course.title: Business Strategy: How Firms Compete
course.description: How firms choose where and how to compete, and how a learner judges those choices: which force holds an industry's profit down, whether an advantage can be copied, whether to make or buy, and why an incumbent missed a shift. Australian cases throughout, from supermarkets and airlines to Wesfarmers, Atlassian and Canva.
course.audience: A capable adult who has met supply, demand, monopoly and game theory, can read a margin in an annual report, and wants to judge a firm's strategic choices with real cases in front of them. No finance or management study is assumed.

paragraphs: How firms choose where and how to compete, and how a learner judges those choices: which force holds an industry's profit down, whether an advantage can be copied, whether to make or buy, and why an incumbent missed a shift. Australian cases throughout, from supermarkets and airlines to Wesfarmers, Atlassian and Canva.
outcomes: You'll be able to tell a strategy from an objective and test whether a claimed trade-off is real.
You'll be able to say which of the five forces holds an industry's profit down and why a firm in it may still do better or worse than its rivals.
You'll be able to judge which obstacles to entry are real barriers and how much bargaining power a buyer or supplier has.
You'll be able to name the position a firm has chosen, test an advantage with VRIO and read where in a firm's chain the profit sits.
You'll be able to say whether a market will tip, how tied in its customers are, and which pricing approach fits.
You'll be able to apply three tests to a diversification, and judge whether a firm should make or buy.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Economics: Markets and Strategy, Accounting: Reading the Numbers of a Business, Decision Theory.

modules.title: Strategy and the industry
modules.description: What strategy is, and how the shape of an industry decides how much profit its firms can keep: the five forces, entry barriers and bargaining power.

modules.title: Advantage inside the firm
modules.description: How a firm earns more than its rivals: cost, differentiation and focus, resources that rivals cannot copy, and the part of the chain where profit sits.

modules.title: Networks, lock-in and price
modules.description: Why some markets tip to one firm, how customers get tied in, and how pricing builds or hides all of it.

modules.title: Where to grow
modules.description: Whether to enter a new business, buy or build it, and whether to make an activity or contract it.

modules.title: Time, change and execution
modules.description: Disruption, first movers and price wars, deciding under uncertainty, and why good plans fail.

concepts.title: Strategy
concepts.summary: A chosen position in an industry, made real by trade-offs about what the firm will not do and by activities that fit together (Porter's three principles).

concepts.title: Trade-off
concepts.summary: A choice that excludes another. It is real when matching it would cost a rival something, and false when it only hides weak execution.

concepts.title: Objective and strategy
concepts.summary: An objective says what the firm wants (a satisfactory return); a strategy says how it will compete to get it.

concepts.title: Sustainable advantage
concepts.summary: An edge rivals cannot copy quickly or cheaply, which is what lets a firm earn more than the average in its industry.

concepts.title: Emergent strategy
concepts.summary: The part of what a firm actually does that no plan set out, formed by decisions made along the way.

concepts.title: The five forces
concepts.summary: Rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power: the pressures that decide how much of an industry's value its firms keep.

concepts.title: Rivalry
concepts.summary: How hard existing firms compete. With few large rivals who watch each other, a price cut is matched and nobody gains share.

concepts.title: Substitute
concepts.summary: A product that meets the same need by a different route, such as video calls for business flights.

concepts.title: Industry profit and firm profit
concepts.summary: The forces describe how much profit an industry can earn; which firm takes it depends on that firm's own position.

concepts.title: Barrier to entry
concepts.summary: A cost an entrant must bear that incumbents do not or did not have to (Stigler, Baumol and Willig).

concepts.title: Sunk entry cost
concepts.summary: Money spent to enter that cannot be recovered if entry fails, which raises the stakes of a wrong bet.

concepts.title: Buyer power
concepts.summary: Rises with the alternatives buyers have and with the share of a supplier's output they take.

concepts.title: Monopsony power
concepts.summary: A buyer large enough to affect the market price, which the ACCC finds most often for perishable fresh produce.

concepts.title: Cost leadership
concepts.summary: Winning on the lowest price in a market by keeping costs lower than rivals, through utilisation, standard no-frills products and tight control of the chain.

concepts.title: Differentiation
concepts.summary: Charging more because customers value something other than price, such as quality or service.

concepts.title: Focus
concepts.summary: Serving one or a few segments, either at lower cost or with a differentiated offer.

concepts.title: Stuck in the middle
concepts.summary: Porter's warning that a firm trying to be everything has no distinct advantage; later research finds some firms combine low cost and differentiation.

concepts.title: VRIO
concepts.summary: Four questions about a resource or capability: is it valuable, rare, costly to imitate, and is the firm organised to capture its value.

concepts.title: Cost of imitation
concepts.summary: Why a rival cannot copy cheaply: unique history, causal ambiguity, social complexity, or patents.

concepts.title: Organised to capture value
concepts.summary: Having a valuable, rare resource is not enough without the structure and systems to exploit it.

concepts.title: Parity and temporary advantage
concepts.summary: A valuable thing that rivals can get as cheaply as you can gives no edge; if it is rare but copyable, the edge is temporary.

concepts.title: Value chain
concepts.summary: The sequence of activities a firm performs to design, produce, market, deliver and support its product.

concepts.title: Product margin and EBIT margin
concepts.summary: Product margin is revenue less the cost of the goods; EBIT margin also deducts operating costs such as wages and rent, so it is lower and closer to profit.

concepts.title: Supplier funding
concepts.summary: Payments suppliers make to retailers for promotions and services; the ACCC finds it contributes significantly to the chains' margins.

concepts.title: Segment margin
concepts.summary: The margin of one part of a firm, which shows where profit sits per dollar of revenue but not how much capital the part uses.

concepts.title: Network effect
concepts.summary: The value of a product depends on how many others use it; direct when users value other users, indirect when one group values the other.

concepts.title: Tipping
concepts.summary: One system pulls away from rivals once ahead; likelier when network benefits beat differentiation, multihoming is costly and switching is costly.

concepts.title: Two-sided platform
concepts.summary: An intermediary with two user groups, each valuing the other's presence; often subsidises one side to get both.

concepts.title: Switching cost and lock-in
concepts.summary: The costs of leaving a supplier, procedural, financial or relational; lock-in is when they are high enough to bind.

concepts.title: Value-based and cost-based pricing
concepts.summary: Value-based pricing sets price by what the customer will pay for the value; cost-based sets it from cost plus a margin.

concepts.title: Penetration and skimming
concepts.summary: Penetration starts low to win share fast and deter entry; skimming starts high to take early adopters' willingness to pay, then lowers.

concepts.title: Freemium
concepts.summary: A free base product with paid extras, which works where the cost of an extra free user is low.

concepts.title: Price discrimination
concepts.summary: Selling the same or similar goods at different prices to different segments.

concepts.title: High-low pricing
concepts.summary: Regular prices with regular periodic specials, which makes the 'real' price harder to judge.

concepts.title: The four growth directions
concepts.summary: Market penetration, market development, product development and diversification, in rising order of risk.

concepts.title: Three tests for diversification
concepts.summary: Is the industry attractive, can the cost of entry be recouped, and will the new unit and the firm each be better off.

concepts.title: Related and unrelated diversification
concepts.summary: Related moves share value-chain links with the existing business; research cited by Morris and Tripathi finds they do better.

concepts.title: Conglomerate discount
concepts.summary: The tendency for a diversified group to be worth less than its parts, because investors can diversify themselves.

concepts.title: Portfolio renewal
concepts.summary: Buying and selling businesses over time, so the group's mix changes.

concepts.title: Vertical integration
concepts.summary: Owning more links of the chain: backward toward suppliers, forward toward customers.

concepts.title: Outsourcing
concepts.summary: Contracting an activity to another firm, usually a non-core one, in exchange for lower cost or specialist capability and less control.

concepts.title: The scale test
concepts.summary: Integration needs enough volume to justify the capital, as Drakes' distribution centre shows.

concepts.title: Credible bypass
concepts.summary: A buyer's real option to supply itself constrains its supplier's pricing even when it is not used on most lines.

concepts.title: Hold-up
concepts.summary: Once one side has invested in a specialised asset, the other can bargain it down.

concepts.title: Sustaining innovation
concepts.summary: Improvement that serves the incumbent's best customers with a better version of what they already buy.

concepts.title: Low-end disruption
concepts.summary: A good-enough product that wins the customers the incumbent finds least profitable and then moves up.

concepts.title: New-market disruption
concepts.summary: A product for customers the incumbent does not serve at all.

concepts.title: The incumbent's dilemma
concepts.summary: A well-managed firm can do everything right for its best customers and still lose, because the early disruptive market is small and unprofitable.

concepts.title: Cannibalising yourself
concepts.summary: Replacing your own profitable product before an entrant does.

concepts.title: First-mover advantage
concepts.summary: The edge gained by the first significant occupant of a segment, from technology leadership, control of resources or buyer switching costs.

concepts.title: Second-mover advantage
concepts.summary: Followers learn from the first mover's costs and mistakes, and sometimes overtake it.

concepts.title: Price war
concepts.summary: Repeated cutting of prices below rivals', which can become unsustainable.

concepts.title: Promotion against cut
concepts.summary: A short-term special is not a long-term price change; mistaking one for the other can start a war.

concepts.title: Scenario planning
concepts.summary: Telling plausible, contrasting stories about the future to test a strategy, not forecasting one.

concepts.title: The official future
concepts.summary: A straight-line projection that ignores qualitative change.

concepts.title: Real option
concepts.summary: The right, not the obligation, to defer, expand, abandon or stage a commitment; most valuable when uncertainty is high and management can act.

concepts.title: Option premium
concepts.summary: The upfront cost of keeping the flexibility.

concepts.title: Implementation
concepts.summary: Aligning people, processes and systems with the strategy.

concepts.title: Strategic drift
concepts.summary: Gradual change that is not noticed until it is too late (Handy).

concepts.title: Alignment of systems
concepts.summary: Targets, measurement, planning and pay that point at the same objective, as Wesfarmers describes.

concepts.title: Emergence
concepts.summary: The weight of what is learned along the way rises as the environment gets harder to forecast.

lessons.title: What strategy is

lead.text: Let's start with what that sentence did to the airline. The ACCC records two changes. Virgin Australia cut its fleet to a single aircraft type, the Boeing 737, and it sold lower fares without complimentary meals. Each of those decisions closed something off: with one type of aircraft it is less able to fly some routes itself, especially regional ones, and without meals it is a weaker choice for the premium corporate travellers whom Qantas serves, so the ACCC concludes that Qantas probably faces less direct competition there.

afterFigure.text: The bottom row of the figure is what turns the sentence into a strategy: a real choice **shows up in what the firm does**. A statement that costs the firm nothing, and that appears in no aircraft, fare or route, is only a hope, whereas this one can be checked against what the airline actually flies and offers. When you read a firm's account of its own strategy, look for that row first.

diagram.alt: A three-row card for Virgin Australia in November 2020. It commits to travellers in the middle of the market who are value-conscious, and to lower airfares. It gives up complimentary meals, routes that need other aircraft types, and a strong hold on premium corporate travellers. What had to change was a fleet cut to one aircraft type, the Boeing 737, and an offer built on low fares without meals.
diagram.caption: Virgin Australia's 2020 choice, set out from the ACCC's report.

lead.text: Michael Porter breaks strategy into three ideas, and each works as a question you can put to a firm's statement. Is there a **position** that is unique and valuable, meaning customers the firm serves in a way its rivals don't? Are there **trade-offs**, which are choices about what the firm will not do? And is there **fit**, so that the firm's activities line up behind its position and don't pull against each other? Virgin's sentence answers the second question in so many words.

Why put so much weight on refusing things? The resources a firm has are limited, so any strategy involves setting priorities, and a firm that tries to serve everyone with everything has set none. Richard Rumelt gives a second test from the other side: a good strategy has a diagnosis of the problem the firm faces, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and coherent actions that carry the policy out. A statement that states a hope and offers no diagnosis of what stands in the way has skipped the part that makes it a strategy.

Wesfarmers, which owns Bunnings, Kmart and Officeworks, has long stated its corporate objective in a single line: to provide a satisfactory return to shareholders. That tells you what the owners want, and it tells you nothing about how the firm will compete to get it. It doesn't say which customers to serve, which businesses to be in or what to refuse, and the annual report goes on to set out the group's value-creating strategies separately, which shows that the firm treats the two as different things.

So an **objective** names a result the firm wants, and a **strategy** names how it will compete to get that result. The two are easy to confuse, because a line such as "become the market leader" sounds bold and strategic, yet it is still a result and any firm could write it. A **tactic** sits at the other end. It is a small move, such as a weekend promotion, which a rival can copy by Monday and which leaves the firm's position where it was.

Why does a strategy have to exclude anything? Because the exclusions are what make it hard to copy. Porter, as Morris and Tripathi summarise him, finds three sources of **real trade-offs**. A product can meet one need well and others badly. Activities can conflict, so that doing one job well gets in the way of another. And a firm's image can be damaged by an offer that doesn't suit it. When the trade-off is real, a rival that matches your offer has to give something up, and that cost is what protects you.

The ACCC's account of the Qantas Group shows the idea at work, though it doesn't say why the group does it. Qantas runs a full-service airline and Jetstar a budget leisure airline, and between them they carry about 60% of domestic passengers. A natural reading is that two brands let each one make its own choices, so that neither has to do the other's job. That is our reading of the evidence, and the ACCC doesn't state it.

afterFigure.text: The opposite mistake is to believe in a trade-off that isn't there. In the figure the dashed line is a claimed trade-off between quality and price. If a rival can sit above it, with more quality at the same price, the line never described the market and only described how well the first firms ran their operations. Morris and Tripathi make the point with Lexus and Cadillac in the 1990s: Lexus offered high quality at a low cost because its manufacturing was far more advanced. A trade-off is **real only when the firms match each other in how well they do things**, and until then a claimed trade-off may be hiding weak operations.

diagram.alt: A chart with quality going up and price falling to the right. A dashed line runs from a first firm, with high quality and high price, to a second firm, with lower quality and low price. In the second view a rival sits above the line, with high quality and a low price, so the line was a false trade-off.
diagram.caption: A claimed trade-off, and a rival that beats it. Use the buttons to compare the two views.

lead.text: A competitive advantage is anything a firm has or does better than its rivals, in a way that customers value. Whether it matters depends on how long it lasts, and that depends on what a rival would have to spend to copy it. Morris and Tripathi use a coffee shop. If the shop's edge is a two-for-one special, a rival matches it at once and the edge is gone. If the edge is an inviting room and friendly baristas who were chosen with care, a rival has to hire and train people and build the atmosphere, which costs money and takes time. An advantage that rivals can't copy quickly or cheaply is a **sustainable competitive advantage**.

Why would a firm go to that trouble? Because it is how the firm earns **above-average returns**, meaning profit above what the typical firm in its industry makes. Investors reward a firm that does with a higher share price and a greater willingness to lend, and such a firm can survive a downturn longer because its finances are less exposed.

A firm doesn't carry out a plan in a world that holds still. Morris and Tripathi describe what a firm actually ends up doing, its realised strategy, as the result of three things: the parts of the plan that were carried out, the parts that were dropped because events made them useless, and the decisions that nobody planned and that managers made along the way. Henry Mintzberg's name for those unplanned decisions is **emergent strategy**.

How much weight emergence carries depends on the world the firm is in. A firm in a stable setting can plan in some detail, whereas a firm whose world can't be forecast can set only a few principles and must let the rest emerge as events unfold. The useful question about an emergent decision is whether it was guided, meaning that managers at every level knew the position the firm had chosen, so that what emerged fitted it.

lessons.orientation: Tell a strategy, which is a chosen position with trade-offs and activities that fit, from an objective or a tactic, and judge whether a claimed trade-off is real and whether an advantage will last.
lessons.nextAction: You can now tell a strategy from an objective and a tactic, test whether a trade-off is real, and judge whether an advantage will last.

blocks.text: In November 2020 Virgin Australia came out of administration with a new owner and a new chief executive, and the ACCC's report on airline competition records what the chief executive said about the plan. Australia already had a low-cost airline and a traditional full-service one, the chief executive said, and Virgin "won't be either". It would aim instead at travellers in the middle of the market who were "value-conscious".
A sentence like that is easy to read as a slogan. What would make that sentence a strategy, and what would the choice have to be like for rivals to find it costly to copy?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell a strategy from an objective, test whether a trade-off is real and judge whether an advantage will last.
intro.whyItMatters: A firm's own account of its strategy is a claim, and these three tests are how you check it.

recap.keyIdea: A strategy is a chosen position held up by real trade-offs and fitting activities, and it earns more than the industry average only while rivals can't copy it quickly or cheaply.

blocks.text: A strategy is a chosen position, made real by what the firm refuses to do and by activities that fit together, as Virgin Australia's refusal showed up in its fleet, its fares and its routes. An objective names a result and a tactic is a move that rivals can copy at once, so neither is a strategy, and a trade-off or an advantage counts only if copying it would cost a rival time and money. What the firm ends up doing is its plan plus whatever emerged along the way.

recap.nextHook: Next we step back from one firm's choices to the industry around it, and ask which forces hold an industry's profit down.

lessons.title: The five forces

lead.text: Porter's five forces framework is a tool for studying the competition that a business faces. Its question is how attractive an industry is, meaning how much profit the firms in it can keep, and it answers by looking at five pressures on that profit. Three of them are **horizontal**, and they come from firms that could take your customers: the rivals already in the industry, new firms that might enter, and substitute products that meet the same need by a different route. The other two are **vertical**, because they come from the firms on either side of the industry in the chain: the suppliers it buys from and the buyers it sells to.

afterFigure.text: The framework describes the industry, so it tells you how hard firms in it will find it to hold on to profit, and it says nothing yet about whether any one firm will do better or worse than the rest. We come back to that difference near the end of the lesson.

diagram.alt: A diagram of the five forces. Rivalry sits in the centre. New entrants press from the left and substitutes from the right, and these are the horizontal forces. Supplier power presses from above and buyer power from below, and these are the vertical forces.
diagram.caption: The five forces. Use the buttons to see which are horizontal and which are vertical.

lead.text: The hook's reasoning has a general form. Rivalry is the force that decides how hard the firms already in an industry compete, and it depends on more than how many firms there are, because how each expects the others to react matters too. Where a price move is easily matched, a cut leaves the firm with a lower margin and no extra share, so prices settle where they are. That is the logic behind the ACCC's finding that Coles and Woolworths have limited reason to undercut each other on price.

The structure fits. Supermarkets capture roughly 85% of consumer spending on groceries, and the two chains between them hold about two-thirds of supermarket sales, with no rival of comparable scope and scale. ALDI is the one real check on them. The ACCC calls it a hard discounter and an important source of price constraint, but only to the extent that its range overlaps theirs, since a low-cost operator doesn't compete head to head on everything they offer.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows two firms of similar size and then a long drop. ALDI's 9% is the largest of the other shares the ACCC lists, which is why its constraint matters, and why it applies only to the products that its stores and the chains' stores both sell.

lead.text: A **substitute** meets the same need as an industry's product by a different route, which is what separates it from a rival. Wikipedia's account of the five forces gives landlines and mobile phones as an example, and lists airlines, cars, trains and ships as substitutes for one another. A new airline on the same route uses the same technology to meet the same need, so it is a rival or a new entrant. The two are worth keeping apart because they weaken profit in different ways: a rival fights you for the customers you have, whereas a substitute gives those customers a reason to leave the industry's product altogether.

The vertical forces turn on alternatives too. **Buyer power** is higher when buyers have many alternatives and lower when they have few, and supplier power is its mirror image, since a supplier gains power when the firms it sells to have few alternatives to it. So when you meet a claim about power, ask who the other side could turn to.

If the forces describe an industry, what do they leave out? They tell you how much profit the industry can hold on to, which you can picture as the size of a pool, and they don't tell you how much of it each firm takes. Two firms facing exactly the same five forces can earn very different profits, because one has a cost advantage or a loyal set of customers that the other lacks.

Morris and Tripathi report research that puts numbers on this: about 20% of the variation in firms' profitability traces to the industry they are in, and about 36% to the firm's own characteristics and actions. Both matter, which makes the choice of industry and the choice of position two separate decisions, and a good industry does not by itself rescue a firm with a weak position.

lessons.orientation: Use the five forces to say which force holds an industry's profit down, and keep that separate from why one firm in the industry earns more than another.
lessons.nextAction: You can now name the force that holds an industry's profit down, tell a substitute from a rival, and keep the industry's profit apart from one firm's.

blocks.text: The ACCC estimates that Woolworths holds 38% of supermarket grocery sales in Australia, Coles 29%, ALDI 9% and Metcash, standing in for the independent stores it supplies, 7%. With two chains holding about two-thirds of supermarket sales between them, you might expect a fierce fight over price.

The ACCC finds the opposite: the two chains have limited reason to undercut each other on price. What does an industry's structure do to the profit its firms can keep, and is that the same question as which firm in the industry does best?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the force that holds an industry's profit down, tell a substitute from a rival and keep an industry's profit apart from one firm's.
intro.whyItMatters: A concentrated industry can look safe for every firm in it, and these distinctions show why it isn't.

recap.keyIdea: The five forces describe how much profit an industry can hold on to, and which firm in it actually takes that profit depends on the firm's own position and choices.

blocks.text: You saw why two big rivals can leave prices alone, since a cut is matched and wins no share, and you read the early-2010s airline price war as what happens when rivalry does turn on. You separated a substitute, which meets the need by a different route, from a rival, which meets it in the same way, and saw that buyer power follows the alternatives a buyer has. The last point is the one to keep: the forces describe the pool of profit, and who takes it is a question about the firm.

recap.nextHook: Next we look closely at two of the forces: what keeps new firms out, and what gives a buyer or a supplier its power.

lessons.title: Barriers to entry and bargaining power

lead.text: What makes something a barrier? George Stigler's definition is that an entry barrier is a cost which a firm entering an industry must bear and which the firms already in it escape. Baumol and Willig put it as anything that needs an expenditure by a new entrant and puts no equivalent cost on an incumbent. Both definitions rest on a comparison, and the comparison is the test: ask *who pays*. A cost that every firm in the industry pays, new or old, can be large without being a **barrier to entry**.

afterFigure.text: Wikipedia's article on entry barriers adds two refinements. A **primary barrier** is a cost that is a barrier on its own, and an **ancillary barrier** is one that isn't a barrier by itself but reinforces the others when they are present. It also notes that firms can create barriers themselves, because the costs that customers face in switching away from a firm count too, and airline frequent flyer programs are its example.

diagram.alt: Two stacks of costs, one for an established firm and one for a new entrant. In the first view both stacks hold the same block, equipment at the market price, so the cost is large but not a barrier. In the second view the entrant's stack also holds a licence that only newcomers must buy, which makes it a barrier.
diagram.caption: An illustration of the test. Use the buttons to compare a cost both pay with a cost only the entrant pays.

lead.text: The ACCC lists four things that a supermarket chain needs for effective large-scale entry or expansion: a supplier network, economies of scale in wholesale buying, capital and access to suitable retail sites. It adds that small local entry is more achievable and does help the shoppers nearby, but is less likely to give the big chains serious price competition. Which of the four are barriers by the test of who pays?

Take sites first. The ACCC finds that the two chains are better placed to secure suitable sites, thanks to their size, reputation and financial resources, so their rivals have a harder time getting the same sites. The two chains also hold more than 150 undeveloped sites intended for future supermarkets, which is the basis of allegations that they engage in land banking. The ACCC did not decide whether those purchases are anticompetitive, since that needs a case-by-case assessment outside the scope of the inquiry. The advantage in sites is a cost that incumbents bear less than an entrant does, and so it passes the test.

Capital is different. The ACCC doesn't treat access to capital as a barrier for large, well-established international supermarket retailers, who are the likeliest entrants, though every entrant needs capital and the smaller ones feel the lack of it most. Economies of scale in wholesale buying are a requirement for a similar reason, since a newcomer starts without the volume that lets an incumbent buy cheaply. That leaves the supplier network, which firms in the inquiry described in opposite ways, and a later screen weighs their accounts.

Capital raises a further question: how much of it comes back if the entry fails? Money spent on assets that can be sold on, such as a delivery truck or an oven, returns in part. Money spent on things that are worth nothing to anyone else, such as a custom fit-out or advertising to introduce a new brand, is gone. We call that second kind a **sunk cost**, and it matters for entry because it raises the price of a wrong bet. An entrant that can sell most of its assets for what it paid risks little by trying, whereas one with large sunk costs has to be much surer of its plan before it starts.

Barriers are often argued over, and the people arguing have a stake. An entrant tends to stress how hard the way in was, which explains its slow start, and an incumbent tends to stress how easy it was, which supports the claim that its position is open to challenge. Either may be right, and each account is still evidence of what the speaker wants believed as well as of what happened, so you look for what an independent party, such as a regulator, found when it weighed both.

A second trap is to read one entrant's success as proof that the barrier is small. The entrants you can see are the ones that got in, and the ones that stayed out, or got in and lost money, don't announce themselves. So ask what the success cost, how long it took, and whether the firms that didn't arrive had the same chance.

Bargaining power follows two things: the alternatives each side has, and how much of the other side's business it takes. Wikipedia's account of the five forces says buyer power is higher when buyers have many alternatives and lower when they have few. The ACCC adds share and perishability when it explains why Coles and Woolworths have **monopsony power**, meaning a buyer so large next to a supplier that the supplier has little choice but to accept its terms, over many fresh produce suppliers. When a chain buys a large share of a product and the product spoils quickly, the supplier can't wait for a better offer and has little else to turn to.

afterFigure.text: Information matters too. In the weekly tender that the chains use for fresh produce, a supplier sees only its own bid while the buyer sees them all, and the ACCC says this imbalance contributes to the chains' power. The process alone doesn't settle the outcome, though: the inquiry heard that ALDI deals with its fresh produce suppliers in a far more constructive way, although it uses a similar weekly tender. And power over suppliers isn't always bad news for shoppers, since a strong bargaining position can win lower wholesale prices, which lower retail prices to the extent that they are passed on.

lessons.orientation: Judge which obstacles are real barriers to entry, weigh conflicting claims about them, and say how much power a buyer or supplier has from its alternatives and its share of the other side's business.
lessons.reviewLabel: Barriers to entry and bargaining power
lessons.nextAction: You can now say which costs are barriers to entry, weigh conflicting accounts of them, and judge how much bargaining power a buyer or supplier holds.

blocks.text: The ACCC's inquiry into supermarkets says that large-scale entry into Australian supermarkets is unlikely in the short to medium term, and it points to what happened to ALDI: more than 20 years to reach the position it holds today. A would-be rival can read that as a warning or as encouragement, since ALDI did get there.

Before deciding which, it helps to be exact about what a barrier to entry is, because many large costs turn out not to be barriers at all, and the firms that describe barriers usually have a stake in how they look.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which obstacles are real barriers to entry, weigh conflicting accounts of them and judge how much power a buyer or supplier holds.
intro.whyItMatters: A large cost isn't automatically a barrier, and the people describing a barrier usually have a stake in how it looks.

recap.keyIdea: A barrier is a cost that only the entrant bears, accounts of barriers come from firms with a stake, and bargaining power follows the alternatives each side has.

blocks.text: A barrier is a cost that an entrant bears and incumbents don't, so a large cost that everyone pays is not one, and a sunk cost raises the price of a wrong bet. When firms with a stake describe a barrier in opposite ways you weigh their stakes and look for an independent view, and one entrant's success doesn't show that entry is easy. Bargaining power follows alternatives, share and perishability, which is why the same wholesaler can be strong over some lines and weak over others.

recap.nextHook: Next we move from the industry to the firm's own position, and ask how a firm chooses to compete on cost, on difference or on focus.

lessons.title: Cost, differentiation and focus

lead.text: Porter described how a firm can win in terms of two choices. The first is the basis of its advantage: it can offer the lowest price, or it can offer something customers value above price, such as quality or service, and charge more for it. The second is scope, which is how many segments of the market it serves. Put the two together and you get three generic strategies. A firm that targets most or all segments on the basis of the lowest price follows **cost leadership**. One that targets most or all segments on the basis of something other than price follows **differentiation**, and it tries to keep costs down wherever it isn't differentiating, so as to stay cost competitive. One that concentrates on a few segments follows **focus**, and it can do so by being cheaper in that scope or by being different in it.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the rows are scope and the columns are the basis of advantage, so focus fills the bottom row twice. A bank that served only veterinary practices, with credit and advice built around how those practices earn, would be a differentiation focus. That bank is an invented illustration, and the next screens use real firms.

diagram.alt: A two by two grid. The columns are lower cost and something other than price, and the rows are most or all segments and one or a few segments. The top row holds cost leadership and differentiation, and the bottom row holds cost focus and differentiation focus.
diagram.caption: Porter's generic strategies, set out by scope and by the basis of advantage.

lead.text: A low price is the visible part of a cost position. Behind it sits a set of activities that produce low cost, and Wikipedia's account of cost leadership groups them in three. The first is high asset utilisation, which means keeping the firm's assets busy, as a restaurant does by turning its tables over quickly or an airline does by turning its flights around fast. The second is low operating cost, which comes from standardised, no-frills products and from limiting customisation. The third is tight control of the whole chain, from buying to inventory, so that cost stays low at every step.

A cost position has risks of its own. Price-sensitive customers will switch once a cheaper alternative appears, so loyalty tends to be low. And a reputation as the cheap firm can turn into a reputation for low quality, which makes it hard to rebrand later if the firm decides to move towards differentiation.

ALDI is the clearest Australian case of a cost position, and the ACCC describes it through its activities as well as its price. A hard discounter, the ACCC's term for a low-cost operator selling at materially lower prices, stocks about 1,800 to 2,000 products in stores of about 1,000 square metres, against the 15,000 to 25,000 products and 1,500 to 4,000 square metres of a standard Coles or Woolworths supermarket. Its stores are only in larger population centres, most of what it sells is its own brand, and it doesn't offer online shopping and delivery, which the ACCC links to its low-cost business model. Each of those choices removes cost, and each gives something up, since a narrow range and no delivery won't suit every shopper.

afterFigure.text: ALDI also does without a loyalty program. It told the ACCC that having none is no disadvantage, because its offer of the best value in the market appeals to customers anyway, and that a program would add cost and complexity. The ACCC notes that ALDI's share of national grocery sales was 2.8% in 2006-07 and had reached 8.1% by 2022-23, and finds that loyalty programs don't at present appear to be a substantial barrier to entry or expansion. Read the case with care: the rise in share and the lack of a program happened *together*, and the ACCC doesn't test whether a program would have helped or hurt.

lead.text: Virgin Blue began as a low-cost airline. Wikipedia describes its formula: it cut costs such as included meals and printed tickets, selling food on board and taking bookings by phone and internet, and it limited the airports it served and flew one type of aircraft, the Boeing 737. In February 2011 it announced that the word 'Blue' would go from its name, part of a push to win more business travellers from Qantas. Predict what followed.

reveal.text: The ACCC describes the transition into a full-service carrier as taking Virgin Australia after Qantas's most profitable customers, the corporate travellers, so it met the incumbent head-on. The two airlines competed hard for share by adding capacity and cutting fares, and the price war proved unsustainable once both had lost heavily.

lead.text: Porter warned that a firm trying to be both the cheapest and the best would lose the focus of its organisation, because differentiation adds costs that cut against a low-cost position. Such a firm is **stuck in the middle**, with no distinct advantage. The warning has had a rough ride since. Wikipedia's article records later empirical research indicating that companies pursuing both differentiation and low cost may be more successful than those pursuing only one, and Morris and Tripathi point to Costco, which pairs low prices built on scale with a differentiated own brand.

Porter's warning is about a firm whose activities pull against each other, such as a hotel with a marble lobby and a budget rate, and a firm that has found activities serving both aims, or that keeps its two offers apart, is not in that position. Whatever label a firm uses, the test is *fit*: do its activities support its position, or work against it?

lessons.orientation: Name the position a firm has chosen from what it does, check whether its activities fit it, and say what the position costs.
lessons.nextAction: You can now name a firm's position from its activities, check whether the activities fit it, and say what the position costs.

blocks.text: In its 2026 annual report Wesfarmers says that in tough times the group leans in to help customers by keeping prices as low as possible, and that this is only possible when it runs its businesses as efficiently as possible and keeps its costs low.
A price is easy to change and a cost is not. What does a firm have to do behind the scenes to hold a low-cost position, and what does it give up when it tries to be everything at once?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the position a firm has chosen from what it does, check whether its activities fit that position and say what the position costs.
intro.whyItMatters: A firm's position is visible in its activities, so you can check a claim about strategy against what the firm does.

recap.keyIdea: A position is chosen by what a firm does, so its activities must fit it, and every position, including the middle of the market, has a cost that the evidence should be asked to show.

blocks.text: You saw that cost leadership, differentiation and focus are positions defined by the basis of advantage and by scope, and that a low-cost position rests on activities such as standard products and busy assets, which ALDI's range and store size show. You also saw that moving into a rival's strongest segment, as Virgin Blue did, meets the incumbent head-on, and that the stuck-in-the-middle warning is best read as a test of fit. When the evidence shows only that a position and a result coexist, it hasn't yet shown that one caused the other.

recap.nextHook: Next we look inside the firm, and ask which of its resources and capabilities rivals can't copy.

lessons.title: Resources and capabilities

lead.text: A resource or capability is anything a firm has or can do that it uses to compete: a route network, a brand, a way of selling, a team that works well together. The VRIO framework asks four questions of any one of them. Is it **valuable**, meaning that it helps the firm exploit an opportunity or blunt a threat, which in practice means raising revenue or cutting cost? Is it **rare**, meaning that the firm controls something limited, so that current and potential competitors lack it? Is it **costly to imitate**, meaning that a firm without it would face a cost disadvantage in getting or building it? And is the firm **organised** to capture the value, with the structures and systems to use it?

afterFigure.text: A resource that isn't valuable can't help however rare it is, and one that anyone can copy as cheaply as you built it gives you at most a short lead, which is why the questions come in this order.

lead.text: The third question decides whether an advantage lasts, and it is asked as a matter of cost: would a firm without the resource pay more than its owners did to get it or build it? Wikipedia gives four reasons the cost can be high. **Unique historical conditions** mean that a firm gained low-cost access to a rare resource at a particular time and place, as a vineyard did that planted its best slopes when the land was cheap (an invented example). **Causal ambiguity** means that an imitator can't tell which factors produced the advantage, so it can't copy the right ones. **Social complexity** means that the advantage rests on relationships, culture or teamwork, which can't simply be hired in. And **patents** protect an advantage by law, which matters in a few industries such as pharmaceuticals.

afterFigure.text: All four make copying cost more than the original did, which is what the third question asks, since a rival who can copy at the same price gets the same resource and no edge.

lead.text: What does a firm have when a resource fails one of the questions? If the resource is valuable but rivals can get it as cheaply as you can, it gives you **parity**: you are as well equipped as they are and no better. If it is valuable and rare but copying it is cheap, it gives you a **temporary advantage**, since Wikipedia's account says that when imitation costs little the advantage doesn't last. Rarity counts only if it persists: a resource has to be in short supply and stay that way to support a lasting edge. A **sustained advantage** needs the resource to pass the first three questions and the firm to pass the fourth.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, follow each case from the top. A no ends the walk at the label beside that question, and only four yeses reach a sustained advantage. A no at the last question leaves a valuable, rare and hard-to-copy resource without its payoff, which is why organisation gets a question of its own.

diagram.alt: A path of four questions, each with a yes arrow to the next and a no arrow to an outcome. Not valuable gives no advantage, not rare gives parity, cheap to copy gives a temporary advantage, and not organised gives an advantage not captured. Four yeses give a sustained advantage.

lead.text: The fourth question asks whether the firm is organised to use what it has. Wikipedia's account lists the parts of organisation: formal reporting structures, management control systems that keep decisions in line with the firm's strategy, and pay policies that reward the behaviour the firm wants. These are complementary resources, which add little value alone and a good deal in combination with the firm's other resources. A firm can hold something valuable, rare and hard to copy and still gain little from it if its reporting lines, controls and pay all point somewhere else. It is also the question that an outsider can least often answer from public documents.

VRIO questions are answered from evidence, and evidence comes in grades. A firm's description of its own model tells you what the firm does and what it values, and it tells you little about whether a rival could copy it. A margin tells you how much profit a firm keeps from each dollar of revenue. A high one is consistent with an advantage, and it is also what a lucky year or a temporary lead would look like. To say that a resource is hard to copy you need evidence about copying, such as rivals that tried and found it costly, or sources of the advantage in history, ambiguity, social complexity or law. When the sources don't hold that evidence, the honest answer is *not shown*, and that is a different answer from *no*.

lessons.orientation: Test a claimed advantage with the four VRIO questions and say whether it is temporary parity or sustainable, and what the evidence can and cannot show.
lessons.nextAction: You can now test a claimed advantage with VRIO, name what makes copying costly, and say what a piece of evidence does and doesn't show.

blocks.text: Atlassian, the software company, tells investors in its annual report on Form 10-K how it finds customers. It lands new customers mainly through its website, where they can buy for themselves, and it uses a commissioned direct sales force only once a customer reaches a certain size. Wikipedia reports the company's principle as software that should be bought, not sold.

It would be easy to call that an advantage, and it may well be valuable. What would you need to know before calling it one that lasts, and what can a firm's description of its own strengths actually show?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to test a claimed advantage with the four VRIO questions, say what makes copying costly and state what a piece of evidence does and doesn't show.
intro.whyItMatters: Firms describe their own strengths in glowing terms, and VRIO gives you a way to test the claim.

recap.keyIdea: A valuable resource gives a sustained advantage only if it is rare, costly for rivals to imitate and used by an organised firm, and a firm's own account of its strengths doesn't show whether it passes.

blocks.text: You tested claimed advantages with four questions and saw that the third, whether copying costs a rival more than it cost you, decides how long an advantage lasts, and that the cost comes from history, ambiguity, social complexity or law. You also saw that a rare, valuable resource can go unused when the firm isn't organised to capture it, and that a firm's description of its model, or a high margin, shows less than it seems to about whether rivals could copy it.

recap.nextHook: Next we read where along a firm's chain of activities the profit sits, and what a margin does and doesn't measure.

lessons.title: Value chains and where profit sits

lead.text: Every product reaches you through a sequence of activities, and that sequence has a name. A **value chain** sets out the activities by which an organisation designs, makes, markets, delivers and supports its goods or services, an idea Michael Porter introduced in his 1985 book *Competitive Advantage*. Porter drew it for a single firm. The same way of looking works along the whole path from grower to shopper, where each link is a different firm doing its own part.

Seen that way, a vague question (where does the money go?) turns into a sharper one: which link keeps a margin, and why that link? The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, the ACCC, asked it about groceries in its 2025 report on supermarkets, and the report gives margins for several links. Suppliers make or grow the products. Coles and Woolworths buy from them and sell to shoppers. Metcash is a wholesaler that supplies independent stores, such as those trading as IGA, and the ACCC describes its business as mainly wholesale supply.

afterFigure.text: A margin tells us how much of each dollar of sales a link keeps, and it says nothing about how much work or risk the link takes on for that dollar. The same number can mean different things at different links, so we keep asking what a margin counts and where it sits.

lead.text: To compare links we need to be clear about what a margin counts, and the ACCC uses two. **Product margin** is what is left of a product's sales revenue after its [[cost of goods sold|The costs directly tied to making or buying a product. Covered in the Accounting course, 'Reading an income statement'.]] is taken away, and for a supermarket that cost is what it paid to acquire the product. On the tin of tomatoes from the opening, the product margin is the 50 cents, before the shop has paid for anything else.

Those other costs are the missing piece. Wages, rent, utilities and marketing are costs of running the business and not of any one product, so the ACCC leaves them out of product margin and counts them in whole-of-business measures such as **EBIT**, earnings before interest and tax. An **EBIT margin** is EBIT divided by revenue, so it has the running costs taken out, and the ACCC says product margins will generally be higher than the profit a supermarket ends up earning.

Coles gives us a figure for the second measure. The report shows Coles' EBIT margin for 2023-24 as 5.20%, and records Coles' point that the year had 53 weeks, so on a 52-week basis the figure would be 5.04%. Both numbers describe the same business in the same year, and the gap between them is only the extra week. A fair reading is that Coles kept about five cents of operating profit, before interest and tax, from each dollar of sales.

reveal.text: The ACCC says the margins *suggest* a conclusion and that product margins *appear* to have contributed. Margins show an outcome, and the reasons behind it need other evidence, so a careful reading keeps the caution.

steps.headline: Where the extra margin comes from

lead.text: Why did product margins at the two big chains rise? The ACCC's analysis of five financial years points to one part of the shop. Average product margins on branded packaged grocery goods rose at both Coles and Woolworths, and those goods sit in some of their highest-revenue departments. In private label goods, in fresh produce and in the meat, seafood and bakery departments, average margins were in general about what they had been five years earlier. The rise was where the chain buys from a brand owner, and where it sells its own label or fresh food the margin barely moved.

The report finds a second source as well. The payments a supplier makes to a supermarket are called **trade spend**, and its main form is **supplier funding** for promotions, which the ACCC says contributes to the product margin. Its analysis is that supplier funding is increasing and contributes significantly to Coles' and Woolworths' margins. So part of what looks like the chain's own margin was paid in by its suppliers, and a payment that is agreed in a negotiation depends on how the negotiation goes.

afterFigure.text: That changes how we read a margin as a sign of where profit sits. A chain's margin comes partly from shoppers and partly from suppliers, and the supplier part is a question about [[bargaining power|The strength a buyer or supplier has in settling a price. Met in 'Barriers to entry and bargaining power'.]]: who needs the other more, and who can ask the other to pay.

The second shows suppliers paying supplier funding for promotions to the chain, and shoppers paying the shelf price.

reveal.text: The ACCC reads the pattern as a sign of position in the chain. A retailer that can widen its own margin while passing on a cost is more than a pipe for the supplier's price.

lead.text: Not every link earns a margin like the chains'. The ACCC reports that Metcash's EBIT margins are much lower than those of Coles and Woolworths, and it explains the gap in one sentence: the difference is likely to reflect the different nature of Metcash's business, which is mainly wholesale supply. A wholesaler does a different job from a supermarket, and the ACCC treats the job as the likely reason for the lower margin.

What follows for reading margins is that **each link has its own normal range**. Setting Metcash beside Coles tells us little about which is better run, while setting it beside other wholesalers would tell us something. A low margin can also pay well when a business turns over a lot of sales for the capital it uses, as the [[asset turnover|Revenue divided by total assets. Covered in the Accounting course, 'Margins and turnover'.]] idea in Accounting showed, though the ACCC's figures here don't say whether that is true of Metcash.

reveal.text: A margin is shaped by the job a link does as well as by how well it does it. Before calling a low margin weak, find out what is normal for that link.

lead.text: A single firm is a chain too, since it is made of activities that each earn at their own rate. Qantas reports a margin for each of its main parts, which gives us a **segment margin**, the margin of one part of a firm. For the 2026 financial year the Group's Domestic flying had a margin of 13%, and Group International flying, which includes freight, had 4%. Loyalty, the frequent flyer program and its partner businesses, had an operating margin of 21.7% on revenue of $2.9 billion and underlying EBIT of $625 million.

Ranked by margin, Loyalty comes first, Domestic second and International last. Qantas gives the flying figures as underlying EBIT margins and Loyalty's as an operating margin, and the figures we have don't show whether the two are built in the same way, so the ranking is a first look and not an exact measurement.

afterFigure.text: A segment margin says what a part keeps from each dollar of its own revenue. It leaves out how many dollars of revenue each part has, how much capital it uses and how far it depends on the other parts. On that last point, Qantas says about 70% of its points are redeemed on Flight Rewards within the Group, so much of what Loyalty does is spent on the airline's own seats. A part can have the highest margin and still be the smallest earner, or earn its margin only because of the others.

From the supplier's side the chain looks different. The margin at the list price is a ceiling, and payments to a retailer come out of it, so a margin always belongs to a place in the chain.

lessons.orientation: Read a firm's margins by activity to say where along its chain the profit sits, what a margin does and does not measure, and what that suggests for strategy.
lessons.reviewLabel: Value chains and where profit sits
lessons.nextAction: Say whether a market is likely to tip toward one firm, which kind of network effect is at work, and how far customers are really tied in.

blocks.text: News stories about supermarkets often quote a margin as though it were the profit, and the two are different things. A margin is a difference or a percentage, and what it means depends on which costs were taken out before it was worked out.

There is a second question behind the first. A tin of tomatoes passes through several firms on its way to you, and each keeps some part of what you pay, so when a profit does exist we also have to ask which link of the chain keeps it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a margin at each link of a chain, say what it counts and leaves out, and say where the profit seems to sit.
intro.whyItMatters: Coles keeps about five cents of operating profit per dollar of sales, and Qantas's loyalty business keeps more per dollar than its flying. Where profit sits depends on what each margin counts.

recap.keyIdea: A margin belongs to one link of the chain and to one definition, so before saying where profit sits we need to know which costs it has taken out and what it leaves out.

blocks.text: You saw that a value chain maps the activities between a product's makers and its buyers, and that grocery margins differ along it. Product margins leave out the costs of running a business, so they run above EBIT margins. The ACCC finds that suppliers pay part of the chains' margins and that a wholesaler such as Metcash earns less per dollar because of the job it does.

You also read Qantas by segment, with Loyalty ahead of Domestic and International on margin. A segment margin says what each part keeps per dollar of its own revenue, and it says nothing about the dollars involved, the capital used or how far one part depends on another.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to markets where a product gets more valuable as more people use it, and asks when one firm ends up with most of the market.

lessons.title: Network effects, platforms and lock-in

lead.text: A messaging app shows what economists call a **network effect**: the value a user gets from a product depends on how many other people use compatible products. It comes in two forms. A *direct* network effect arises when each user gains from every other user of the same product, as with a telephone or a messaging app, because each person who joins is one more person you can reach.

An *indirect* network effect arises when two groups need each other and one group's gain grows with the size of the other. Hardware becomes more valuable to buyers as compatible software appears, and software makers in turn want the hardware with the most buyers.

It is easy to mistake a network effect for **economies of scale**, which describe a producer's average cost falling as its output grows. The two sit on opposite sides of the market. Scale lowers what a unit costs the firm, while a network effect raises what each customer will pay, which is why a network effect is sometimes called a demand-side economy of scale.

afterFigure.text: Only the third case in the figure changes the firm's costs. The first two change what customers are worth to each other.

diagram.alt: Three diagrams. A direct network effect: five users, each connected to every other. An indirect network effect: a group of hardware buyers and a group of software makers, each connected to the other. A scale economy: a tall bar for the average cost per unit at low output and a shorter bar at high output.

cases.label: Scale economy
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 266"><text x="320" y="28" class="t-small t-bold" text-anchor="middle">Scale economy: the firm's cost per unit falls as output grows</text><line x1="180" y1="50" x2="180" y2="200" class="s-line w1"/><line x1="180" y1="200" x2="560" y2="200" class="s-line w1"/><text x="168" y="54" class="t-small t-muted" text-anchor="end">Average cost per unit</text><rect x="220" y="80" width="100" height="120" class="f-sunken s-line w2" rx="3"/><text x="270" y="224" class="t-small" text-anchor="middle">Few units</text><rect x="400" y="140" width="100" height="60" class="f-accent-soft s-accent w2" rx="3"/><text x="450" y="224" class="t-small" text-anchor="middle">Many units</text><text x="320" y="250" class="t-small t-muted" text-anchor="middle">The firm's cost changes. What any customer will pay does not.</text></svg>

reveal.text: A network effect is about what users gain from other users. Cost per unit is a separate matter that belongs to the producer.

lead.text: When [[network effects|The value of a product to each user rises with the number of others using compatible products. Met earlier in this lesson.]] are strong, a market can **tip**: once one system has gained a first edge, it moves ahead of its rivals in popularity, and a single firm, or a very few, ends up serving most users. The first obstacle is **critical mass**. Early on there is little reason to adopt a new network, because few others are on it. Once enough people have adopted it, joining becomes the sensible choice for each new person, and growth feeds itself.

A network effect doesn't guarantee a tip, though, because three conditions have to hold together. The value users get from the network has to outweigh what they value in the differences between rival products. Users have to face high costs of using more than one network at once, which is called **multihoming**. And users have to face high **switching costs**, the costs of changing from one network to another. If any one fails, several products can keep significant shares. The United States instant messaging market stayed an oligopoly despite strong network effects, and the explanation given is that its users faced low multihoming and switching costs.

afterFigure.text: If a market does tip, the shape of competition changes. The ACCC, writing about digital platforms, says the most effective competition may then be competition for the market and not in it, and that the main threat to the leader is likely to be disruptive entry, on a scale that could displace it.

diagram.alt: A market tips only when three conditions hold: network benefits outweigh differences between products, multihoming costs are high, and switching costs are high. The first view shows all three holding and the market tipping. The second shows the case of United States instant messaging, where multihoming and switching costs were low and several firms kept large shares.
diagram.caption: Use the buttons to compare a market where all three hold with one where two conditions failed.

lead.text: [[Indirect network effects|Effects in which two groups each gain from the other's size. Met earlier in this lesson, in 'Network effects'.]] are the engine of the **two-sided platform**, an intermediary with two distinct groups of users who each give the other network benefits. Both sides are customers, and the platform's job is to bring them together. Atlassian's Marketplace is an example. It is an online marketplace, hosted by Atlassian, where free and paid apps extend its products, and its thousands of apps come from a widening circle of outside vendors and developers. Forge is the cloud platform developers use to customise and extend its products. The pattern fits the definition: customers gain from more apps, and developers gain from more customers to sell to.

The structure creates a start-up problem, because neither side wants to join first. A platform's usual answer is to subsidise one side to attract the other, charging the side that comes because of it. The operator charges one group little or nothing so that the other group has a reason to arrive.

afterFigure.text: That makes the price on one side part of the cost of winning the other, so a platform's prices can look odd until you look at both sides together.

diagram.alt: A two-sided platform sits between two groups. The first view shows Atlassian's Marketplace between customers, who buy apps, and third-party developers, who list them. The second shows the general pattern of starting up: one side pays little or nothing, and its presence draws in the side that pays.

reveal.text: The platform needs both groups. The question is which group a new platform should pay to arrive first.

lead.text: Whether a firm can hold its customers is a separate question from whether its market tips. Switching costs, the costs a customer meets in leaving one supplier for another, are also the raw material of **lock-in**, the condition in which they are high enough that the customer depends on the supplier and cannot use another without substantial cost.

How would we know whether customers are locked in? A customer who stays might be locked in or might simply be happy, and a survey can't settle which. The ACCC surveyed Australians aged 14 and over about their mobile operating systems in October and November 2024. 92% agreed they were happy with their system. 49% agreed that a new one would be hard to learn. 59% said their friends and family mostly use the same one, and 73% agreed they could see no significant benefit in switching.

afterFigure.text: Read them one at a time. The 92% fits satisfaction, and it fits lock-in just as well, because a locked-in customer can still be content. The 49% points to a cost of learning, which is a switching cost, and the 59% to a network effect among the people a user deals with. The 73% fits a good product or a costly move equally. The answers that name a cost are the stronger evidence of lock-in, and the happiness figure alone proves little.

diagram.alt: Four findings from the ACCC's survey of Australian mobile phone users: 92% happy with their system, 49% say a new one would be hard to learn, 59% say friends and family use the same, and 73% see no significant benefit in switching. The second view shows what each could point to: satisfaction, a switching cost, a network effect, or more than one explanation.

reveal.text: A cost of leaving is one kind of evidence about lock-in, and a count of who stays is another. They are worth keeping apart.

lead.text: Loyalty programs are a familiar attempt at lock-in, and the ACCC's supermarket inquiry tested how well they work. Its survey found that 51% of respondents belonged to two or more grocery-related programs. The ACCC considers the lock-in risk from free programs *low*, because members can sign up to several at once and enough of them seem willing to shop at different retailers. A program that **costs nothing to join costs nothing to leave**, so it ties a customer in only weakly, and holding several at once is multihoming at work.

reveal.text: The fee is a cost, and costs change what customers are willing to do. Ask what the fee does to the number of programs a member holds.

lessons.orientation: Say whether a market is likely to tip toward one firm, which kind of network effect is at work, and how much customers are really tied in.
lessons.nextAction: Judge which pricing approach fits a case, read what a firm's price pattern says about its position, and spot when a price is built to be hard to judge.

blocks.text: Most products are worth the same to you whether or not anyone else owns one. A toaster works as well if you are its only owner. A few products are different, and a messaging app is the plainest case: it is worth nothing to you if nobody you want to talk to has it, and a little more with every friend who joins.

That difference changes how markets behave, because a product that improves as it grows can run away from its rivals. It also changes how we should read a customer who stays, since staying might mean the customer is happy or might mean that leaving costs too much, and the evidence for the two looks alike.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which kind of network effect a case shows, whether its market is likely to tip, and how far its customers are really tied in.
intro.whyItMatters: In an ACCC survey, 92% of Australians said they are happy with their phone's operating system. That alone cannot show whether they are satisfied or locked in.

recap.keyIdea: A network effect raises the value of a product with its use, but a market tips only if multihoming and switching are costly, and a customer who stays may be happy and not locked in.

blocks.text: You sorted network effects into direct, indirect and scale economies, and saw that a market tips only when network benefits beat differences and users face high multihoming and switching costs. A two-sided platform has to start with one side, and subsidising it is the usual way.

You also read lock-in from evidence. Costs of leaving, such as technical barriers, fees and lost work, are stronger evidence than contentment or staying put, and a free loyalty card binds weakly because members can hold several.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to pricing, and asks which approach fits a case and when a price is built to be hard to judge.

lessons.title: Pricing strategy

steps.headline: Two ways to set a price

lead.text: Every price is built on something, and two foundations are common. **Cost-based pricing** sets the price from what it costs to produce and deliver the product, with a target margin added, so it starts from the firm's own spending. **Value-based pricing** starts from the buyer instead, and sets the price from the value the buyer sees in the product, measured by willingness to pay, whether in money or in the time and resources the buyer would give up.

The two answer different questions. Cost sets a floor, because below it the firm loses money on each sale, and value sets a ceiling, because above it buyers walk away. A pricing strategy is a way of choosing a point between them and of moving that point over time or between customers, and the rest of the lesson looks at the choices firms make: where to start, whether to charge at all, and whom to charge differently.

A new product has to be priced before anyone knows what it is worth. One choice is **penetration pricing**: the price starts low, to reach a wide fraction of the market quickly and start word of mouth, in the hope that customers will move to the new brand for the sake of its lower price. The low price also helps to discourage rivals from entering, since a low price acts as a barrier to entry.

The opposite choice is **price skimming**. The firm starts with a high price, so that the buyers with the strongest desire and the money to act on it buy first, and then lowers the price to reach the next layer of demand. Skimming collects the most from the buyers who value the product most, and penetration reaches the most buyers.

afterFigure.text: Which fits depends on the case. Where a product's value rises with the number of users, as with the networks of the last lesson, a low or free start can carry the firm to [[critical mass|The point at which enough people have adopted a product that joining becomes the sensible choice for each new person. Met in 'Network effects, platforms and lock-in'.]] and discourage rivals. Where early buyers want the product badly and can pay for it, skimming takes more from them before the price comes down.

diagram.alt: Two price paths over time, drawn without numbers. Under penetration pricing the launch price is low, which reaches many customers quickly, and the later price is the firm's choice. Under price skimming the launch price is high, then steps down so that each lower price reaches the next layer of buyers.

reveal.text: The launch price has to fit the problem the product faces. Here the problem is getting enough people on board.

lead.text: Zero can be a price too. **Freemium**, a blend of free and premium, provides a basic product free of charge and charges for additional features, services and goods that extend it. It is sometimes used to build a customer base when the marginal cost of producing another copy is low, because then little is lost by giving the basic version away, provided the free version does not eat into sales of the paid one.

Canva, from the opening, shows the shape. Its additions over time include print services and video editing tools, so there is more to pay for, and in December 2019 it announced Canva for Education, which gives educational institutions a free product. The two user counts in the opening are not a conversion rate. One counts monthly active users and the other counts paid users, and nothing in our sources says how many free users move up to paid.

Atlassian makes its pricing part of how it wins customers. It says automated service, product quality and transparent pricing bring in new customers and their first expansion, and that this keeps its costs of acquiring customers lower.

reveal.text: Freemium has two conditions. One is about cost, and the other is about what the free version leaves out.

lead.text: **Price discrimination** means selling the same or largely similar goods at different prices to different buyers, according to the market segment each buyer is seen to belong to. The word carries no accusation here. It describes a pricing pattern, and the pattern is common wherever a seller can tell its segments apart.

Airlines show it in their fares. The ACCC reports price indices from BITRE for different kinds of domestic ticket, and between January 2013 and January 2020, before the pandemic, the index for restricted economy fares rose 41% in real terms while the index for business class rose 26%. The seats on a flight are alike, and the fare classes sell them to different segments at different prices, which then moved by quite different amounts.

afterFigure.text: The report gives the figures and doesn't explain them. A pattern like this fits segments with different willingness to pay, but it can't by itself say why a particular class rose by more or less, and a careful reader keeps the pattern and the explanation apart.

reveal.text: Look for what separates the buyers, and ask whether that is the same as what separates the costs.

lead.text: Supermarkets use two pricing patterns together. Under everyday low pricing a product's price stays low and steady. Under **high-low pricing** the regular price is higher and is cut from time to time, which shoppers see as a special. The ACCC found that Coles, Woolworths and the Metcash banner stores all use both, and it says the two work together to bring shoppers in and lift sales.

The ACCC also saw a pattern across the two big chains. High-low pricing tends to be cyclical, with products coming on and off special regularly, and for particular products the specials alternate between Coles and Woolworths. For one Coles store and one Woolworths store in a common location, between June 2023 and June 2024, prices moved in opposite directions about 12% of the time. The ACCC reports the pattern. It does not say, in the sections we have, that the chains coordinated.

afterFigure.text: A special always compares a price with another price, and that other price is its **reference price**. If the shopper cannot tell what the usual price is, the size of the saving cannot be judged, which is why the usual price matters so much to how a special is read.

reveal.text: A reference price is a claim about what the usual price is. The question is how far a shopper can check it.

lead.text: A loyalty program is a price written in another currency. The ACCC's example comes from Coles' and Woolworths' programs. Leaving aside bonus points offers, a member has to spend $2,000 to collect a $10 discount, which works out at **0.5c off for each $1 spent**. A discount stated in points has to be turned into cents before it can be set beside a shelf price, and that conversion is work the shopper has to do.
