lessons.orientation: Judge which pricing approach fits a case, read what a firm's price pattern says about its position, and spot when a price is built to be hard to judge.
lessons.nextAction: Judge a move into a new business with the three tests, say when a diversified group is worth more together than apart, and read a portfolio's history as strategy.

blocks.text: Canva, the Australian design software company, counted over 265 million monthly active users and over 31 million paid users by the end of 2025, according to its own reports. It gives its basic product away and charges for extra features.

A firm that gives much of its product away can look as if it has no pricing strategy. A price of zero is a price all the same, and it is one of the strategic choices a firm makes about which customers it wants, how fast it wants them and what it hopes they will do once they are in.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which pricing approach fits a case, read what a pattern of prices shows, and judge when a comparison price is hard for a shopper to check.
intro.whyItMatters: Supermarket specials alternate between Coles and Woolworths, and a loyalty program that sounds generous returns half a cent in the dollar. Reading a price well means knowing what it is built to do.

recap.keyIdea: A price is a strategic choice built on value or on cost, set low or high at launch, free or charged, uniform or by segment, and some prices are built so that the comparison is hard to judge.

blocks.text: You saw that a price can start from cost or from value, and that penetration pricing reaches many buyers while skimming takes more from eager ones. Freemium works when a free copy costs little and a paid tier offers something extra, and Canva and Atlassian show two entry strategies.

You also read price patterns. Fares for similar seats moved by different amounts across classes, which fits segments with different willingness to pay and doesn't show why. Specials need a reference price a shopper can judge, and points turn a discount of half a cent in the dollar into something harder to value.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks when a firm should diversify, using three tests and the history of Masters and Wesfarmers.

lessons.title: Diversification and acquisition

lead.text: A firm that wants to grow has four basic directions, and they depend on whether the product and the market are ones it already has. In **market penetration** the firm sells more of what it already sells to the customers it already has. In market development it takes the same product to a new market, and in product development it sells a new product to its existing market. In **diversification** both are new, and the firm introduces new offerings in new markets.

A furniture retailer (invented) shows all four. Opening more stores in cities it already serves is penetration, taking its stores into a new state is market development, and adding a garden range for its current shoppers is product development. Starting a café chain is diversification. Firms often diversify by buying a business that already exists, which brings its customers and skills and also a [[price paid|What an acquirer pays for a business. Covered in Corporate Finance, 'Acquisitions and the price paid'.]], and the price belongs to that course. Here we ask whether the move itself makes sense.

afterFigure.text: The directions differ in risk. Market penetration is generally the least risky of the four, because it builds on the firm's established strengths and market knowledge. Diversification is at the other end, because it means venturing into uncharted territory where the firm may have little or no prior experience.

diagram.alt: A two by two grid of existing and new product against existing and new market. Penetration is existing product and market, market development is a new market, product development is a new product, and diversification is both new. The second view marks penetration as least risky and diversification as uncharted territory.

lead.text: A diversification move can be tested before it is made, and Morris and Tripathi, in their strategic management textbook, give **three tests** that a move should pass or be turned down. The first is *attractiveness*: an industry without strong profit potential is a risky place to enter, so we ask whether the industry is [[attractive|An industry is attractive when its structure lets firms keep a profit. Met in 'The five forces'.]]. The second is the *cost of entry*: the firm has to be able to earn back what it spends to get in. The third is whether both sides are *better off*, meaning that the new unit and the firm each gain from the other, because a move in which neither gains an edge has no reason behind it.

Masters, from the opening, can be set against the first two. Hardware had long been dominated by Bunnings, which raises the question of how much profit a new chain could win. Woolworths planned 150 stores in five years, which was a large commitment to earn back. In 2015 Masters posted a loss of $227.4 million, and in January 2016 Woolworths announced it would sell or wind up the business, with its chairman saying that the business would need years to reach profit and that its continuing losses were unsustainable.

diagram.alt: Three tests for a diversification move: attractiveness (can the industry earn a profit), cost of entry (can the firm earn back what it spends) and better off (will the new unit and the firm each gain). The second view sets what we know of Masters against the first two tests and leaves the third for the next screen.

reveal.text: The third test is the one the first two do not reach. The extract bears on whether the unit and its parent gained from each other.

lead.text: The third test brings in a distinction between two kinds of move. A **related** diversification goes into a business that shares something important with the firm's existing ones, such as customers, suppliers, skills or logistics. An **unrelated** diversification goes into one that shares nothing important. A related move has something to leverage, so the new unit and the firm are likelier to gain an edge from each other.

The research Morris and Tripathi cite points the same way. Firms that diversify in related directions do better and last longer than firms with a narrower scope, which suggests that what pays is the strategic fit between the businesses.

reveal.text: The better-off test asks for an advantage that runs both ways. Ask which move has more in common with what the chain already does.

lead.text: A firm that owns many unrelated businesses is a conglomerate, and it has a respectable argument. Diversification lowers investment risk, because a downturn in one subsidiary can be offset by stability or growth in another. The trouble is that an investor can get the same spread without the firm's help, by holding shares in several separate companies. So a conglomerate can be worth less than its businesses would be apart, which is called the **conglomerate discount**.

Other disadvantages count too. A conglomerate can lose focus and find it hard to run unrelated businesses equally well, and a brand can be diluted when it stretches too far from what it stood for. So the test of a diversified group is whether it adds something that its investors cannot add for themselves, such as skills, discipline about capital or links between businesses that make each worth more inside the group than outside it.

reveal.text: Ask what an investor can do alone, and what the group would then have to bring.

lead.text: A diversified group is not a fixed collection of businesses. Wesfarmers lists among the ways it seeks a satisfactory return for shareholders that it will acquire or divest businesses where doing so raises long-term shareholder value, so buying and selling are part of the method and not exceptions to it. Wesfarmers calls this renewing the portfolio through value-adding transactions, and we will call it **portfolio renewal**.

Its history shows the pattern. In July 2007 Wesfarmers declared its intention to buy Coles Group for $22 billion, which made it Australia's biggest takeover bid, and in November 2018 Coles Group was spun off from Wesfarmers and listed separately on the stock exchange. The sources we have say what happened and when, and they do not say why Wesfarmers chose to spin Coles off, so we can read the record and cannot yet read the reasons.

diagram.alt: A timeline with two events. In July 2007 Wesfarmers announced a $22 billion bid for Coles. In November 2018 Coles was spun off and listed on its own. A note says the reasons for the spin-off are not in the sources used here.

reveal.text: A share of profit changes with the business and with everything else in the group. Ask what the extract can and cannot tell you.
A record of a purchase and a sale shows what happened. A reason for it is a separate claim, and it needs its own evidence.

lessons.orientation: Judge a move into a new business with the three tests, say when a diversified group is worth more together than apart, and read a portfolio's history as strategy.
lessons.nextAction: Judge whether a firm should do an activity itself or contract it, using scale, alternatives, control and the cost of getting it wrong.

blocks.text: In August 2009 Woolworths unveiled a plan to move into hardware retailing in Australia, through a joint venture with the American chain Lowe's, with 150 stores to open within five years. Hardware had long been dominated by Bunnings, which belongs to Woolworths' rival Wesfarmers. By December 2016 every Masters store had closed, after losses of more than $3.2 billion over seven years.

Woolworths knew how to run supermarkets, and capable firms have failed at moves like this one before. A careful board could have asked questions at the start that would have shown how much risk it was taking, and the answers would also tell us what a failure like this does and does not prove.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to apply three tests to a diversification move, say when a diversified group adds value, and read a portfolio's history without inventing reasons for it.
intro.whyItMatters: Wesfarmers once earned about 55% of its profit from fertiliser and now earns about 1%. Reading a portfolio like that means asking what the record shows and what it leaves out.

recap.keyIdea: A diversification should pass three tests, related moves tend to pass the third more often, and a diversified group has to add something investors cannot add alone.

blocks.text: You met the four directions of growth, with diversification the one where both product and market are new, and three tests for a move: an attractive industry, a cost of entry that can be earned back, and a gain for both the unit and the firm. Masters showed how a failed entry can be traced to one test and not to the industry as a whole.

You also saw why investors discount a conglomerate, since they can spread risk themselves, and how Wesfarmers renews its portfolio by buying and selling. A record of purchases and sales shows what a group did, and its reasons need their own evidence.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks when a firm should do an activity itself and when it should contract it, with Drakes and Qantas as cases.

lessons.title: Make or buy

lead.text: Every firm sits in a chain of activities, as the lesson on [[value chains|The activities between a product's makers and its buyers, read link by link. Met in 'Value chains and where profit sits'.]] showed, and it has to decide how many of them to do itself. **Vertical integration** is an arrangement in which a company owns more of the links in its own supply chain. It can move backward, controlling subsidiaries that produce some of the inputs it uses, or forward, controlling the distribution centres and retailers that sell its products. The alternative is to buy the activity from another firm.

Owning a link has gains. The ones usually listed include lower transaction costs, a closer match between supply and demand along the chain, capture of the margin that sits upstream or downstream, and some independence where an input is rare or volatile in price. It has costs too: higher costs of switching to other suppliers or buyers, weaker motivation at the start of the chain once its sales are guaranteed, and the strain of building skills in a business the firm does not know. Morris and Tripathi make the same two points. Integration is attractive when a firm's suppliers or buyers hold too much power over it, and it risks taking the firm into a business where its skills are of little use, as when a timber merchant begins building houses.

Drakes is the ACCC's case study. It has traded since 1974 and now runs 68 independent stores in South Australia and Queensland, and it took on for itself the wholesale step that Metcash performs for the independents it supplies, which is backward integration toward its suppliers. On 26 September 2019 it opened its own distribution centre in Adelaide, a $125 million investment that marked its independence from Metcash in South Australia. In Queensland it is still supplied by Metcash, under an agreement that runs until at least 3 June 2029.

afterFigure.text: The ACCC draws two lessons. The first is scale. In its judgement, few independent groups are likely to be able to copy the move, because Drakes is among the biggest of them and so had the volume to justify the capital spent. The second is what the move did to Metcash. A review of internal documents indicates that losing Drakes' custom had a significant effect on the viability of Metcash's South Australian wholesale business, and the ACCC concludes that customers' ability to go around Metcash may be a realistic constraint on its wholesale pricing. A **credible bypass** like this can constrain a supplier even where it has been used in only one state.

diagram.alt: Three views of how Drakes' supermarkets are supplied. Before, a wholesaler, Metcash, supplies the stores. In South Australia Drakes opened its own distribution centre on 26 September 2019, a $125 million investment, and Metcash is not used there. In Queensland Drakes is still supplied by Metcash, under an agreement that runs until at least 3 June 2029.

reveal.text: The scale test asks whether a firm has enough business to cover what making the activity itself costs.

lead.text: The other choice is to buy the activity. **Outsourcing** means contracting an activity to another firm, usually one that is not at the core of the business, and the reasons firms give are to cut the cost of peripheral activities, to take advantage of differences in labour cost or tax, to reach top talent and to meet compliance requirements. A recent Australian case is Qantas, which in 2020, during the pandemic, outsourced ground handling at ten airports and affected about 1,800 employees. The sources we have do not say how the decision turned out, so it is an example of the choice and not of its result.

Contracting out costs control. The main difference between doing a job in-house and outsourcing it is who owns it, and a firm that outsources usually has little or no control over a process that another firm owns. That is the price of the savings, and it is one reason a firm might keep the activity itself.

reveal.text: A survey of reversals counts firms that changed course. Ask what that can and cannot show about outsourcing.

lead.text: Buying from another firm has a risk that doesn't show up in the price. Suppose a supplier competes hard to win a contract to make a component, and to make it the supplier has to build specialised machinery that can't be used for anything else. Once the contract is awarded the two firms are no longer in a competitive market. Each depends on the other, and the customer can bargain the supplier's price down because the supplier has no other use for its machinery.

That risk is called **hold-up**: once one side has made a specialised investment, the other side can use that to bargain it down. It also runs the other way, since a customer with only one possible supplier is exposed in a mirror-image way. This is one reason firms own an activity, and another way to limit the risk is to keep a credible alternative, the kind of bypass that constrained Metcash.

reveal.text: Hold-up is about who has made an investment that cannot be used elsewhere.
A bypass need not be used much to matter. What it changes is the supplier's expectations about the customer.

lessons.orientation: Judge whether a firm should do an activity itself or contract it, using scale, alternatives, control and the cost of getting it wrong.
lessons.nextAction: Say whether an entrant is a disruptor, explain why a well-run incumbent may rationally ignore it, and judge the incumbent's possible responses.

blocks.text: Metcash estimates that about 74% of all purchases by IGA stores go through it. Metcash is the wholesaler that supplies the IGA network, and the stores source the remainder from fresh markets, specialist wholesalers and direct supply.

Every business has to decide which of the things it needs it does itself and which it buys. The answer shapes its costs, how much control it keeps and how much it depends on others, and the IGA owner's pattern is one answer to the question.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to weigh whether a firm should make or buy an activity, say what scale and alternatives add to the answer, and name the risk of the choice it makes.
intro.whyItMatters: Drakes built its own $125 million distribution centre, and in a 2005 survey a quarter of the firms that had outsourced reversed course. Each choice carries a cost that the price does not show.

recap.keyIdea: Doing an activity yourself needs scale and brings control and risk, and contracting it out brings savings and a loss of control, so the choice depends on volume, alternatives and what could go wrong.

blocks.text: You saw that vertical integration means owning more links of the chain, and that Drakes could justify its own distribution centre because it was one of the largest independents. Its move also showed that a credible bypass can constrain a supplier even when used in only one state.

You also weighed the other side. Outsourcing saves on peripheral work and gives up control, a quarter of firms in one survey reversed it, and a specialised investment exposes its owner to hold-up when the contract comes up again.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks whether an entrant is a disruptor and why a well-run incumbent might rationally ignore it.

lessons.title: Disruption and the incumbent's dilemma

lead.text: Suppose a company sells a product and its best customers keep asking for a better one. Improving it is the sensible response, and every improvement goes to the customers who already pay the most. Clayton Christensen, whose work Wikipedia summarises, called innovation of this kind **sustaining innovation**, since its goal is to improve the performance of an existing product. He set against it **disruptive innovation**, a product or service made with a different set of customers in mind. Its early versions offer less of what the leader's customers want, so those customers rarely use it at first.

How impressive the technology is doesn't decide which kind an innovation is. Wikipedia's example is the car. The first automobiles of the late nineteenth century were revolutionary, but they were expensive luxury items and left the market for horse-drawn transport alone. The mass-produced automobile did disrupt that market, because it changed how people travelled, which the cars of the first thirty years had never done. Wikipedia describes disruption as a process that runs from the nascent to the mainstream, so the useful question about a new product is who it serves first and where it goes from there.

reveal.text: Disruption turns on who an entrant serves first and what it does next. The next screen describes the two ways in.

lead.text: Christensen described two routes by which an entrant gets a foothold, and neither begins with the leader's best customers.

In **low-end disruption**, products improve faster than customers can use the improvement, until a product does more than some customers need. An entrant then offers lower performance than the leader's that still exceeds what those customers require, and it wins them first. They are the leader's least profitable customers, happy with a good enough product and unwilling to pay a premium for more. With that foothold the entrant improves and moves towards customers who will pay a little more. The leader earns little at the bottom and retreats up-market, and after several rounds it is squeezed into smaller markets until the entrant meets the needs of its most profitable customers as well.

In **new-market disruption** the product fits a segment that existing firms don't serve at all. It begins in a niche, and it starts to define the industry once it can draw customers across from the old market into the new one.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets the three side by side. What sorts an entrant is who its first customers are: the leader's best buyers, the buyers the leader earns least from, or people who weren't buying at all.

diagram.alt: A box for the leader's customers, in three bands from most profitable at the top to least profitable at the bottom, beside a box for people who are not its customers. A sustaining entrant starts in the top band. A low-end entrant starts in the bottom band and later moves up. A new-market entrant starts in the box of non-customers and later draws customers across.

steps.headline: Why a good firm looks away

lead.text: Why would a well-run leader let the entrant in? The easy answer is that the leader missed the technology. Christensen called that the technology mudslide hypothesis, the idea that a firm fails because it can't keep up technologically, and Wikipedia says he and his colleagues showed it to be wrong. Well-run firms generally know about the innovations. What stops them is their business environment, which doesn't allow them to pursue an innovation when it first appears, for two reasons. The new product isn't profitable enough at first, and developing it would take scarce resources away from the [[sustaining innovations|Improvements that give the leader's best customers a better version of what they already buy. Met earlier in this lesson.]] the leader needs in order to compete with the rivals it already has.

Put yourself on the leader's side of the table. Your customers are asking for improvements, and meeting them keeps your sales and profit growing, while the newcomer's market has tight margins and is too small to give a large firm a good growth rate. A small entrant can live in that niche and improve while you are busy elsewhere. Christensen concluded that successful, well-managed firms can lose their lead this way, which means the common advice to stay close to the customer can be strategically counterproductive. Morris and Tripathi say much the same: incumbents tend to wave early disruptors away and concentrate on gradual improvements for their core customers.
We call this the **incumbent's dilemma**: a firm can do everything right by its best customers and still lose its place.

reveal.text: The committee's reasoning holds up on its own terms, which is what makes the dilemma hard. Kodak shows what it can cost.

lead.text: Kodak shows the dilemma from the inside. In 1975 its engineer Steven Sasson built the first handheld digital camera prototype that ran on batteries, and a report from 1979 forecast that photography would be fully digital by 2010. Wikipedia says its executives were reluctant to commit strongly to digital, since it meant a large outlay for a small market and would set Kodak against established makers of computer hardware.

Film went on growing meanwhile, and began to fall only in 2001. Kodak then moved aggressively into digital cameras, and by 2005 it ranked first in US sales. But the cameras earned low margins, because competition was strong and cheaper makers undercut them, and many were sold at a loss, while the film business, where Kodak had earned high margins, kept falling. Wikipedia names the combination as the cause of the decline in profits, and by 2007 Kodak had dropped to fourth place in US digital camera sales.

Selling a product that replaces your own profitable one is called **cannibalising** it, and the pull of the old business is a real cost of moving. An empirical study of the hard disk industry, reported in Wikipedia's article on *The Innovator's Dilemma*, found that incumbents innovate less than entrants mainly because cannibalising their own products reduces their incentive. So Kodak invested in digital, and the trouble was that the new business earned much less than the old one it replaced. The Kodak article doesn't use Christensen's terms, so reading the case as an example of the dilemma is our own step.

Blockbuster adds a difficulty of another kind. As Netflix's mail-order rentals grew in popularity, Blockbuster launched Blockbuster Online on 11 August 2004, a nationwide rent-by-mail service, and later a plan called Total Access, which let a customer rent a DVD online and swap it for a new one at a Blockbuster store.

Blockbuster had franchise operators as well as its own stores. On 5 January 2007 Southern Stores Inc., one of its largest US franchise operators, sued in a US federal court, claiming that the launch of Blockbuster Online and Total Access had undercut its franchise agreement. In Australia franchisees ran most of the outlets: when Blockbuster sold its network to Video Ezy in February 2007, 341 of the 370 outlets were owned by franchisees.

The new service wasn't a poor idea, since Wikipedia reports that Total Access grew past three million customers. The franchisees' complaint shows another cost of an answer to a new model, which can land on the firm's own partners. Wikipedia lists poor leadership, the Great Recession and competition from Netflix, video on demand and Redbox kiosks as major factors in the decline, so the dispute is one strand of a larger story.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the two moves that pulled against each other.

diagram.alt: A timeline with three dates. In August 2004 Blockbuster Online starts renting DVDs by mail. In January 2007 a large US franchise operator sues, saying the online services undercut its franchise agreement. In September 2010 Blockbuster files for bankruptcy protection. The second view colours the first date as serving the new model and the second as pushing back for the old one.

reveal.text: A response that works against part of the firm's own business can still be right. It brings a second negotiation, and the franchisees are the other party to it.

lead.text: What can a leader do once it has looked? Two answers appear in the cases we have, and a price cut on the main product isn't one of them.

The first is a separate unit. Virgin Blue entered the domestic market in 2000 as a new discount airline, Qantas's market share fell, and Qantas created the budget airline Jetstar in 2001 to compete. The ACCC describes the result as a dual brand strategy, with Qantas and QantasLink as the full-service brand and Jetstar as the budget brand for leisure travellers, together generally carrying about 60 per cent of domestic passengers. The sources don't call Virgin Blue a disruptor in Christensen's sense, so we take Jetstar as an example of the response and leave the label open.

Christensen advised the same kind of arrangement, an autonomous organisation that can be rewarded for small wins and small customer sets, and Wikipedia reports that he attributed the failure of Woolworth's discount chain Woolco to a lack of organisational and cultural separation from the high-margin Woolworth stores.

The second answer is to end your own product before an entrant can. The firm cannibalises itself and chooses the timing, at the cost of revenue it could have kept for longer and the risk that customers who can't or won't move to the replacement leave. The alternative is to wait until the entrant has reached your customers, when the best a leader can do is a me-too entry, which Wikipedia says can secure survival but not growth.

reveal.text: Ending a profitable product on purpose is the second answer, and the filing shows what it costs. Not everything called disruption fits the pattern, which the next screen takes up.

lead.text: The idea is older than Christensen. Joseph Schumpeter's creative destruction describes innovation that keeps tearing down old economic structures and building new ones, and Morris and Tripathi's example is steel: low-cost rails made with the Bessemer process wrecked the market for iron rails and the firms that made them.

The pattern isn't a law. Jill Lepore, whose critique Wikipedia reports, points out that some companies the theory named as casualties of disruption years ago, among them Seagate Technology, U.S. Steel and Bucyrus, remain dominant in their industries today. She asks whether the theory has been oversold, as if it could explain everything, and Wikipedia notes that its reliance on selected case studies as the main evidence has also been challenged. Success isn't a requirement of the pattern either: a business can fit it and still fail.

So use the pattern as a set of questions to put to a case: who the first customers are, whether the leader has a reason to look away, and what each possible answer costs it. Where the sources don't settle them, as they don't for Kodak's cameras or for Virgin Blue, a careful reader says what the evidence leaves open.

reveal.text: A product can look like a new-market entrant from its design alone, and the pattern still needs evidence about what its users did before. That habit carries to any case that is labelled disruption.

lessons.orientation: Say whether an entrant is a disruptor, explain why a well-run incumbent may rationally ignore it, and judge the incumbent's possible responses.
lessons.nextAction: Judge whether being first will give a lasting edge, and whether to match a rival's price cut.

blocks.text: Kodak built a prototype of a digital camera in the mid-1970s, and in 2005 Kodak ranked first in the United States in digital camera sales, which rose 40 per cent that year to $5.7 billion. In January 2012 the company filed for bankruptcy protection. Wikipedia reports all of this, and it also calls the popular explanation, that Kodak refused to invest in digital cameras, a misconception.
How does a firm lead in the new technology and still lose its place? We'll look at what kind of newcomer can do that to a well-run leader, and at what the leader can do about it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say whether an entrant is disruptive, explain why a well-run leader may sensibly ignore it, and judge the responses open to the leader.
intro.whyItMatters: Calling every new product disruptive, or every fallen leader complacent, leads to the wrong response. Asking who the entrant serves first, and what each answer costs the leader, gives a sounder reading of a case.

recap.keyIdea: An entrant is disruptive when it starts with customers the leader earns least from or doesn't serve, and a well-run leader has good reasons to look away until the newcomer has improved.

blocks.text: You sorted entrants by their first customers: the leader's best buyers for sustaining innovation, its least profitable buyers for low-end disruption, and people who weren't buying for new-market disruption. You saw why a well-run firm looks away, since the early market is small and thin in profit and the firm's resources are wanted for improvements its best customers have asked for.

Kodak showed a transition that cost the leader its own profits, because digital cameras earned little while its film business shrank, and Blockbuster showed an answer that fell on the firm's own franchisees. A separate unit, as with Jetstar, and ending your own product are the two answers in the cases, and the theory has critics, so it works best as a set of questions to put to each case.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks whether being first brings a lasting edge, and whether to match a rival's price cut.

lessons.title: First movers and price wars

lead.text: Moving first into a market can give a firm an edge. Wikipedia defines **first-mover advantage** as the competitive advantage that goes to the first significant occupant of a market segment, and it names three main sources. Each works by making the pioneer's position hard for a later entrant to match.

The first is **technology leadership**. A first mover that cuts the cost of making a product holds a cost advantage over anyone who follows, and it can apply for patents and similar protection, or make the product too complicated for a rival to reverse engineer. Wikipedia adds a warning: when technology changes fast, patents give weak protection, and a patent race can ruin a slower first mover.

The second is **control of resources**. The first firm can take the best of what the business needs, and Wikipedia's example is the first restaurant of a new type in a town, which can take the prime location. A first mover can also build capacity that discourages others from entering.

The third is **buyer switching costs**. Where customers find it expensive or awkward to change brands,, the firm that wins them first holds the advantage, because buyers sensibly stay with the first brand that does the job well enough, and satisfied customers seldom look further. Wikipedia names Coca-Cola, Kleenex and Nestlé as pioneering brands whose dominance often lasts.

afterFigure.text: In each view the advantage is something a later entrant must overcome, and being early only lets the pioneer build it.

diagram.alt: Three views of a pioneer beside a later entrant. Technology leadership gives the pioneer a lower cost per unit and protection, so the entrant starts with higher costs. Control of resources gives the pioneer the prime sites and suppliers, so the entrant gets what is left. Buyer switching costs leave the pioneer's customers settled in, so the entrant must give buyers a reason to move.

reveal.text: Each edge had a source, and a firm that was merely early had none. The next screen looks at why even a real edge can fade.

lead.text: Does the first mover's edge last? The name suggests that pioneers stay more profitable than followers, and the evidence is less tidy. Wikipedia says that products first to market sometimes fail, and that a pioneer's profits can fall close to zero when a patent expires, which often leads to the patent being sold or the firm leaving the market. Pioneers also pay for going first: they often meet high research and development costs, and the cost of teaching the public what a new kind of product is.

A follower can learn from all of this. It can spend less on research and on educating the market, run less risk that customers reject the product and spend less on winning customers, and it can use what it saves to make a better product or to out-market the pioneer. That is **second-mover advantage**, and Wikipedia calls such firms fast followers.

Studies disagree about whether pioneers do better overall. Wikipedia reports two conclusions that have been widely accepted: first movers on average tend to end up unprofitable, and the pioneers that survive do keep lasting advantages in market share. So whether the first mover wins depends on whether it has one of the three sources, and whether it lasts long enough to use it.

reveal.text: A first-mover claim needs a source behind it. The next screen looks at how a follower can take on a pioneer.

lead.text: A follower that wants to challenge a pioneer has choices of its own. Wikipedia says that attacking head on, with heavy advertising, has usually worked only against smaller pioneers short of resources and recognition, and that a me-too strategy otherwise tends to fail because the follower lacks the brand name and the awareness. The alternative it describes is to start in a new segment, through a new channel, to gain a foothold, and then to widen out. The case after this one shows a follower whose route owed more to timing than to any of these choices.

Virgin Blue gives us a case to read. It started flying on 31 August 2000 with a pair of aircraft serving one route, in a market where Qantas and Ansett were the established airlines. Wikipedia says its timing was fortunate, because it could fill the vacuum left when Ansett failed in September 2001, and that the failure let it grow quickly into Australia's second domestic carrier, where it might otherwise have remained a low-priced alternative to the big incumbents. When Virgin Blue's entry took market share from Qantas, the Qantas Group answered by creating Jetstar in 2001, as the last lesson described.

So Virgin Blue's way to second place ran through an incumbent's failure as well as through its own low-cost formula, and being first isn't part of that story. The ACCC's account of ALDI shows the same thing from another side. ALDI arrived in the Australian grocery market in 2001 and the ACCC says its impact has been significant, and yet the ACCC cites the more than 20 years it took ALDI to reach its present position as evidence that large-scale entry isn't likely in the short to medium term.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the part that each event played in Virgin Blue's story.

diagram.alt: A timeline of three events. On 31 August 2000 Virgin Blue starts flying with two aircraft on one route. In 2001 Qantas creates Jetstar. In September 2001 Ansett fails and Virgin Blue grows quickly. The second view labels the first as a later entrant, the second as a reaction by an incumbent and the third as a rival's failure that opens space.

reveal.text: A report that describes an opportunity hasn't described a result. Reading the difference is most of the skill in reading an industry's history. The next screen turns from timing to prices.

lead.text: A **price war** is a form of competition in which firms keep cutting prices below their rivals', and each tries to match or undercut the other. Wikipedia lists several causes. Where products are alike and customers can switch easily, a firm that cuts its price forces the others to follow or lose share. A firm entering an established market may set a low price to tempt customers across. And in an oligopoly, where a few large firms dominate, each watches the others' prices and is ready to answer any cut, which is the [[rivalry|With few large rivals who watch each other, a price cut is matched and nobody gains share. Met in 'The five forces'.]] that the five forces describe.

Kodak's fight with Fuji shows what a war can cost. Fuji broke through in the 1980s by selling film more cheaply, and Wikipedia says its aggressive marketing and price cutting took share from Kodak, raising Fuji's own from about 10 per cent in the early 1990s to 17 per cent in 1997. A price war between the two began in 1997 and, the article says, cut into Kodak's profits: its revenue went from $15.97 billion in 1996 down to $14.36 billion the next year, and its net earnings from $1.29 billion to $5 million. The article ties the fall to the war and doesn't separate it from other causes.

Wikipedia's summary of the research is that price wars can do real damage. Short-term gains, such as moving stock quickly, are outweighed by longer-term losses in margins, in the value of the customer base and in the ability to innovate, and consumers gain only for a while, because they come to expect unrealistically low prices.

What should a firm do when a rival cuts its price? Wikipedia says the first thing to ask is whether the cut is a long-term decision or a short-term promotion. If it's a promotion, the ideal response is to watch the rival's prices and keep your own where they are, because price wars often begin when a simple promotion is taken for a major change of strategy.

If the cut is long term, there are four reactions. You can **reduce your price**, the most popular reaction, which keeps things as they were and cuts your profit in proportion. You can **maintain your price** in the hope that the rival has made a mistake, but if the rival's move does take share, customers can lose confidence in you. You can **split the market**, dividing a product into a premium version and a basic one, as Heublein did with Smirnoff vodka. Or you can **react with other measures**, such as better quality or more promotion, since price isn't the only weapon.

afterFigure.text: None of the four fits every case. The choice rests on what your own customers value and on what the rival can afford to keep up.

diagram.alt: A decision map. When a rival's price falls, first ask whether it is a short promotion or a long-term cut. For a promotion, watch the rival's prices and hold your own. For a long-term cut there are four reactions: reduce your price, maintain it, split the market into premium and basic versions, or react with other measures such as quality or promotion.

lessons.orientation: Judge whether being first will give a lasting edge, and whether to match a rival's price cut.
lessons.nextAction: Choose the uncertainties that should drive a set of scenarios and judge when staging a commitment is worth its cost.

blocks.text: Virgin Blue started flying on 31 August 2000 with a pair of aircraft serving one route, in a domestic market where Qantas and Ansett were already established. Ansett failed in September 2001, and Virgin Blue suddenly emerged as a major airline. By 2023 the ACCC could report that, going back to 2002, over nine in every ten domestic passengers had flown with Qantas or Virgin Australia.

Virgin Blue wasn't first in its market, and an established firm failed around it. Does an early start matter? We'll look at what being first can give a firm and why the edge so often fades, and then at what a firm should do when a rival cuts its prices.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to judge whether being first will give a lasting edge, and decide whether to match a rival's price cut.
intro.whyItMatters: A pioneer's lead and a rival's price cut both invite a quick reaction, and the quick reaction can cost more than it earns. Asking what protects an early lead, and what kind of price cut a rival has made, gives you a better first question.

recap.keyIdea: Being first helps only where something makes the lead hard to copy, and a rival's price cut calls first for a check on whether it is a short promotion.

blocks.text: You saw three sources of first-mover advantage: a technology that rivals can't match, resources that a firm controls, and costs of switching that tie customers in. A pioneer's lead can fade through heavy early costs, a patent that runs out and followers who learn from its mistakes. Virgin Blue grew into a major airline through timing and an incumbent's failure as well as its own formula, and ALDI took more than twenty years to reach its position.

When a rival cuts its price, the first check is whether it is a short promotion, since a war often starts when a promotion is mistaken for a lasting change. For a lasting cut a firm can reduce its price, hold it, split the market or answer with other measures, and Kodak's fight with Fuji shows how much a war can cost.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks how to plan when the future is uncertain, and when it is worth paying to keep choices open.

lessons.title: Strategy under uncertainty

lead.text: Every plan rests on a picture of the future, and the simplest picture is a straight line that carries current trends forward. Wikipedia calls this the **official future**, and says strategic plans have often considered only that, with trend lines drawn by the accounting department and no discussion of demographics or of qualitative changes in society. Such a rough guess usually works. It fails when the world changes in kind, because a straight line has no place for a change of that sort.

**Scenario planning** is a method that some organisations use to build plans that can flex over the long term. It combines known facts, such as demographics and resource reserves, with the main driving forces in the business environment, and tells a few contrasting stories about how the future could go. Wikipedia credits its practical development for business to Pierre Wack at Royal Dutch Shell in 1971, and says the oil shock of 1973 gave it impetus.

Each story is a **scenario**: a plausible combination of facts and social changes. Wikipedia says scenarios usually describe situations that are plausible but unexpectedly important, and that already exist in some early form today. Any one scenario is unlikely. No scenario is a forecast of the one that will happen. The aim is to help a firm anticipate change and prepare responses, with strategies that hold up in more than one future.

Which facts go into the stories? Wikipedia gives a test: the factors must be genuinely variable, with significant alternative outcomes. A factor whose outcome is predictable but important can't separate one story from another, so it is stated at the start, where it can't be ignored. In the process Wikipedia describes at Shell, the work starts with seven to nine mini-scenarios and reduces them to two or three that differ in the ways that matter.

Take an invented ferry company serving a river town. Two things about its future are open: whether the council builds a bridge, and whether the mine across the river expands or closes. Each could go either way and each would change the company's fortunes, so they are the two uncertainties that drive its scenarios. Whatever happens, the ferries will need fuel and crews, and that goes in the introduction. The colour of the hulls is a minor detail and appears nowhere.
Crossing the two uncertainties gives four scenarios. The company then asks how each of its options would fare in each one, and an option that pays in only one of them is a bet on that story.

The cells are a crowded crossing, a bridge that takes the traffic, a quiet river and an empty crossing. In the third view a second ferry pays only in the crowded crossing and sits idle in the other three.

reveal.text: Only a factor that is both important and open drives a scenario. The next screen asks what scenarios can and cannot do.

lead.text: Scenarios are easy to oversell. Critics say the method is subjective and heuristic, that it hasn't been examined rigorously and that scientific evidence has influenced it too little, and they caution against using it to predict. Wikipedia also says the evidence offered for the value of scenarios has been only anecdotal, and that most of it comes from one company, Shell. Even Shell's case has a complication. When Arie de Geus's team audited its use of scenarios in the early 1980s, the weak point proved to be the decisions that followed the scenarios, which were the main reason the strategy went unimplemented.

Wikipedia adds a point about prediction. People who predict are part of the world they predict, and their forecasts can change it: a scenario about growing cyber-security trouble may lead firms to improve their security and so prevent the trouble. Wikipedia treats this as a difficulty and also a strength of building scenarios.
So the sensible use of scenarios is to challenge a firm's assumptions and prepare responses, with the odds of any one story left aside. They shouldn't be treated as proof that scenario planning pays.

reveal.text: Scenarios prepare a firm for several futures. The next screen turns to a way of acting on them, which is to pay for flexibility.

lead.text: Scenarios say what could happen, and a **real option** is a way of acting on that. It is the right, though not the obligation, to do something with an investment, such as defer it, expand it, abandon it, stage it or contract it. Wikipedia says real options earn their keep when uncertainty is high, when management has real flexibility to change course, and when it is willing to use the option.

Three kinds matter here. An **option to expand** means building a project with more capacity than its expected output needs, so that it can produce more if conditions turn out well. An **option to abandon** means being able to stop a project and sell what is left, which makes sense when what the project will still earn drops below what its assets would fetch. An **option to defer** means choosing when to start, as when a firm waits to mine a deposit until market conditions are favourable.

Flexibility isn't free. Wikipedia calls the non-recoverable spending that buys it the **option premium**. A project built with room to expand costs more to establish, and the extra is the premium, though the project is worth more than the same project without the room. Waiting has its own price: a firm that defers can find a rival has moved first, as the last lesson showed.

Staging is the option that matters most when a firm doesn't know whether a whole plan fits. Wikipedia's account of sequencing says that if projects are taken one after another, watching how the first turns out resolves part of the uncertainty, and the firm can then decide whether to go on. If they are taken in parallel, the money is already spent and the chance to hold back that spending has gone.

The opening case fits this. Woolworths announced in 2009 a plan for 150 stores within five years. Staging would have meant opening some stores and then deciding whether to go on, and a mismatch with the seasons is the kind of fact the first few stores could show. That is our own reasoning about a plan whose actual staging the sources don't describe.

afterFigure.text: The figure compares the three ways in.

diagram.alt: A table of three ways to enter a market under uncertainty. Committing fully risks all the money at once, teaches nothing before it is spent and risks a large mistake. Staging risks a small part first, teaches how it does, and costs the premium and a slower start. Waiting risks nothing yet, teaches what rivals and customers do, and risks a rival moving first.

reveal.text: The staged plan buys learning at a price. The next screen looks at a real company that credits its flexibility, and at what that flexibility did not prevent.

lead.text: Qantas gives a company's own account of flexibility at work. Its FY26 results presentation describes the group's response when fuel prices escalated during a conflict in the Middle East, which it says effectively closed hubs there and created spillover demand on other routes. It lists the actions: capacity moved to capture the spillover traffic, fare rises and domestic capacity cuts to offset fuel, a debt raise for the following year arranged early, a paused share buy-back, lower capital spending and restructured fuel hedging. The company credits its multi-gauge fleet, a fleet of mixed aircraft, with giving it operational flexibility in its response.

Two cautions come with it. The account is the company's own, and the sources we have include no outside test of how much the fleet's flexibility helped. And flexibility didn't make the group immune, because the same slide puts the net impact on the group at about $420 million in the second half of FY26. An option limits a loss, and it doesn't remove one.

reveal.text: Qantas and Virgin each show flexibility with a limit attached. The last step asks what a company's own description can show.
A company's description of its investments can't show how they are staged unless it says so. Reading what a passage leaves open is part of judging a firm's flexibility.

lessons.orientation: Choose the uncertainties that should drive a set of scenarios and judge when staging a commitment (a real option) is worth its cost.
lessons.nextAction: Diagnose why a plan failed from a case: a mismatch with the market, an organisation that did not carry it out, or a plan that was not revised as the world changed.

blocks.text: On 25 August 2009 Woolworths announced a joint venture with the US chain Lowe's to enter Australian hardware, with a plan to develop 150 stores within five years. The first store opened in 2011. In 2016 all the stores were closed, after losses of over $3.2 billion across seven years, and Wikipedia names as a main reason that the stores' product schedules followed the seasons of the US northern hemisphere.

Could a firm in Woolworths's position have found that out more cheaply, and what would finding out have cost? We'll look at how a firm plans when it can't know what will happen, and when it is worth paying to keep choices open.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose the uncertainties that should drive a set of scenarios, and judge when paying to stage a commitment is worth it.
intro.whyItMatters: A plan built on one forecast fails when the world changes in a way the forecast left out. Testing a strategy against several futures, and pricing the flexibility that keeps choices open, makes a firm's commitments easier to defend.

recap.keyIdea: Scenarios test a strategy against several futures, and a real option keeps a choice open at a price that is worth paying when uncertainty is high and the firm would use the option.

blocks.text: You saw why a straight-line official future misses change in kind, and how scenarios built around factors that matter and could go either way, with the predetermined ones stated as givens, let a firm test its options against more than one story. Any one scenario is unlikely, and the evidence that the method pays is anecdotal and mostly from Shell.

A real option such as expanding, deferring or abandoning is flexibility with a premium, and staging is worth paying for when uncertainty is high and an early stage would teach the firm something it would act on. Qantas's response to a fuel shock showed flexibility at work and still cost it about $420 million, by its own figure.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson asks why plans that looked sound still fail, and how to tell a mismatch with the market from a failure to carry the plan out.

lessons.title: Why good plans fail

lead.text: A plan can go wrong in three places, and a cure for one does nothing for the others. It can fail to fit the market it was made for. It can fit and still not be carried out, because the organisation isn't set up to do what the plan asks. Or it can fit and be carried out and then outlive its world, because nobody revises it as conditions change. The loop in the figure shows where each failure sits.

Masters, from the last lesson, is the clearest mismatch in our sources. Wikipedia names as a main reason for its failure that company leadership didn't localise the range to the Australian market, so that product schedules followed the northern hemisphere's seasons, which run opposite to Australia's. The chain also tried to stand out, with bright, colourful stores, buzzers that called staff to a customer and an emphasis on attracting women shoppers, and it lost more than $3.2 billion over seven years. A fair reader could also call it a failure to carry out a plan, since the article puts the blame on the leadership. The three places are for finding the main weakness, and one case can show more than one.

diagram.alt: A loop of four steps: analyse, plan, act and learn, with the last feeding back into the first. The first view shows a break between analysing and planning, where a plan doesn't fit the market. The second shows a break at acting, where the organisation doesn't carry the plan out. The third shows a break at the return from learning to analysing, where results don't change the plan.

lead.text: **Implementation**, as Wikipedia describes it, is aligning and mobilising an organisation's resources, meaning its people, processes and IT systems, behind its objectives. It covers how the organisation is structured, who leads it, how it communicates, which incentives it offers and how progress is monitored. A plan breaks here when these pull in different directions.

Wesfarmers's chair describes what carrying a plan out looks like when it works. In the 2026 annual report he names the corporate objective adopted in 1984, 'To provide a satisfactory return to shareholders', as the single most important factor in the company's success, once good fortune is put aside. He says that bringing more than 100,000 team members into line with it meant structuring the company's systems to reinforce it: how targets are set, how the accounts are kept for management, what is measured and reported, how plans are drawn up and how people are paid, all built around return on investment. Growth in assets or revenue matters, he says, but it can pull attention away from the returns. We call this **alignment** of systems. The account is the chair's own, and the sources we have include no outside test of how far the alignment explains the results.

afterFigure.text: The second view shows an invented firm in which each system rewards something else.

diagram.alt: Six systems of a firm: its targets, management accounts, measures, reports, planning and pay. In the first view all six point at one measure, return on investment, as Wesfarmers describes. In the second, for an invented firm, each system rewards a different measure and none points at a shared aim.

diagram.caption: Use the buttons to compare systems that point one way with systems that pull apart.

reveal.text: Alignment means that targets, measurement and pay all push the same way. The next screen turns to a plan that was well carried out and still failed.

lead.text: A plan can fit its market and be carried out well and still fail later. Mintzberg argued in 1987 that a strategy works as a filter that sorts the signals reaching an organisation, which is why it also shuts some of them out. Because a strategy points the organisation in one direction, that direction may match the environment badly at first, if the strategy is a bad one, or over time as circumstances change.

Charles Handy separated two kinds of change in 1989. **Strategic drift** is gradual change that happens so subtly that nobody notices until it is too late, and transformational change is sudden and radical. Richard Pascale's maxim was 'Nothing fails like success': yesterday's strength turns into the source of tomorrow's weakness, because firms keep to what worked and prevailing strategies become self-confirming. Masters was slow to change course. Wikipedia says that by 2013 it was plain the chain was struggling, the roll-out plan was revised in August 2014, and in January 2016 Woolworths announced that it would 'either sell or wind up' the chain.

Woodhouse and Collingridge offer a remedy, which is intelligent trial and error: lay out the general path and leave the precise steps to be found. Morris and Tripathi describe how this works inside a firm. A firm's realised strategy is made of what it planned, plus the [[emergent strategy|The part of what a firm does that no plan set out. Met in 'What strategy is'.]] decisions that managers make as they interpret the plan and adapt, minus the parts abandoned on the way, and the weight of emergence grows as the environment gets harder to forecast.

reveal.text: Revising a plan is part of planning. The next screen asks what the evidence says about whether planning pays.

lead.text: Does planning work at all? Wikipedia reports a 2019 meta-analysis that pooled results from nearly 9,000 firms in the public and private sectors. It found that strategic planning has a positive effect on performance, and the effect is strongest on a firm's ability to reach its goals. Having a plan wasn't enough on its own. Planning worked when it had some formality, with a look at both the firm and its surroundings, when it was comprehensive, with many strategic options produced before one was chosen, and when it managed stakeholders carefully.

That fits what Morris and Tripathi say about how much to plan. A firm in a stable environment can plan in detail. A firm whose environment can't be forecast can fix only a few principles and guidelines, and the rest has to emerge as events unfold. So how much a firm should plan depends on how the plan is made and on how much detail the environment will bear.

reveal.text: The amount of detail a plan can carry depends on how predictable the environment is. The last step puts that together with the evidence on planning.
One failed plan is a single case. The evidence on planning looks at thousands, and it says how a plan is made matters as well.

lessons.orientation: Diagnose why a plan failed from a case: a mismatch with the market, an organisation that did not carry it out, or a plan that was not revised as the world changed.
lessons.nextAction: You can now diagnose why a plan failed from a case, judge whether a firm's systems are aligned with its objective, and weigh the evidence on planning against a single failed plan.

blocks.text: Under two successive chief executives, Kodak tried to diversify its chemical operations. Wikipedia says the new ventures were given large budgets, but there was little long-term planning or help from outside experts, and most of them lost heavily. In 1988 Kodak bought Sterling Drug for $5.1 billion, and the drug company, the article says, was overvalued and soon lost money.
Money wasn't what Kodak lacked, so where do good plans go wrong? We'll ask how to tell a plan that didn't fit from one that was never carried out, or one that was never revised.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to diagnose why a plan failed, judge whether a firm's systems are aligned with its objective, and weigh the evidence on planning.
intro.whyItMatters: A failed plan invites a quick verdict, either that planning is useless or that the people carrying it out were careless. Asking where the plan broke gives a more useful answer.

recap.keyIdea: A plan can fail because it doesn't fit its market, because the organisation doesn't carry it out, or because nobody revises it as the world changes, and the evidence supports planning when it is done well.

blocks.text: You sorted failures by where the plan broke. Masters's mismatch with Australian seasons was a plan that didn't fit, Wesfarmers's systems showed what it takes to carry a plan out, and strategic drift described a plan that outlived its world. A firm's targets, measures and pay have to point the way its objective does, or the plan stalls inside the organisation.

The 2019 meta-analysis found that planning helps on average and that how it is done matters, so one failed plan doesn't show that planning is useless. How much to plan in detail depends on the environment: more where it is stable, and a few fixed principles where it is volatile and the rest has to emerge.

questions.prompt: Virgin Australia's new chief executive said this about the airline's plan in 2020. Which reading is best?
hints: Ask whether the sentence names a result the firm wants or a way of competing it has chosen.
Think about what an airline that is neither low-cost nor traditional full-service would have to do differently from both.

extracts.text: New CEO Jayne Hrdlicka said at the time that ‘Australia already has a low-cost carrier and a traditional full-service airline, and we won’t be either’.
extracts.who: ACCC, Airline competition in Australia, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.when: published June 2023, recording a statement made in 2020
extracts.kind: A report by Australia's competition regulator, quoting the airline's chief executive

questions.onCorrect: A refusal narrows a firm's position, and the narrowing shows up in what it flies, charges and offers.

acceptedIdeas: A position defined partly by what Virgin refuses to be, with consequences for how it operates
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A position defined partly by what Virgin refuses to be, with consequences for how it operates

choices.label: A target to grow faster than both rivals, which names a result and gives no clear way of competing
A slogan that changes nothing about how the airline is run, since every airline simply sells seats
A position defined partly by what Virgin refuses to be, with consequences for how it operates

misconceptions.feedback: A target would name a result, such as a share of passengers. The sentence names what the airline will not be, which is a choice about how it competes.
The ACCC records what followed from it: a single aircraft type, lower fares without meals and less ability to fly some regional routes. It did change how the airline runs.

questions.prompt: A regional tyre retailer (invented) has six statements in its board papers. Which kind of statement is each one?
hints: For each statement ask whether it names a result, commits the firm to some customers and shuts out others, or is a move a rival could copy next week.
A statement can sound ambitious and still be only a result. Ask whether it says how.
questions.onCorrect: An objective names the result, a strategic choice commits the firm to a position and shuts out another, and a tactic is a move a rival can copy at once.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Objectives: becoming the biggest seller and out-earning the best retailer. Strategic choices: serving only fleets, and sending fitters to depots while closing the shops. Tactics: the free alignment and the banner.

items.label: Become the biggest tyre seller in the state
items.explanation: It names a result and says nothing about how to reach it.

items.label: Serve only businesses that run vehicle fleets, and turn away walk-in customers
items.explanation: It commits the retailer to one kind of customer and shuts out another.

items.label: Give a free wheel alignment with every set of four tyres this month
items.explanation: A rival can match it at once, and the retailer's position stays the same.

items.label: Send fitters to customers' depots, and close the walk-in shops
items.explanation: It reshapes the activities around one position and gives up the walk-in trade.

items.label: Earn more profit each year than the best-run tyre retailer in the country
items.explanation: It is a target for results and says nothing about how to beat that retailer.

items.label: Put a banner outside the shop on wet days
items.explanation: A small move that changes neither the customers served nor the offer.

questions.prompt: A bank (invented) says that low fees and fast service can't go together, because each costs the other. A rival (also invented) gives both on the same products by running a simpler process. What does that show?
hints: Ask where the first bank's costs come from. Is it the product, or the way the bank gets the work done?
If one firm can offer both with the same products, what does that say about the claim that they can't go together?
questions.onCorrect: When a rival matches the offer without paying a penalty, the trade-off was hiding how the first firm operates.

acceptedIdeas: That the first bank's trade-off was false, because its higher cost came from how it works
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the first bank's trade-off was false, because its higher cost came from how it works

choices.label: That the first bank's trade-off was false, because its higher cost came from how it works
That the rival must lose money on every customer, since nobody can offer both for long
That trade-offs never exist in any business, since a clever enough process removes every one

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the case says the rival loses money. It says the rival runs a simpler process, which is how it can charge less and answer faster.
Real trade-offs exist where a product serves one need and not another, where activities conflict or where an image would be damaged. The case shows only that this one wasn't real.

questions.prompt: Two independent plumbing supply merchants (both invented) compete for the same tradespeople. Merchant A runs a one-weekend sale. Merchant B has spent years learning each regular customer's jobs and keeps the parts they need on the shelf. Which advantage is more likely to last, and why?
hints: Picture each rival trying to match the advantage. How long would that take, and what would it cost?
A sale and a stock of the right parts are very different things to copy. Which needs time and money?
questions.onCorrect: An advantage lasts in proportion to what it costs a rival to copy it, and a promotion costs almost nothing.

acceptedIdeas: B's, because a rival can copy a sale at once but must spend time and money to match the knowledge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: B's, because a rival can copy a sale at once but must spend time and money to match the knowledge

choices.label: A's, because a sale reaches every customer at once, and customers nearly always choose the lower price
B's, because a rival can copy a sale at once but must spend time and money to match the knowledge
Both, because any advantage that draws customers away from rivals lasts for as long as it keeps drawing them

misconceptions.feedback: Reaching customers quickly doesn't help if a rival can match the sale by Monday. Lasting depends on how costly the copy is.
That treats lasting and drawing customers as the same thing. An edge that a rival can match overnight stops drawing customers as soon as it does.

questions.prompt: A cable channel (invented) was planned to cover sport in one state. Its early success opened options nobody had planned, and it grew into a national network. A board member says that was luck and so isn't part of the channel's strategy. What is the best reading?
hints: Ask whether the national network came from the plan, or from decisions made once the early success was known.
Strategy as the firm actually practises it includes more than the written plan.
questions.onCorrect: What a firm ends up doing is its plan, less what it dropped, plus whatever emerged along the way.

acceptedIdeas: It is the emergent part of the realised strategy, made up of decisions taken after the plan
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is the emergent part of the realised strategy, made up of decisions taken after the plan

choices.label: It is outside the strategy, since only what was written down in advance can count as strategy
It shows the original plan failed, so planning adds nothing to what a firm's strategy turns out to be
It is the emergent part of the realised strategy, made up of decisions taken after the plan

misconceptions.feedback: Realised strategy is what the firm actually does, and that includes decisions that nobody planned.
The plan was carried out first, and the growth came from decisions made on the back of it. Whether planning is worth doing is a separate question.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain's annual report (invented) says: "Our strategy is to be the country's most trusted grocer." What is the best comment on that sentence?
hints: Does the sentence say how the chain will compete, or only what it wants to become?
A strategy excludes something. What does this sentence exclude?
questions.onCorrect: Being trusted is a result the chain wants. How it competes to get there is the strategy, and the sentence doesn't say.

acceptedIdeas: It is an objective, since it names a result and no way of competing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is an objective, since it names a result and no way of competing

choices.label: It is a strategy, since it names the customers the chain wants to win
It is an objective, since it names a result and no way of competing
It is a tactic, since any grocer could say the same thing next week

misconceptions.feedback: It names a result and no customers. A strategy would say which shoppers the chain will serve and what it will refuse to do.
A tactic is a specific move, such as a promotion. This sentence is a goal, and its weakness is that it says nothing about how to reach it.

questions.prompt: Six businesses (all invented) each claim a trade-off. Which claims describe a real trade-off, and which hide weak operations?
hints: For each claim, ask whether a rival has shown that both can be had at once.
A trade-off is real when the activities conflict, one product can't meet two needs or an image would be damaged.
questions.onCorrect: A trade-off is real when copying it would cost a rival something, and false when a rival gets both and the claim only hid weak operations.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Real: the funeral home, the shoe maker and the bookshop. False: the small airline, the cafe and the tailor.

items.label: A funeral home known for quiet dignity says it can't also run a cheerful party-hire business, because the two would damage its image
items.explanation: The image of one business would suffer from the other, so a rival copying both would pay for it.

items.label: A small airline says quick turnarounds and full meal service can't go together, yet a rival with a better-organised ground crew offers both
items.explanation: A rival offers both, so the claim described the first airline's ground operations.

items.label: A shoe maker says it can't build cheap running shoes and elite racing shoes in one factory, because the machines are set up in different ways
items.explanation: The activities conflict, so doing one job well gets in the way of the other.

items.label: A cafe says it can't serve good coffee and be quick, yet the cafe across the road does both with the same number of staff
items.explanation: The rival does both, so the claim hid how the first cafe is run.

items.label: A bookshop that sells only rare editions says it can't also stock cheap paperbacks, because browsers would stop seeing it as a specialist
items.explanation: The cheap stock would damage the image that draws rare-book buyers.

items.label: A tailor says it can't make suits both well and quickly, yet a rival with a smarter cutting process delivers in half the time at the same quality
items.explanation: A rival matches both, so the supposed trade-off came from the tailor's own process.

questions.prompt: A small bookshop (invented) lists three advantages: a loyalty card that gives a discount, staff who have spent years learning customers' tastes, and a bright window display. Which is most likely to last?
hints: Imagine a rival trying to match each of the three. Which would take the longest and cost the most?
An advantage that customers can see isn't necessarily one that rivals can't copy.
questions.onCorrect: The staff's knowledge builds slowly through experience, so a rival can't buy it quickly or cheaply.

acceptedIdeas: The staff knowledge, since a rival would need years and money to build it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The staff knowledge, since a rival would need years and money to build it

choices.label: The staff knowledge, since a rival would need years and money to build it
The loyalty discount, because customers can see exactly how much it saves them
The window display, because it is the first thing every passer-by sees

misconceptions.feedback: A discount is visible to customers, and just as visible to rivals who can offer the same card within weeks.
A display is easy to see and easy to copy. What matters for lasting is the cost to a rival, and a display costs little.

questions.prompt: The ACCC explains how an oligopoly can dampen competition on price. What does its reasoning depend on?
hints: Read what the first chain believes will happen if it cuts prices. What does the other chain do?
Ask what a cut costs the chain, and what it gains if the rival matches it.

extracts.text: For example, in circumstances where there are 2 major supermarkets, and one believes that a reduction in prices (through a reduction in profit margins) will provoke an equal price reduction by the other, this may result in a lower profit margin without the growth in market share that was sought.
extracts.who: ACCC, Supermarkets inquiry, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A final report by Australia's competition regulator

questions.onCorrect: If a cut will be matched, it lowers both margins and shifts no customers, so neither chain gains by starting one.

acceptedIdeas: That the other chain is expected to match any cut, so the cut lowers margin and wins no share
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the other chain is expected to match any cut, so the cut lowers margin and wins no share

choices.label: That shoppers rarely notice a price cut, so a cut never brings a chain any additional customers
That the other chain is expected to match any cut, so the cut lowers margin and wins no share
That each chain is too small to afford a price cut, so neither of them is really able to try one

misconceptions.feedback: The reasoning doesn't depend on shoppers missing the cut. It depends on the other chain answering with an equal cut.
The extract describes a chain that can cut prices by accepting a lower margin. The point is that a cut which is matched wins nothing.

questions.prompt: Between the early 2010s and the end of the decade the domestic airline industry went through the episode this extract describes. Which force strengthened, and what did it do to profit?
hints: Who is competing with whom in the extract, and what moves do they make?
Look at what the airlines had to say about the result. What happened to their finances?

extracts.text: In the early 2010s, low-cost carrier Virgin Blue’s transition into full-service carrier Virgin Australia meant that it was competing more directly with Qantas, including for the highly profitable corporate customer segment. The 2 airlines competed vigorously for market share by adding capacity and bringing down airfares. However, the price war proved to be unsustainable and was abandoned in the latter part of the decade after both airlines had incurred significant financial losses.
extracts.who: ACCC, Airline competition in Australia, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A report by Australia's competition regulator

questions.onCorrect: Two rivals added capacity and cut fares to win share from each other, and the fight cost both of them money.

acceptedIdeas: Rivalry, because the two airlines fought for share and that pushed down the profit of both
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rivalry, because the two airlines fought for share and that pushed down the profit of both

choices.label: Supplier power, because suppliers raised the airlines' costs and that cut the profit of both
Buyer power, because passengers organised themselves and forced both airlines to cut their fares
Rivalry, because the two airlines fought for share and that pushed down the profit of both

misconceptions.feedback: The extract gives no story about suppliers raising costs. It describes two airlines adding capacity and cutting fares to win share from each other.
Passengers appear only as the ones who gained from lower fares. What the extract describes is a fight for share between the two airlines.

questions.prompt: A new airline (invented) starts flying Sydney to Melbourne, and the ACCC makes this observation about business travel. Which of the airline and the online technology is a substitute for a business flight?
hints: Ask what need a business flight meets, and which of the two meets it in a different way.
A product that uses the same technology to meet the same need is a rival or an entrant, whatever its name.

extracts.text: Some of the lag in recovery may also be due to a structural change in which online technology continues to replace some business travel.
extracts.who: ACCC, Airline competition in Australia, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
