extracts.kind: A report by Australia's competition regulator

questions.onCorrect: A substitute takes the need away by another route, so it can cut an industry's profit without a single new rival appearing.

acceptedIdeas: The online technology, because it meets the need to do business at a distance another way
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The online technology, because it meets the need to do business at a distance another way

choices.label: The online technology, because it meets the need to do business at a distance another way
The new airline, because it competes for the same passengers on the same route
Neither, because a substitute exists only for cheap goods that buyers can drop without much loss

misconceptions.feedback: A new airline meets the need in the same way, by flying people, so it is a rival or a new entrant. A substitute meets the need by a different route.
Substitutes exist for any product. Wikipedia's examples include airlines, cars, trains and ships, which are far from cheap.

questions.prompt: The ACCC reports this estimate, made by the Qantas Group itself. What can the five forces not tell you about it?
hints: Which of the three questions is about the industry, and which is about one firm in it?
The extract gives one firm's share of a pool. What decides a firm's share of it?

extracts.text: Further, while profits in the airline industry can fluctuate greatly from year‑to‑year, the Qantas Group earned most of the profits made by the domestic airline industry. The Qantas Group estimates that it earned around 70% of the domestic industry profits (earnings before interest and taxation, EBIT) between the 2011 and 2015 financial years, which increased to around 90% between the 2015 and 2019 financial years.
extracts.who: ACCC, Airline competition in Australia, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.when: published June 2023, giving the Qantas Group's own estimate
extracts.kind: A report by Australia's competition regulator

questions.onCorrect: The forces describe the pool. Who takes it depends on the firm's own position and choices, which they don't cover.

acceptedIdeas: How the industry's profit is shared among the firms in it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How the industry's profit is shared among the firms in it

choices.label: How closely the few large rivals watch each other's prices
How well barriers to entry protect the industry's profit
How the industry's profit is shared among the firms in it

misconceptions.feedback: That is what the rivalry force is for, so the forces can tell you this. It describes the industry's structure and says nothing about one firm's share.
That is the entrants force, so the forces can tell you this. They describe how well the industry's profit is protected and say nothing about who collects it.

questions.prompt: Six industries (all invented) each have one force that holds profit down more than the others. Which force is it in each?
hints: Ask what is pressing on profit in each case: firms already there, firms that could arrive, a product from another route, or a firm on one side of the chain.
For the vertical forces, ask which side has few alternatives to the other.
questions.onCorrect: The binding force is the one that presses hardest on profit, and each force has its own signature, such as price matching, easy entry or a single source.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rivalry: the plumbers. New entrants: gutter cleaning. Substitutes: the cinema and the rail operator. Buyer or supplier power: the bakery, where one buyer has other bakers to turn to, and the brewer, where one grower has no rival.

items.label: Forty plumbers in one town all quote for the same jobs and match each other's prices
items.explanation: Firms already in the industry fight for the same customers and answer each other's prices.

items.label: Anyone with a van and a ladder can start a gutter-cleaning business next week
items.explanation: Nothing stops new firms from joining, so profit is competed away from outside.

items.label: A regional cinema whose audiences increasingly stream films at home
items.explanation: Streaming meets the need for a film by a different route.

items.label: A bakery that sells most of its bread to one supermarket chain, which could switch to another baker at any time
items.explanation: One buyer takes most of the output and has other bakers to turn to.

items.label: A craft brewer that must buy one rare hop variety from a single grower
items.explanation: The only supplier of an input has no rival, so it can set the terms.

items.label: A rail operator whose passengers can drive, fly or take a coach for the same trip
items.explanation: Each of those meets the need to travel by a different route.

questions.prompt: Source A describes the structure of the domestic airline industry and Source B describes one of its two big firms in 2020. What do the two together show?
hints: Source A is about the industry and Source B is about one firm. What can a firm's result tell you about the industry's structure?
Ask what else, besides the industry's structure, could decide how a firm in it fares.

extracts.text: The duopoly market structure of the domestic airline industry has made it one of the most highly concentrated industries in Australia, other than natural monopolies.
extracts.who: ACCC, Airline competition in Australia, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A report by Australia's competition regulator

extracts.text: Virgin Australia then went into voluntary administration in April 2020 with significant levels of debt.
extracts.who: ACCC, Airline competition in Australia, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A report by Australia's competition regulator

questions.onCorrect: The structure of an industry shapes how much profit is available. How well a firm does within it also depends on the firm.

acceptedIdeas: Concentration doesn't make every firm profitable, since a firm's earnings also depend on its own position
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Concentration doesn't make every firm profitable, since a firm's earnings also depend on its own position

choices.label: Concentration doesn't make every firm profitable, since a firm's earnings also depend on its own position
Concentration has no effect on profit, since Virgin lost money in a duopoly and nothing else matters
The pandemic alone explains Virgin's trouble, so the two sources say nothing about the firm's position or debt

misconceptions.feedback: That goes too far. The ACCC's description of the structure is why it expects limited price competition. The two sources show only that structure doesn't guarantee profit to every firm.
Source B states the administration and the debt without giving a cause, so it can't show that the pandemic was the only reason, and a reader can't set the firm's own position aside.

questions.prompt: A ferry company (invented) carries commuters across a harbour. A second ferry operator starts the same crossing, and a road tunnel opens under the harbour. Which of the two is the substitute, and why?
hints: Which of the two crosses the harbour in the way the first company does, and which in a different way?
A substitute can take customers away from the whole industry as well as from one firm.
questions.onCorrect: The tunnel pulls commuters away from ferries as a category, which is what marks a substitute. The second operator only splits them.

acceptedIdeas: The tunnel, because it meets the need to cross by a different route and gives commuters a reason not to take a ferry at all
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tunnel, because it meets the need to cross by a different route and gives commuters a reason not to take a ferry at all

choices.label: The second ferry operator, because it competes for the same commuters on the same crossing and so is the closest alternative
The tunnel, because it meets the need to cross by a different route and gives commuters a reason not to take a ferry at all
Both of them, because anything that takes commuters away from the first company counts as a substitute for its ferries

misconceptions.feedback: The second operator meets the need in the same way, so it is a rival or a new entrant. A substitute is defined by a different route to the same need.
A substitute is defined by meeting the need in a different way. The second operator offers the same service, so it is a rival or an entrant.

questions.prompt: Six facts (all invented) are listed about the brick industry. Which describe the industry, and which describe one firm's position in it?
hints: Ask whether every firm in the industry faces the fact, or only one of them.
The forces describe pressures that fall on the whole industry. Anything only one firm has is about its position.
questions.onCorrect: A fact about the industry presses on every firm in it, and a fact about one firm's position decides how much of the industry's profit that firm takes.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The industry: four large firms, the licence and the timber substitute. One firm's position: the quarry, the delivery record and the loyal builder.

items.label: Four large firms make almost all the bricks, and each watches the others' prices
items.explanation: It is the structure of rivalry, which every firm in the industry faces.

items.label: Only one brick maker has a quarry next to its kilns, so its freight costs are the lowest
items.explanation: It is an advantage that only one firm holds, so it explains that firm's share of the profit.

items.label: New brickworks need a licence that takes years to obtain
items.explanation: It limits entry for every newcomer, so it protects the industry's profit.

items.label: One brick maker has a reputation for delivering on the day promised
items.explanation: It belongs to one firm and helps it win more of the industry's profit.

items.label: Homebuilders can switch between brick and timber frame for most houses
items.explanation: A substitute pressures every brick maker alike.

items.label: One brick maker's biggest customer is a builder who buys from it whatever the price
items.explanation: It is a relationship that one firm has, and it doesn't describe the industry.

questions.prompt: What does this extract best support about entry into Australian supermarkets?
hints: Read what the extract says about how long ALDI took, and then about how likely large-scale entry is soon.
One firm's success shows that entry can happen. Ask what it can't show about the firms that didn't arrive.

extracts.text: Small-scale local entry and expansion is more achievable and delivers benefits to those in the local market, but is less likely to deliver significant price competition to incumbent chains than large-scale new entry of a supermarket chain. Achieving large-scale new entry is not likely in the short to medium-term, as demonstrated by the time taken (more than 20 years) for ALDI to achieve its current market position.
extracts.who: ACCC, Supermarkets inquiry, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A final report by Australia's competition regulator

questions.onCorrect: A barrier can slow entry for decades without stopping it, and one entrant's success says little about how hard the way in was.

acceptedIdeas: Large-scale entry is possible but slow, so barriers can delay a rival without ruling it out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Large-scale entry is possible but slow, so barriers can delay a rival without ruling it out

choices.label: Entry is impossible, since a single success after more than two decades shows how rare it is
Barriers must be small, since ALDI got there in the end and any other chain could do the same
Large-scale entry is possible but slow, so barriers can delay a rival without ruling it out

misconceptions.feedback: ALDI did enter and succeed, and the extract adds that small local entry is more achievable. The barriers slow large-scale entry, and they do not rule it out.
One success after more than 20 years says little about entrants who never arrived, and the extract concludes that large-scale entry isn't likely in the short to medium term.

questions.prompt: A new airline (invented) wants to fly the main domestic routes. Using the test of who pays, which of these costs are barriers to its entry? The fuel, wage and leasing items are invented, and the other three come from the ACCC's account.
hints: For each cost, ask whether the established airlines pay it too, or whether they already have what the entrant must build.
A cost can be the biggest on the page and still not be a barrier, if every airline pays it.
questions.onCorrect: A cost is a barrier only if the entrant bears it and incumbents don't, however large it is, so fuel and wages fail the test and reputation and slots pass it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Barriers: the reputation for reliability, the slot preference and the terminal and route legacy. Not barriers: fuel, wages and aircraft leased on equal terms.

items.label: Building a reputation for reliable service that the established airlines already hold
items.explanation: The ACCC lists the need to establish this reputation among the barriers. Incumbents already have it and the entrant must build it.

items.label: Winning slots at a busy airport, where incumbents seeking to change a slot time get a preference over new entrants' requests
items.explanation: The ACCC identifies this preference, which gives incumbents an advantage that an entrant doesn't have.

items.label: Reaching terminal access and routes that Qantas secured when only two airlines were permitted to fly domestically
items.explanation: The ACCC traces part of Qantas's position to this legacy. An entrant must now build what the incumbent acquired then.

items.label: Buying jet fuel at the market price, as every airline does
items.explanation: Incumbents pay the same price, so the cost is large but isn't a barrier.

items.label: Paying pilots and engineers market wages, as every airline does
items.explanation: The incumbents' wage bill is the same kind of cost, so it doesn't favour them over an entrant.

items.label: Leasing aircraft on the same terms that the established airlines are offered
items.explanation: The terms are the same for everyone, so the cost falls equally on entrant and incumbent.

questions.prompt: The ACCC made this estimate about a retailer's entry into Australian supermarkets. What does it show about entry barriers?
hints: Look at how much of the money was spent and how much of it was recovered.
Ask what the unrecovered part does to the risk of trying, as against what it says about the retailer's skill.

extracts.text: From Kaufland’s ASIC filings, we estimate it invested approximately $500m in its Australian entry, of which approximately $300m was unrecovered or, in other words, sunk costs.
extracts.who: ACCC, Supermarkets inquiry, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A final report by Australia's competition regulator, estimating from company filings

questions.onCorrect: Money that can't be recovered turns an entry from a bet that can be unwound into one that can't, which raises the stakes.

acceptedIdeas: That sunk cost raises the price of a wrong bet, so an entrant must be surer than its capital suggests
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That sunk cost raises the price of a wrong bet, so an entrant must be surer than its capital suggests

choices.label: That sunk cost raises the price of a wrong bet, so an entrant must be surer than its capital suggests
That capital is the main barrier for every entrant, so the retailer with the biggest fund always wins entry
That the retailer was badly managed, since an entrant that loses money has made avoidable mistakes

misconceptions.feedback: The ACCC doesn't treat capital as a barrier for large international retailers. The figure shows what was at stake, and it doesn't show a wall that money can't climb.
The extract says nothing about management or about why the entry ended. A large sunk cost shows what was at stake and nothing more.

questions.prompt: These are two accounts of the same barrier, supplier networks. Source A is the ACCC's account of what ALDI told the inquiry, and Source B is what Woolworths said at a public hearing. What matters most in weighing them?
hints: Ask what each speaker would gain from how it describes the barrier.
If you wanted a judgement that neither side had a reason to shade, whom would you ask?

extracts.text: One of the barriers ALDI faced when opening in Australia was building a supplier network.
extracts.who: ACCC, Supermarkets inquiry, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: The regulator's summary of the entrant's account

extracts.text: Woolworths in the public hearings stated building a supplier network is not a barrier because ‘suppliers always look for opportunities to sell their products across a range of different retailers and offerings’
extracts.who: ACCC, Supermarkets inquiry, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.when: published in 2025, recording a public hearing
extracts.kind: The incumbent's account, as reported by the regulator

questions.onCorrect: Both accounts are interested, so weight goes to an independent weighing. The ACCC judged supplier networks a less significant barrier.

acceptedIdeas: Neither account settles it alone, because each speaker has a stake in how it describes the barrier
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Neither account settles it alone, because each speaker has a stake in how it describes the barrier

choices.label: Woolworths is right, because the larger firm has more data on how suppliers behave toward every retailer it deals with
Neither account settles it alone, because each speaker has a stake in how it describes the barrier
ALDI is right, because it faced the barrier at first hand, and a first-hand account settles the question

misconceptions.feedback: Size isn't accuracy. Woolworths is also the party that gains from a weak barrier, and its account needs the same scrutiny as ALDI's.
First-hand experience is evidence, but it comes from a party with a stake, and one entrant's experience doesn't show how typical it was.

questions.prompt: Metcash estimates that about 74% of what IGA retailers buy goes through it, and that they source 50% to 90% of their fresh groceries elsewhere. Sources A and B add to that. What do they say about Metcash's bargaining power over an IGA store?
hints: Ask separately about packaged groceries and about fresh produce: how many alternatives does a store have for each?
Source B is Metcash's own account. Does it help its claim about power or weaken it?

extracts.text: We consider Metcash-supplied independent supermarkets currently have little or no choice aside from Metcash for their supply of certain packaged groceries.
extracts.who: ACCC, Supermarkets inquiry, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: The regulator's own finding

extracts.text: the barriers to entry to supply fresh produce are relatively low, in that anybody can go to the market who has a market licence and buy produce.
extracts.who: Metcash, evidence at an ACCC public hearing, recorded in the Supermarkets inquiry final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: Evidence from the wholesaler whose position is being assessed

questions.onCorrect: Bargaining power follows the alternatives for each line, so the same wholesaler can be strong on one and weak on another.

acceptedIdeas: Strong on some packaged lines, since stores lack choice there, and weak on fresh, where they have many suppliers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Strong on some packaged lines, since stores lack choice there, and weak on fresh, where they have many suppliers

choices.label: Strong on some packaged lines, since stores lack choice there, and weak on fresh, where they have many suppliers
Strong on everything, because Metcash is the largest wholesaler to the independent supermarkets it supplies in Australia
Weak on everything, because each IGA store is locally owned and can walk away from Metcash at any time it likes

misconceptions.feedback: Size isn't the test. Power depends on the alternatives for each line, and the stores buy a large share of their fresh groceries elsewhere.
Source A finds that the stores have little or no choice but Metcash for certain packaged groceries, so on those lines they can't simply walk away.

questions.prompt: Two firms (both invented) are weighing entry into a regional bus market, and both plan to spend about the same total. Firm P would spend mostly on second-hand buses that it could resell. Firm Q would spend mostly on a custom depot and on advertising to introduce a new brand. Which faces the higher stakes if entry fails, and why?
hints: Imagine each firm abandons the market after a year. What does each get back?
Equal spending doesn't mean equal risk if some of it can be sold on.
questions.onCorrect: A sunk cost is the part that can't be recovered, and the more of it an entrant has, the more it stands to lose.

acceptedIdeas: Firm Q, because most of its spending could not be recovered if it left the market
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Firm Q, because most of its spending could not be recovered if it left the market

choices.label: Firm P, because buses are the most expensive items either firm would buy
Neither, because firms that plan to spend the same total face the same risk
Firm Q, because most of its spending could not be recovered if it left the market

misconceptions.feedback: The totals are the same. What differs is how much comes back, and the buses can be sold on.
The risk depends on how much of the spending can be recovered as well as on its total.

questions.prompt: A city's craft distilling trade (invented) has several established distillers. Which of these costs are barriers to a new distiller, by the test of who pays?
hints: For each cost, ask whether established distillers pay it too.
Some barriers are costs that incumbents already paid at an earlier time or on better terms.
questions.onCorrect: A barrier is a cost that the entrant bears and the incumbent doesn't, or didn't have to, so costs paid equally by everyone are not barriers however large.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Barriers: the licence bought at today's price, the grain contracts and the customers' reluctance to switch. Not barriers: copper stills, award wages and excise duty.

items.label: A distilling licence that the established distillers obtained years ago for a small fee and that newcomers now buy at today's price
items.explanation: Only the newcomers pay today's price, so it is a cost the incumbents don't bear.

items.label: Copper stills, which every distiller buys at the same price
items.explanation: The same price for everyone means the incumbents bore the same cost when they started.

items.label: Long-term contracts in which the established distillers locked in the best grain at old prices
items.explanation: A newcomer pays the higher price for the grain that the incumbents secured cheaply.

items.label: Paying staff the award wage that applies to every distiller
items.explanation: Every distiller pays it, so it doesn't favour the incumbents.

items.label: Regular customers who stay with an established brand unless a newcomer offers a large discount
items.explanation: The newcomer must pay, in discounts, for a switching cost that the incumbents' customers carry.

items.label: Paying the same excise duty on every bottle sold
items.explanation: The duty is identical for entrant and incumbent, so it is large but not a barrier.

questions.prompt: A would-be entrant to a city's food-truck trade (invented) says that the permit system is a heavy barrier. An established operator says the permit system is light. A reviewer paid by neither has not yet reported. What should you do first?
hints: Both speakers describe the same process. What does each have to gain from the way it describes it?
Whose account would carry the most weight if neither side had a stake?
questions.onCorrect: An account from a party with a stake is evidence of what it wants believed as well as of what happened, so an independent view carries the most weight.

acceptedIdeas: Ask what each speaker stands to gain from its account, since both have a stake, and wait for the review
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ask what each speaker stands to gain from its account, since both have a stake, and wait for the review

choices.label: Take the established operator's view, since it knows how the permit process works from long experience
Ask what each speaker stands to gain from its account, since both have a stake, and wait for the review
Take the midpoint of the two accounts, since the truth must lie somewhere halfway between the two of them

misconceptions.feedback: Experience is useful, but the operator is also the party that gains if the barrier looks low. Its account needs the same scrutiny as the entrant's.
Accounts aren't numbers to be averaged. One of them may simply be right, and the way to find out is an independent weighing.

questions.prompt: A small vineyard (invented) sells almost all its grapes to one large winery that has many other vineyards to buy from, and its grapes must be picked and sold within days. A second vineyard (invented) grows a rare variety that three wineries want. Which has less bargaining power, and why?
hints: Count each grower's alternatives, and ask what share of its crop each buyer takes.
A crop that must be sold within days weakens a grower's ability to wait for a better offer.
questions.onCorrect: Alternatives, share of output and perishability all point the same way here, so the first vineyard has the weaker hand.

acceptedIdeas: The first, because it relies on one buyer with other places to turn, and its crop can't wait
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first, because it relies on one buyer with other places to turn, and its crop can't wait

choices.label: The second, because a rare variety is worth less when several wineries compete to buy it from the grower
Neither, because bargaining power depends only on how large each firm happens to be
The first, because it relies on one buyer with other places to turn, and its crop can't wait

misconceptions.feedback: Several buyers wanting the same rare crop raises the grower's power, because the grower has alternatives and the buyers don't.
The ACCC's factors are alternatives, the share of output a buyer takes and how quickly the product spoils, and not size alone.

questions.prompt: Wesfarmers says that keeping prices low is possible only when it keeps its costs low. Why does a firm that wants to hold low prices need more than a pricing decision?
hints: Think about what a low price does to the margin on each sale, unless something else changes.
A price can be changed in an afternoon. What can't?
questions.onCorrect: A price is a decision and a cost is the result of how the firm works, so lasting low prices need low-cost activities behind them.

acceptedIdeas: Because a price is held only if costs sit low enough to earn a return, which takes activities built for it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because a price is held only if costs sit low enough to earn a return, which takes activities built for it

choices.label: Because a low price is only a promise, so the firm must advertise heavily before customers will believe it
Because rivals copy a price cut at once, so the firm must keep changing its prices to stay one step ahead
Because a price is held only if costs sit low enough to earn a return, which takes activities built for it

misconceptions.feedback: The problem is the margin that a low price leaves, and advertising doesn't change it. The firm needs costs low enough that the price still pays.
A rival can match a price. Whether the firm can go on charging it depends on its costs, which are much harder for a rival to match than a price tag.

questions.prompt: A budget inn chain (invented) wants to keep a low-cost position. Which of its possible features fit that position, and which belong to a full-service position?
hints: Ask for each feature whether it lowers the cost of serving a guest or adds to it.
A low-cost position keeps products standard, keeps assets busy and drops what the customer isn't paying for.
questions.onCorrect: Each feature of a cost position removes cost or keeps assets busy, so features that add personal service belong to a full-service position.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Low-cost: the standard rooms, quick turnover and no restaurant. Full-service: the concierge desk, the custom decoration and the spa and bar.

items.label: Standard rooms of one size, reset to the same checklist each day
items.explanation: A standard product with little customisation keeps operating costs low.

items.label: Rooms filled through the week by quick check-in and check-out
items.explanation: Keeping the assets busy is the first source of low cost.

items.label: No restaurant on site, with vending machines instead
items.explanation: It removes a whole set of costs that a low-cost guest isn't paying for.

items.label: A concierge desk staffed around the clock
items.explanation: Personal service adds cost in return for a higher price.

items.label: Rooms decorated differently, with fittings chosen for each guest's tastes
items.explanation: Customisation is what a low-cost position limits.

items.label: A spa and a bar open to every guest
items.explanation: They add costs that only a premium price can pay for.

questions.prompt: What does the ACCC say followed the 2011 campaign to win Qantas's corporate customers?
hints: Think about which activities the low-cost formula depends on, and which of them business travellers wouldn't accept.
Ask where Qantas was strongest and most profitable, and what it would do when a rival came after those customers.
questions.onCorrect: A firm that moves into a rival's strongest segment meets the rival where it is best defended, and it must add costs its old formula avoided.

acceptedIdeas: It met Qantas head-on for its profitable corporate customers, and the fight over share proved unsustainable
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It met Qantas head-on for its profitable corporate customers, and the fight over share proved unsustainable

choices.label: It found a niche that Qantas had left unserved, and so it escaped any direct competition for several years
It met Qantas head-on for its profitable corporate customers, and the fight over share proved unsustainable
It became a cost leader in business travel, because adding business services lowered its costs on every seat

misconceptions.feedback: The ACCC says the move brought Virgin into more direct competition with Qantas, including for the corporate segment. That is the opposite of finding an unserved niche.
Services for business travellers are a differentiation feature, and they add cost. They don't lower unit costs, and they pull against the low-cost formula.

questions.prompt: A commentator says that Virgin Australia's 2020 choice to target the middle of the market is exactly the stuck-in-the-middle position Porter warned about. What does this extract let you say?
hints: Look for any result in the extract, such as profit or market share. Is there one?
Ask what the extract does record, and whether that is the same as a verdict on the position.

extracts.text: The new strategy employed by Virgin Australia has had several consequences for competition. While Virgin Australia continues to seek to attract business travellers, its new offering based around lower airfares but without complimentary meals has likely meant that Qantas faces less direct competition in the premium corporate customer segment. Separately, with a less diverse fleet of aircraft, Virgin Australia is less capable of directly servicing certain routes, especially in regional areas.
extracts.who: ACCC, Airline competition in Australia, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A report by Australia's competition regulator

questions.onCorrect: The ACCC records what the position costs the airline and what it gives Qantas. A verdict on whether it works needs results that the extract doesn't give.

acceptedIdeas: That it names real costs of the position but gives no result for Virgin's profit, so the claim is not shown
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That it names real costs of the position but gives no result for Virgin's profit, so the claim is not shown

choices.label: That it names real costs of the position but gives no result for Virgin's profit, so the claim is not shown
That the claim is shown, since the ACCC lists costs of the position and any costly position is a failed one
That the claim is refuted, since Virgin Australia survived and later research favours firms that combine low cost and difference

misconceptions.feedback: Every position has costs, including successful ones. The extract names consequences and gives no outcome for Virgin's profit, so it can't show that the position failed.
The extract says nothing about how Virgin fared, and the later research is general evidence that gives no verdict on one airline, so the claim stays untested.

questions.prompt: A regional bank (invented) serves only veterinary practices. It builds its credit and advice around how a practice earns, and it charges more than the big banks. Which generic strategy is it following?
hints: Check the scope first: does the bank serve most segments or one? Then check the basis of its advantage: price or something else?
A premium price for an offer built around one segment is the signature of one of the two focus strategies.
questions.onCorrect: Narrow scope plus an offer built for that segment's needs, sold above the going price, is a differentiation focus.

acceptedIdeas: Differentiation focus, because it serves one segment with an offer built around that segment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Differentiation focus, because it serves one segment with an offer built around that segment

choices.label: Cost leadership, because it concentrates on one customer type and so should have the lowest costs
Differentiation focus, because it serves one segment with an offer built around that segment
Stuck in the middle, because it serves neither all customers nor the cheapest ones in the market

misconceptions.feedback: A cost leader sells on the lowest price across most segments. This bank charges more and serves a single segment, so it isn't one.
The warning was about firms with no distinct advantage. A narrow scope with an offer built for that segment is a focus, which is a clear position.

questions.prompt: A discount electronics chain (invented) runs bare stores with a narrow range. It plans to win customers who want advice and installation by adding in-store technicians and a premium brand. What does that move cost it, in the terms of this lesson?
hints: Which of the chain's low-cost activities would technicians and a premium brand work against?
Think about who already serves those customers well, and how they will respond.
questions.onCorrect: A move up-market adds costs that the old formula avoided, and it brings a fight with firms that already do the new job well.

acceptedIdeas: Its low-cost formula, because technicians and a premium brand add costs that conflict with it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its low-cost formula, because technicians and a premium brand add costs that conflict with it

choices.label: Its low-cost formula, because technicians and a premium brand add costs that conflict with it
Nothing, because a firm that already has low costs can add whatever service it likes without any trade-off
Its customers, because a discount chain can never sell to anyone who is not a price-sensitive shopper

misconceptions.feedback: Low costs come from specific activities, such as a narrow range and bare stores, and technicians and a premium brand pull against them. Every position has a price.
Nothing makes that impossible. The cost is that the new offer adds expense and sets the chain against rivals already strong in that segment.

questions.prompt: A discount pharmacy chain (invented) refuses to run a loyalty card, saying it would add cost and complexity. Its share has risen since. A manager says the refusal caused the rise. What can you conclude?
hints: Ask what other things could have raised the chain's share over the same period.
Seeing two things together isn't the same as seeing one cause the other.
questions.onCorrect: A case can show that two things coexist, and showing that one caused the other needs a comparison the case doesn't offer.

acceptedIdeas: That the missing card and the rising share coincided, which doesn't show that one caused the other
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the missing card and the rising share coincided, which doesn't show that one caused the other

choices.label: That the refusal caused the rise, since the chain's share kept on growing after the decision was taken
That loyalty cards can never help any retailer, since this discount chain grew without having one
That the missing card and the rising share coincided, which doesn't show that one caused the other

misconceptions.feedback: Growth after a decision isn't evidence that the decision caused it. Many other things changed over the same years, and nothing here tests the refusal.
One chain growing without a card says nothing about retailers with other strategies, and a card may suit a firm whose position depends on it.

questions.prompt: A low-cost furniture retailer (invented) is considering six moves. Which fit its low-cost position, and which work against it?
hints: For each move, ask whether it lowers the cost of each sale or adds to it.
A cost position keeps products standard, overheads low and assets busy.
questions.onCorrect: Moves that standardise the product, keep overheads low or keep assets busy fit a cost position, and moves that add personal service or customisation work against it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fits: flat-packs, a few standard models and warehouse stores in low-rent areas. Works against: home design visits, expensive showrooms and made-to-order sofas.

items.label: Selling flat-packed furniture that customers assemble themselves
items.explanation: It cuts handling and delivery costs and keeps the product standard.

items.label: Offering free home design visits to every shopper
items.explanation: A personal service adds cost on each sale and sits with a premium offer.

items.label: Limiting the range to a few standard models made in large runs
items.explanation: Long runs of standard products lower the cost of each item.

items.label: Opening showrooms in the most expensive shopping streets
items.explanation: High rents add overhead that the retailer would have to pass on in its prices.

items.label: Building large warehouse stores in low-rent areas
items.explanation: Cheap sites keep overheads low.

items.label: Making each sofa to order in the customer's chosen fabric
items.explanation: Customisation is what a cost position limits.

questions.prompt: Atlassian's annual report describes its sales model in these words. What can an analyst conclude about whether it is a sustained advantage?
hints: Separate what the extract says Atlassian does from what it says about rivals.
An advantage is sustained when copying it costs a rival more than it cost you. Does the extract say anything about that?

extracts.text: By focusing on an automated, easy-to-use web-based purchasing process, we enable customer self-service and data-driven targeting. This approach means we do not have to solely rely on a traditional, commissioned direct sales force until a customer reaches a specific size, thanks to the automation and efficiency built into our sales model.
extracts.who: Atlassian Corporation, FY2026 Annual Report on Form 10-K
extracts.kind: A company's annual report to investors, describing its own business

questions.onCorrect: A firm's own account shows what it does and values. Whether a rival could copy it is a separate question that needs its own evidence.

acceptedIdeas: That it is valuable to Atlassian, while whether rivals can copy it isn't in the source and has to be tested
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That it is valuable to Atlassian, while whether rivals can copy it isn't in the source and has to be tested

choices.label: That it is sustained, because Atlassian describes it as central to the business and says it has worked for years
That it is valuable to Atlassian, while whether rivals can copy it isn't in the source and has to be tested
That it is only parity, because every software company sells over the web in much the same way

misconceptions.feedback: The extract doesn't say it has worked for years or that rivals can't match it. A firm's description of its model isn't a test of whether it can be copied.
Nothing in the extract says what other software companies do. A claim about rivals' practice needs evidence that this source doesn't give.

questions.prompt: The ACCC traces part of the Qantas Group's position to the legacy this extract describes. Which reason for costly imitation does it best match?
hints: Ask what made the access cheap for Qantas, and whether a new airline could be in that position now.
Compare the three reasons: a moment in history, a tangle of relationships or a legal right. Which does the extract describe?

extracts.text: Qantas benefited from merging with Australian Airlines in 1992, which was one of only 2 airlines (along with Ansett Australia) permitted to operate domestic flights prior to market liberalisation in the 1990s. This legacy provided Qantas with advantages such as the early establishment of routes as well as access to both airport terminals and take‑off and landing slots.
extracts.who: ACCC, Airline competition in Australia, final report (© Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A report by Australia's competition regulator

questions.onCorrect: Access won when only two airlines could fly domestically can't be bought now, so copying it costs a rival far more than it cost Qantas.

acceptedIdeas: Unique historical conditions, since the access came from a moment that can't recur
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Unique historical conditions, since the access came from a moment that can't recur

choices.label: Unique historical conditions, since the access came from a moment that can't recur
Social complexity, because the advantage rests on culture and relationships among the staff
Patents, because Qantas holds exclusive legal rights over its network of routes and terminals

misconceptions.feedback: Social complexity would be an advantage built from teamwork and relationships. The ACCC describes access to routes, terminals and slots won at a moment that can't recur.
The extract describes a head start from market rules before liberalisation. It doesn't describe a legal right that an authority has certified to Qantas as an invention.

questions.prompt: A gym chain (invented) is the first in its city to install a new kind of training equipment that members love. The equipment is on sale to any gym at the same price. What does VRIO say the chain has?
hints: Run the four questions in order, and stop at the first no.
Ask what rivals would have to pay to get the same equipment, compared with what the chain paid.
questions.onCorrect: A valuable, rare resource that is cheap to copy gives a lead only until rivals buy it, after which the firm is level with them.

acceptedIdeas: A temporary advantage at most, since rivals can buy the same equipment at no disadvantage
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A temporary advantage at most, since rivals can buy the same equipment at no disadvantage

choices.label: A sustained advantage, because anything valuable and rare will hold up against rivals
A permanent disadvantage, because rivals gain the same equipment at no extra cost to them
A temporary advantage at most, since rivals can buy the same equipment at no disadvantage

misconceptions.feedback: That stops after two questions. The chain is rare only until rivals buy the equipment, and nothing about the equipment is costly to copy.
Rivals matching the chain leaves it level with them, which is parity and not a loss. The chain keeps its lead until they buy, and then it has none.

questions.prompt: Kodak struggled with the move from film to digital photography, as this extract records. What does the extract let you say about Kodak and the four VRIO questions?
hints: Which of the four questions does the extract give any evidence about?
Ask whether the extract explains why Kodak struggled, or only that it did.

extracts.text: Kodak began to struggle financially in the late 1990s as a result of increasing competition from Fujifilm. The company also struggled with the transition from film to digital photography, even though Kodak had invented integral color image sensors and had developed the first self-contained digital camera prototype in the mid-1970s.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Kodak" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: A general encyclopaedia article

questions.onCorrect: The extract shows Kodak had something rare, and the later struggle leaves the other questions open. Holding a resource doesn't show it was used or couldn't be copied.

acceptedIdeas: That Kodak was first with the technology, while the extract shows nothing about copying or about how well Kodak used it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That Kodak was first with the technology, while the extract shows nothing about copying or about how well Kodak used it

choices.label: That Kodak failed to organise itself, since it invented the first digital camera prototype and then still struggled badly
That the technology wasn't valuable, since a firm that really held it could not have struggled afterwards anyway
That Kodak was first with the technology, while the extract shows nothing about copying or about how well Kodak used it

misconceptions.feedback: The extract gives no reason for the struggle. Reading a failure to organise out of the result is a leap, because the same facts fit other explanations too.
Being first with a technology and then struggling doesn't show the technology lacked value. The extract says Kodak struggled with the transition, and it doesn't say why.

questions.prompt: In its FY26 results Qantas reported that Qantas Loyalty had 18.9 million members and an operating margin of 21.7% on $2.9b of revenue, against a Group Domestic margin of 13%. All are company figures. Which statement do they support?
hints: A margin compares profit with revenue. Does it also tell you the total profit?
Which of the four VRIO questions would a margin help with, and which would it leave open?
questions.onCorrect: The figures compare margins and leave imitation untested, which needs evidence about what rivals would have to spend to match the program.

acceptedIdeas: That loyalty's reported margin is higher than domestic flying's, and the figures don't show whether rivals could copy it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That loyalty's reported margin is higher than domestic flying's, and the figures don't show whether rivals could copy it

choices.label: That the program is a sustained advantage, since a margin as high as 21.7% could not survive imitation by any rival
That loyalty's reported margin is higher than domestic flying's, and the figures don't show whether rivals could copy it
That Qantas earns more in total from the program than from flying, since the program's margin is so much higher

misconceptions.feedback: A margin is an outcome. Whether a high one survives depends on how costly imitation is, and the figures say nothing about that.
A margin is profit per dollar of revenue. The figures give no totals for flying, and a higher margin on a smaller revenue can be a smaller profit.

questions.prompt: A family restaurant (invented) is known for dishes that rivals can't reproduce, even after hiring away one of its cooks. The cooks have worked as a team for twenty years. Which reason for costly imitation fits best?
hints: Hiring one cook didn't work. What is it that the rivals couldn't hire?
Match the case to a reason: a moment in history, a tangle of relationships, an unclear cause or a legal right.
questions.onCorrect: When an advantage lives in how people work together, buying one part of it doesn't buy the whole.

acceptedIdeas: Social complexity, because the advantage lives in a team, which can't be hired in
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Social complexity, because the advantage lives in a team, which can't be hired in

choices.label: Patents, because the restaurant's recipes must be legally protected from copying
Social complexity, because the advantage lives in a team, which can't be hired in
Unique historical conditions, because the restaurant was the first of its kind in its city

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the case says the recipes are patented. The rivals' trouble is that hiring one cook doesn't bring the team with them.
Being first isn't the reason given in the case. The advantage lies in twenty years of cooks working together, which is a social matter.

questions.prompt: A mining company (invented) holds a rich deposit that no rival can reach and that would cost any rival a fortune to match. Its structures and pay reward short-term output, so the mine is run in ways that damage the deposit's value. Which VRIO question is the firm failing?
hints: Check the first three questions against the case. Which does the firm pass?
Which question is about structures, controls and incentives?
questions.onCorrect: A resource can pass the first three questions and still pay nothing if the firm's structures and pay point away from using it.

acceptedIdeas: Whether it is organised to capture the value, since its pay and structures work against using the deposit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whether it is organised to capture the value, since its pay and structures work against using the deposit

choices.label: Whether the resource is valuable, since a resource that is run badly can't really be valuable to the firm
Whether the resource is costly to imitate, since poor management would make the deposit easy for any rival to copy
Whether it is organised to capture the value, since its pay and structures work against using the deposit

misconceptions.feedback: The deposit is rich, so it is valuable. The failure lies in how the firm uses it, which is the fourth question.
The case says matching the deposit would cost any rival a fortune, so imitation is costly. Management quality doesn't change that.

questions.prompt: A listed firm (invented) tells investors that its operating margin is above its industry's average and credits its in-house training academy. For each item, does the statement tell you this, or does it leave it open?
hints: For each item, ask whether the firm's own words contain it, or whether it needs evidence from somewhere else.
A firm saying that something explains its result shows what it believes, and doesn't show that it is true.
questions.onCorrect: A firm's own statement shows what it reports and believes, and it leaves open the cost of copying, the cause and the future.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The statement tells you the firm's reported margin and the firm's own credit to the academy. It leaves open the cost of copying, the cause, the future of the margin and the firm's organisation.

items.label: That the firm reports a margin above its industry's average
items.explanation: It is what the firm says about its own result.

items.label: That the firm credits its training academy
items.explanation: It is the firm's stated explanation, which tells you what it believes.

items.label: Whether a rival could build a similar academy at the same cost
items.explanation: Imitability needs evidence about the cost of copying, and the statement gives none.

items.label: Whether the academy, and not something else, causes the higher margin
items.explanation: A firm's credit isn't a test of the cause.

items.label: Whether the margin will stay above average in later years
items.explanation: A margin from one period doesn't show that the lead will last.

items.label: Whether the firm is organised to use what the academy produces
items.explanation: The statement says nothing about structures, controls or pay.

questions.prompt: A supermarket pays a supplier $1.00 for a tin of tomatoes and sells it for $1.50 (an invented example). A news story calls the 50 cents the shop's profit on the tin. What does that leave out?
hints: Ask what the shop has to pay for besides the tin itself.
The $1.00 covers the tin. Who pays the people who stock the shelf and the landlord who owns the building?
questions.onCorrect: The 50 cents is the price gap on one product. The shop's running costs come out of it before anything is left as profit.

acceptedIdeas: The cost of running the shop, such as wages and rent, which has to be paid out of the 50 cents
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cost of running the shop, such as wages and rent, which has to be paid out of the 50 cents

choices.label: The cost of running the shop, such as wages and rent, which has to be paid out of the 50 cents
Nothing, since whatever a shop charges above what it paid for a product is its profit
The supplier's own costs, which the shop must also cover before it keeps any of the 50 cents
Inflation, which makes the 50 cents buy less each year and so shrinks the real profit on the tin

misconceptions.feedback: A shop has costs besides the products it buys. Staff, rent and power are paid from the gap between the two prices, so the gap is not yet profit.
The shop's $1.00 already pays for the supplier's costs and the supplier's own margin. The costs missing from the story are the shop's.
Inflation changes what money buys, but it does not turn a price gap into a profit. The gap still has to pay the shop's running costs first.

questions.prompt: The ACCC looked at ALDI, Coles and Woolworths over five years, a period in which their costs rose and in which they may have acted to moderate that growth. What does the ACCC conclude from the EBIT margins?
hints: Read the verbs. Does 'suggest' mean the same as 'prove'?
The extract makes two points, one about what EBIT margins suggest and one about what product margins appear to have done. Which option has both?
questions.onCorrect: The ACCC reads stable or rising EBIT margins as a sign that savings were kept, and says higher product margins appear to have contributed.

acceptedIdeas: That the chains kept part of their savings, and that higher product margins appear to have helped
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the chains kept part of their savings, and that higher product margins appear to have helped

choices.label: That the chains passed every saving on to shoppers, so the rise in their prices reflects rising costs alone
That the chains' EBIT margins rose every year, which proves that they acted unlawfully in setting prices
That the chains kept part of their savings, and that higher product margins appear to have helped
That EBIT margin and product margin are one and the same measure, so the two rises are a single finding

misconceptions.feedback: The extract says the opposite: stable or rising EBIT margins suggest the full benefit of the savings did not reach shoppers.
The ACCC's wording is cautious. Margins that were stable or increasing suggest a conclusion, they do not prove one, and the extract says nothing about the law.
They are different measures. The extract treats the rise in product margins as one contributor to the rise in EBIT margins, which is a separate claim.

extracts.text: Stable or increasing EBIT margins over this period suggest that – even if ALDI, Coles and Woolworths have acted to moderate cost growth – they have not passed on to consumers the full benefit of savings from those initiatives. Increasing product margins appear to have contributed to the increasing EBIT margins.
extracts.who: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, Supermarkets inquiry final report (CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A final report of a public inquiry, written for government and the public

questions.prompt: Quenda Biscuits (an invented supplier) raises its wholesale price. A big chain accepts only if its retail margin is held or raised in percentage terms, and the shelf price then rises by more than the wholesale price did. The ACCC reported a pattern of this kind at Coles and Woolworths. What does it say the pattern indicates?
hints: Compare the size of the shelf price rise with the size of the wholesale price rise. What would a pure pass-through look like?
Ask who gains when the retail margin widens by more than the cost rise required, and what that says about who has the stronger position.
questions.onCorrect: A retailer that can widen its own margin while passing on a cost is acting from a position of some strength in the chain.

acceptedIdeas: That the chains have some market power in retail, since they can widen their margin and pass a cost on
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the chains have some market power in retail, since they can widen their margin and pass a cost on

choices.label: That the chains have some market power in retail, since they can widen their margin and pass a cost on
That the supplier holds the market power, because it managed to push its whole price rise through to shoppers
That the chain made an error, since a shelf price ought to rise by exactly the amount the wholesale price did
That the chain has no influence over its own margin, since it only passes on the cost it is given

misconceptions.feedback: The extract says the chains' ability to widen the retail margin indicates their market power. Nothing in it describes the supplier forcing a rise through.
Nothing requires shelf prices to track wholesale prices dollar for dollar. The ACCC reads the extra widening as evidence about the chain's position.
A retail margin that grows by more than a cost rise needs is a margin the chain has shaped. The ACCC says that ability indicates market power.

extracts.text: Coles’ and Woolworths’ apparent ability to increase retail margins for packaged grocery products by more than is necessary to accommodate a wholesale price increase indicates they have – and sometimes exercise – a level of market power in retail markets.
extracts.who: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, Supermarkets inquiry final report (CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A final report of a public inquiry, written for government and the public

questions.prompt: Merriwa Flour Mills (invented) mills grain and sells flour by the tonne to bakeries. Its EBIT margin is far below the bakeries' EBIT margins, and a commentator concludes that Merriwa is badly run. What does the ACCC's reading of Metcash suggest about that conclusion?
hints: Metcash earns much lower margins than Coles. Did the ACCC say that made Metcash badly run?
If every link's margin should look alike, why would a wholesaler and a retailer be compared? Ask who the fair comparison is with.
questions.onCorrect: Each link has its own usual range of margins, so a fair comparison is with firms doing the same job.

acceptedIdeas: A margin belongs partly to the link, so compare Merriwa with other millers before calling it weak
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A margin belongs partly to the link, so compare Merriwa with other millers before calling it weak

choices.label: The commentator is right, since a margin far below its customers' margins always means weaker management
A margin belongs partly to the link, so compare Merriwa with other millers before calling it weak
EBIT margin is a measure for retailers, so it says nothing about a miller and should not be quoted
Merriwa's margin should match the bakeries', so the gap shows that it is underpricing its flour

misconceptions.feedback: A different position in the chain can produce a different normal margin, as the ACCC says of Metcash. A gap alone does not show weak management.
EBIT margin can be worked out for any firm. The ACCC uses it for Metcash, a wholesaler. What matters is what you compare it with.
Nothing makes margins equal along a chain. Links do different jobs, and each has its own usual range.

questions.prompt: Skerry Air (invented) publishes segment margins of 6% for Passenger flights, 17% for Cargo and 11% for Charter. A student writes four conclusions. Which one does the table alone support?
hints: A segment margin is a share of that segment's own revenue. Does the table give any revenue?
Test each conclusion by asking whether it needs dollars of revenue or capital. Which one does not?
questions.onCorrect: A segment margin ranks the parts by what they keep per dollar of revenue, and nothing more.

acceptedIdeas: Cargo keeps more of each dollar of its own revenue than Passenger flights do
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cargo keeps more of each dollar of its own revenue than Passenger flights do

choices.label: Cargo earns the airline more profit in dollars than Passenger flights do
The airline as a whole keeps about 11% of its revenue, the average of the three margins
The airline should put its next dollar of capital into Cargo, because Cargo has the highest margin
Cargo keeps more of each dollar of its own revenue than Passenger flights do

misconceptions.feedback: A margin is a share of a part's own revenue. A part with a high margin and small revenue can earn fewer dollars than a part with a low margin and large revenue.
Each part counts in proportion to its revenue, so the whole-firm margin is not the plain average. The table gives no revenue to weight it with.
Margins do not show how much capital each part uses, so the table cannot say where the next dollar earns most.

questions.prompt: Bluegum & Co (an invented maker) sells packaged soup to a big supermarket chain, and the chain asks it to contribute to a promotion each quarter. Using the ACCC's findings on supplier funding, which reading of the maker's position is best supported?
hints: Follow the money. In supplier funding, who pays whom?
Ask whose margin gets bigger when the payment is made, and whose gets smaller.
questions.onCorrect: A payment from supplier to retailer lifts the retailer's margin and lowers the supplier's.

acceptedIdeas: Its margin on a tin may be thinner than the list price suggests, since promotion payments come out of it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its margin on a tin may be thinner than the list price suggests, since promotion payments come out of it

choices.label: Its margin is unaffected, because the promotion is the chain's own cost and shoppers end up paying for it
Its margin is protected, since supplier funding is the way the chain pays the maker for shelf space
Its margin on a tin may be thinner than the list price suggests, since promotion payments come out of it
The payments show that the maker holds the stronger position, since the chain only asks those it needs

misconceptions.feedback: Supplier funding is a payment from the supplier to the retailer. The maker pays it, so it comes out of the maker's margin.
The ACCC describes supplier funding the other way round: suppliers pay the chains, and it adds to the chains' margins.
The ACCC finds that supplier funding contributes significantly to the chains' margins, which fits their position being the stronger one.

questions.prompt: Halden Group (invented) reports segment margins of 3% for Shipping, 9% for Warehousing and 24% for Software. A reader draws six conclusions from the margins. Which of them do the margins alone support?
hints: A segment margin is a share of a part's own revenue. Ask of each conclusion whether it only compares those shares.
Dollars of profit, a whole-group average and a decision about capital each need something the margins do not contain. What is it in each case?
questions.onCorrect: A segment margin compares what parts keep per dollar of their own revenue, and it does not give dollars, group totals or capital.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The margins support the three rankings of what each part keeps per revenue dollar. The dollar profit, the group margin and the use of capital all need revenue or capital figures.

items.label: Software keeps the most of each dollar of revenue it earns
items.explanation: That is exactly what a segment margin measures.

items.label: Shipping keeps the least of each dollar of revenue it earns
items.explanation: The three margins rank the parts by the share of their own revenue they keep.

items.label: Warehousing keeps more of each revenue dollar than Shipping does
items.explanation: Nine cents in the dollar against three, so the ranking follows from the margins.

items.label: Software earns the group the most profit in dollars
items.explanation: A high margin on a small revenue can still be a small profit, so dollars of revenue are needed.

items.label: The group's overall margin is the average of the three margins
items.explanation: Each part counts in proportion to its revenue, which the margins do not give.

items.label: The next dollar of capital should go into Software
items.explanation: A margin leaves out how much capital each part uses to earn it.

questions.prompt: A columnist writes that Yarran Pharmacy (invented) keeps a third of every sale as profit, because its product margin is 33%. Its EBIT margin is 4%. The ACCC says the following about product margins. What is the fairest view of the columnist's claim?
hints: Which costs has the 33% already taken out, and which costs has the 4% taken out as well?
The extract says product margins give an indication. Ask of what, and compared with what.
questions.onCorrect: A product margin shows what a shop makes over what it paid for a product. It runs above the profit the business keeps.

acceptedIdeas: The 33% overstates profit, yet it still shows what the pharmacy makes on each product above its cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 33% overstates profit, yet it still shows what the pharmacy makes on each product above its cost

choices.label: The 33% overstates profit, yet it still shows what the pharmacy makes on each product above its cost
The claim is sound, since a product margin is the share of every sale that a shop keeps as its profit
The claim is empty, since a product margin tells us nothing at all about what a business actually earns
Both figures are profit margins, so together they show that Yarran earns somewhere between 4% and 33%

misconceptions.feedback: A product margin leaves out wages, rent and the other costs of running the business, so it runs above profit. The 4% EBIT margin is nearer the profit.
The extract says product margins give an indication of what a shop makes on each product compared with what it paid. That is limited, and it is not nothing.
They are different measures. One counts only the cost of the goods, and the other counts the costs of running the business, so they do not mark the ends of one range.

extracts.text: Nonetheless, product margins provide an indication of the profit a supermarket makes on each product compared to what they paid for it.
extracts.who: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, Supermarkets inquiry final report (CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A final report of a public inquiry, written for government and the public

questions.prompt: Frostline (invented) is a ski resort with three businesses: lift tickets, a ski school and a hire shop. The ski school reports the highest margin, and nearly all its pupils hold a Frostline lift ticket. A rival says it will copy the ski school alone and earn the same margin. What does that reading miss?
hints: Ask where the school's pupils come from, and what happens to its revenue if the rival has no lifts.
A margin describes a part as it sits inside its firm. Can it be lifted out unchanged?
questions.onCorrect: A part of a firm may earn its margin because of the other parts, so copying it alone may not copy the margin.

acceptedIdeas: The school's margin may depend on the lifts supplying pupils, so copying the school may not copy it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The school's margin may depend on the lifts supplying pupils, so copying the school may not copy it

choices.label: Nothing, since a segment margin belongs to the activity itself, so any firm running it earns the same
The school's margin may depend on the lifts supplying pupils, so copying the school may not copy it
That the school's margin is overstated, because segment margins are never reliable enough to compare
That a ski school cannot be run without lifts, since lessons are always sold together with tickets

misconceptions.feedback: A segment's margin depends on the whole firm around it as well as on the activity. Here the pupils come from the lifts.
Segment margins are fair measures of what a part keeps per dollar of its own revenue. The question is whether the part can be separated from the rest.
That goes beyond what is given. The point is only that this school's pupils mostly come from the lifts, so its margin may not travel alone.

questions.prompt: A new payments app, Fernpay (invented), is free to join and lets you pay another person only if they have it too. You are deciding whether to sign up. Which fact about it matters most?
hints: Fernpay works only between two people who both have it. Who has to be on it for it to be useful to you?
Compare a toaster, which works the same no matter how many people own one, with this app. What is different?
questions.onCorrect: A product whose value rises with the number of others using it is worth most when your own contacts are on it.

acceptedIdeas: How many of the people you pay or get paid by have already joined
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How many of the people you pay or get paid by have already joined

choices.label: How many features it offers compared with the payment apps you already use
How many of the people you pay or get paid by have already joined
How much it costs Fernpay to run each account that joins the app
How many people in total have downloaded it, whoever those people are

misconceptions.feedback: Features count for something, but this app is useful only between two people who both have it. A rich app with none of your contacts is of no use to you.
That is a cost to the company and not a benefit to you. Its value to you depends on who else is on it.
Downloads by strangers add little. The value to you comes from the people you actually pay.

questions.prompt: Each of these cases is invented. Which kind of effect is at work in each?
hints: Ask whether the case is about what a user gains from other users, or about what a unit costs the firm to make.
If it is about other users, is it one group of users, or two groups who each need the other?
questions.onCorrect: A direct effect comes from users of one product, an indirect effect from two groups needing each other, and a scale economy from a lower cost per unit.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Direct: the video-call app and the language app. Indirect: the games console and the marketplace app. Scale economy: the bakery and the printing firm.

items.label: A video-call app is useful only if the people you want to call have it too
items.explanation: Each user gains from the other users of the same product.

items.label: A language app where you practise with other learners, so each new learner is a possible partner
items.explanation: Each user gains from every other user of the same product.

items.label: A games console: more games draw more players, and more players draw more game makers
items.explanation: Two groups, players and game makers, each gain from the other's size.

items.label: A marketplace app where more sellers draw buyers and more buyers draw sellers
items.explanation: Two interdependent groups, each valuing the other's growth.

items.label: A bakery's cost per loaf falls as it bakes more loaves in the same ovens
items.explanation: The firm's cost per unit falls with output, and no customer is better off for others' use.

items.label: A printing firm's cost per page falls as it runs longer print jobs
items.explanation: Again it is the firm's average cost that falls, which is a supply-side effect.

questions.prompt: A market can tip only if three conditions hold. The ACCC found the following about the App Store and the Play Store in Australia. Which condition for tipping does it weaken?
hints: The extract says most top apps are available in both stores. Which side of the platform is using both at once?
Using more than one platform at the same time has a name. Which condition is it part of?
questions.onCorrect: When developers can easily list on both stores, using both is cheap on that side, which weakens a push to tip.

acceptedIdeas: That users and developers face high costs of multihoming
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That users and developers face high costs of multihoming

choices.label: That network benefits must outweigh the value of differences between products
That consumers must face high costs of switching between the two stores
That users and developers face high costs of multihoming
That a market must contain a network effect before it can tip at all

misconceptions.feedback: That condition is about how much users value network size against differences. Developers listing on both stores says nothing about it.
The extract is about the apps available in each store. It does not say how costly it is for a consumer to switch phones.
App stores do have strong indirect network effects. The extract bears on whether using both is costly, not on whether a network effect exists.

extracts.text: The ACCC’s Report on App Marketplaces found that around 90% or more of the top 100 apps available in Australia in each of the App Store and the Play Store, were also available in the other app marketplace.
extracts.who: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, Digital platform services inquiry final report (CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A final report of a public inquiry, written for government and the public

questions.prompt: Microsoft's new operating system faced a start-up problem: users wanted applications, and software firms wanted users. The extract describes how it responded. What was the logic of the move?
hints: Who got the steep discount, and what did that group then do?
The platform needs both users and applications. Which side did Microsoft decide to pay to arrive first?
questions.onCorrect: Cheap tools drew developers in, and the applications they built made the platform worth more to users.

acceptedIdeas: It subsidised the side whose arrival would draw in the other, so the platform became worth more
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It subsidised the side whose arrival would draw in the other, so the platform became worth more

choices.label: It charged developers the same as users, so that neither side felt it was treated unfairly
It waited until applications existed on their own, then priced the toolkit to match their value
It matched Apple's price for the toolkit, since a platform must follow its rival's price on everything
It subsidised the side whose arrival would draw in the other, so the platform became worth more

misconceptions.feedback: The extract says developers were charged less, relative to Apple. Equal prices would not have lowered the barrier for developers.
The extract describes a discount that made applications appear. It did not wait for them.
The extract says Microsoft's toolkit was discounted relative to Apple's pricing, which is the opposite of matching it.

extracts.text: In the operating systems market for home computers, created in the early 1980s with the introduction of the Macintosh and IBM PC, Microsoft decided to steeply discount the software development toolkit (SDKs) for its operating system, relative to Apple pricing at that time, lowering the barrier to entry to the home computer market for software businesses. This resulted in a big increase in the number of applications being developed for home computers

extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.prompt: The ACCC describes the position of customers of cloud infrastructure services in this extract. What kind of evidence about lock-in does it give?
hints: Look at the verb in the extract. Does it say customers are locked in, or that they may face costs?
A cost of leaving is one kind of evidence and a count of customers who stay is another. Which one does the extract give?
questions.onCorrect: A switching cost is a reason to expect lock-in. Whether customers are locked in also depends on what they do.

acceptedIdeas: It names costs of leaving, which are reasons for lock-in, and does not count who has stayed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It names costs of leaving, which are reasons for lock-in, and does not count who has stayed

choices.label: It shows that most cloud customers are locked in, since they so rarely move
It names costs of leaving, which are reasons for lock-in, and does not count who has stayed
It shows that cloud customers are satisfied, since only satisfied customers would pay egress fees
It shows that lock-in is absent, since customers can use several providers at once

misconceptions.feedback: The extract says customers may face high costs of switching. It gives no count of how many stay or move.
Egress fees are charged when data leaves, and they are a cost of moving. They do not measure how pleased a customer is.
The extract says the opposite: it names high impediments to using several providers, including technical barriers and fees.

extracts.text: Existing users of cloud infrastructure services may face high impediments to switching or ‘multihoming’ across different service providers, including technical barriers to interoperability, and high egress fees when moving data out of a cloud ecosystem.
extracts.who: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, Digital platform services inquiry final report (CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A final report of a public inquiry, written for government and the public

questions.prompt: Lorne Chemist (invented) replaces its free loyalty card with a paid annual membership that gives bigger discounts. Using the ACCC's reasoning about free loyalty programs, how is the change likely to affect lock-in?
hints: Why did the ACCC think free programs bind customers weakly? Think about how many a customer can hold.
What does a fee do to the incentive to join several programs at once?
questions.onCorrect: A fee discourages members from joining several programs at once, so a paid program can bind more than a free one.

acceptedIdeas: Lock-in may rise, because the fee gives members a reason not to join rival programs as well
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Lock-in may rise, because the fee gives members a reason not to join rival programs as well

choices.label: Lock-in may rise, because the fee gives members a reason not to join rival programs as well
Lock-in will not change, since a program binds customers only through the size of its discounts
Lock-in will fall, since a fee is a cost of joining and so tends to drive customers away
Lock-in will rise because a paid program holds more data about each of its members
