misconceptions.feedback: The ACCC's reasoning is about multihoming, not discount size. Free programs bind weakly because members can join several.
A fee may lose some members, but those who pay have less reason to hold several programs at once, which is where free programs fail to bind.
The ACCC's reasoning does not rest on data. It rests on the cost of joining discouraging members from joining many programs.

questions.prompt: A consultant says the market for small-business accounting software, with packages such as Penwell Books and Tallis Ledger (both invented), must tip to a single winner because software has network effects. Small firms mostly choose a package for features suited to their trade, and few ever need to share files with another firm. What is the weakest part of the consultant's claim?
hints: The first condition for tipping compares network benefits with the value users put on differences. Which is larger for these firms?
If few firms ever share files with each other, how much does a package gain from being the most popular?
questions.onCorrect: When users value differences between products more than network size, a network effect alone does not tip the market.

acceptedIdeas: It assumes network benefits beat differences, though users here value features far more
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It assumes network benefits beat differences, though users here value features far more

choices.label: It assumes that software can have network effects at all, which software never has
It assumes that switching costs are high, though the case gives no facts about them
It assumes network benefits beat differences, though users here value features far more
It assumes that multihoming is costly, though the case gives no facts about it

misconceptions.feedback: Some software does have network effects. The claim fails here because of how little they matter to these users.
The case gives no facts about switching costs. The facts it does give bear on whether network benefits outweigh the value of differences.
The case gives no facts about multihoming either. The facts it does give bear on network benefits against differences.

questions.prompt: Harbourhost (invented) hosts websites for small businesses. A researcher collects six findings about its customers. For each, is it evidence of satisfaction, evidence of lock-in, or consistent with both?
hints: Ask of each finding whether it would be true of a customer who stays only because leaving costs too much.
A finding that is true of both a happy customer and a trapped one cannot separate the two.
questions.onCorrect: Contentment and staying put fit satisfaction and lock-in alike, while costs of leaving point to lock-in and quality points to satisfaction.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Satisfaction: the independent test and the recommendations. Lock-in: the weeks of work with the export fee, and the add-ons that must be rebought. Both: contentment and few changes of host.

items.label: In an independent test its sites ran faster and were down less often than rivals' sites
items.explanation: It shows quality, and says nothing about what it costs a customer to leave.

items.label: Most customers say they would recommend it to a friend
items.explanation: Recommending is a sign of satisfaction, which is a reason to stay.

items.label: Most customers say they are content with the service
items.explanation: A locked-in customer can be content as well, so the answer fits either.

items.label: Few customers have changed host in five years
items.explanation: Staying fits a happy customer and a trapped one equally well.

items.label: Moving a site means weeks of work and a fee to export its data
items.explanation: These are costs of leaving, which are what lock-in is made of.

items.label: Customers must rebuy the add-ons they have built when they change host
items.explanation: Losing what they have built is a cost of switching.

questions.prompt: Hirelark (invented) is a job site where employers post vacancies and job seekers apply. Most employers post the same vacancy on several sites, and most seekers browse more than one. Which statement is best supported?
hints: Is it one group gaining from itself, or two groups gaining from each other?
Which of the three tipping conditions is weakened when both sides use several sites?
questions.onCorrect: Two groups that each gain from the other give an indirect effect, and cheap use of several sites on both sides makes a tip unlikely.

acceptedIdeas: It has an indirect effect, but the market is unlikely to tip because both sides use several sites
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has an indirect effect, but the market is unlikely to tip because both sides use several sites

choices.label: It has a direct network effect, and the market will tip because seekers gain from other seekers
It has no network effect, because employers and seekers are different groups of people
It has an indirect network effect, so the market will tip because every such effect ends in one winner
It has an indirect effect, but the market is unlikely to tip because both sides use several sites

misconceptions.feedback: The two groups are different, employers and seekers, and each gains from the other. That makes the effect indirect, and seekers gain little from other seekers.
Two groups that value each other's numbers are exactly what an indirect network effect describes.
A network effect does not guarantee a tip. Using several sites at once makes multihoming cheap on both sides, which weakens the push.

questions.prompt: Canva gives its basic design product away and charges for extra features. What is the most plausible reason a firm would choose that price?
hints: A free tier has to be paid for somehow. What would make giving the basic version away cheap, and where would the revenue come from?
Think about what one more user of a piece of software costs the firm, compared with what one more loaf costs a baker.
questions.onCorrect: A free basic product can pay when serving another free user costs little and enough users move up to a paid tier.

acceptedIdeas: Serving one more free user costs it little, and some free users move up to the paid features
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Serving one more free user costs it little, and some free users move up to the paid features

choices.label: The free product is only an advertising expense, since free users almost never become paying customers
Free users cost as much to serve as paying ones, so the free tier is a loss the firm plans to end
Serving one more free user costs it little, and some free users move up to the paid features
A free product locks users in, so the firm can raise the price of the free version later on

misconceptions.feedback: If free users never paid, the free tier would be a pure cost. Freemium works because some of them move up to the paid features.
Freemium suits cases where one more free user costs little. If each cost as much as a paying user, the free tier would not last.
A free version stays free. The money comes from charging for the additional features, not from raising the price of the basic product.

questions.prompt: Passdown (invented) is a new online marketplace for second-hand school uniforms. Parents will list uniforms only if buyers are there, and buyers will come only if many uniforms are listed. Which launch price fits, and why?
hints: The marketplace is worth little until many people are on it. Which launch price helps it get past that point?
Think about which approach reaches many customers quickly, and which waits for the few who will pay most.
questions.onCorrect: A product that is worth more as more people use it can justify a low start, to reach critical mass and keep rivals out.

acceptedIdeas: A low launch price, to reach critical mass quickly and discourage rivals
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A low launch price, to reach critical mass quickly and discourage rivals

choices.label: A low launch price, to reach critical mass quickly and discourage rivals
A high launch price, to take the most from early users before any rival appears
A price set at cost plus a fixed margin, so each user pays what serving them costs
A price held steady while the marketplace grows, because a network needs no pricing strategy

misconceptions.feedback: Skimming suits buyers who want the product badly. Here the product is useless until many users are on it, so a high price would keep the network from forming.
A cost-based price ignores that the product's value comes from the other users. It would not help the marketplace reach critical mass.
A network has to get past critical mass, and price is one of the ways to get there. Leaving it alone leaves that problem unsolved.

questions.prompt: Four invented firms are each weighing a free basic version of their product. Which is best placed to make freemium work?
hints: Freemium depends on what it costs the firm to serve one more free user. Which firm has that cost close to zero?
A free version must leave users something worth paying for. Which firm keeps back features for paying users?
questions.onCorrect: Freemium suits a product that is cheap to copy and keeps something back that free users will pay for.

acceptedIdeas: A note-taking app that costs almost nothing per extra user, with paid team features
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A note-taking app that costs almost nothing per extra user, with paid team features

choices.label: A meal-kit company whose ingredients cost it real money for every free box it ships
A note-taking app that costs almost nothing per extra user, with paid team features
A photo app whose free version already includes every feature the paid version has
A courier that would carry each customer's first ten parcels free, at its normal cost

misconceptions.feedback: Each free box costs the company its ingredients. Freemium works when producing another copy is cheap.
With nothing extra to buy, free users have no reason to pay, and the free version eats into sales of the paid one.
Every free parcel costs the courier a driver and fuel. The cost of serving one more free customer is far from small.

questions.prompt: Gull Island Ferries (invented) sells flexible tickets that can be changed up to departure, and cheaper fixed tickets that cannot. Business travellers mostly buy the flexible ones. What best describes this pricing?
hints: The seats are alike, and the prices differ. What separates the buyers who pay each price?
Is the difference driven by what each seat costs the ferry, or by who is buying it?
questions.onCorrect: When similar seats go to different segments at different prices, the pattern is price discrimination.

acceptedIdeas: Similar seats are priced by the segment that buys them, which is price discrimination
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Similar seats are priced by the segment that buys them, which is price discrimination

choices.label: The fares simply follow cost, since a flexible ticket is dearer to run than a fixed one
It is penetration pricing, because the cheaper fixed ticket is meant to win new riders
It is an error in the timetable, because one seat on one ferry should have a single fare
Similar seats are priced by the segment that buys them, which is price discrimination

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the case says a flexible seat costs more to carry. The gap tracks who is buying, which is a segment, and not what each seat costs.
Penetration is a low launch price to reach many customers. Here two fares are sold side by side to two kinds of buyer.
Selling similar goods at different prices to different segments is a deliberate pricing strategy, and a common one.

questions.prompt: Mallee Sofas (invented) marks every sofa 'was $1,200, now $799' and has done so all year. The ACCC raised a concern about stated comparison prices in its supermarkets inquiry. What do its words say about this kind of pricing?
hints: The ACCC speaks of the 'real' or 'standard' price. What would a shopper need to know to judge a special?
Look at the verbs and nouns. Does the extract say comparison prices are false, or that they raise concerns?
questions.onCorrect: A comparison is only as good as the reference price it points to, and shoppers may find that hard to judge.

acceptedIdeas: That shoppers may not know the real price, so the legitimacy of a comparison can be questioned
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That shoppers may not know the real price, so the legitimacy of a comparison can be questioned

choices.label: That every 'was' price is false, since a seller may never show a second price next to a sale price
That shoppers may not know the real price, so the legitimacy of a comparison can be questioned
That a special is a real saving whenever a price falls, whatever the earlier price had been
That specials show the sellers have agreed their prices with each other in advance

misconceptions.feedback: The extract raises concerns about what the real price is and whether comparisons are legitimate. It does not say that every comparison is false.
The extract is about the opposite worry: that a stated earlier price may not be the real or standard one.
The extract is about shoppers' difficulty in judging comparison prices. It says nothing about sellers agreeing prices.

extracts.text: Information received during the inquiry indicates that 2-price comparison representations can be particularly challenging for consumers, and we consider they are inherently risky for traders. Specific concerns have been raised (particularly in the context of high-low pricing) about what the ‘real’ or ‘standard’ price for grocery products is and, accordingly, the legitimacy of stated comparator prices.
extracts.who: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, Supermarkets inquiry final report (CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A final report of a public inquiry, written for government and the public

questions.prompt: A shopper keeps using one chain's card because the points keep adding up, although a rival's shelf prices on her usual items are lower. Which reading do the ACCC's words support?
hints: The extract says shoppers may rely on mental shortcuts. What would a shortcut that favours points accumulation lead a shopper to do?
Which option stays within what the extract says, and does not add a judgement about the shopper or the rival?
questions.onCorrect: A price stated in points is hard to compare with a shelf price, so shoppers may follow the points instead of the best value.

acceptedIdeas: Points can lead shoppers to favour collecting them, even when other products or shops give better value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Points can lead shoppers to favour collecting them, even when other products or shops give better value

choices.label: She is acting irrationally, and the ACCC finds that shoppers cannot be trusted with loyalty programs
The rival's lower prices must be a trick, since a lower shelf price on usual items cannot be a real saving
Points can lead shoppers to favour collecting them, even when other products or shops give better value
Points cannot change what she buys, since shoppers always work out the value of each offer exactly

misconceptions.feedback: The extract says shoppers may lack the time or ability to do the calculations. It does not call them irrational or untrustworthy.
The extract says the shopper may be unaware of better value elsewhere. It gives no reason to doubt a lower price.
The extract says the opposite: shoppers may lack the time or the skill to do the sums, and may rely on shortcuts.

extracts.text: Even if members are aware (or broadly aware) of these conversion rates, they may not have the time or ability to make the related calculations when making purchasing decisions, and may instead rely on mental shortcuts to favour points accumulation if unsure. In many cases, a consumer may not be aware that they could obtain better value for money by purchasing a different product, shopping elsewhere or waiting until an item is on promotion.
extracts.who: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, Supermarkets inquiry final report (CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A final report of a public inquiry, written for government and the public

questions.prompt: Eight invented firms each choose a pricing approach. Which approach is each one using?
hints: Ask first whether any buyers pay nothing. Then ask whether the price changes over time or between kinds of buyer.
Low then wide reach points one way. High first and lower later points another. Different prices at one time for different buyers points a third.
questions.onCorrect: Each approach answers a different case: low to reach many fast, high to take early willingness to pay, free with paid extras, or different prices for different segments.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Penetration: the delivery start-up and the streaming service. Skimming: the headset and the fashion label. Freemium: the video-editing tool and the language app. Price discrimination: the theatre and the software licence.

items.label: A delivery start-up opens at a very low price to reach many suburbs fast and put off copycats
items.explanation: A low launch price aimed at wide reach and at discouraging rivals.

items.label: A streaming service charges almost nothing for six months to win subscribers quickly
items.explanation: The price starts low to reach a wide share of the market fast.

items.label: A firm launches a first-of-its-kind headset at a high price, then cuts it once early buyers have bought
items.explanation: Eager buyers pay first, and the price then falls to the next layer of demand.

items.label: A fashion label prices a new collection high for enthusiasts and marks it down later in the season
items.explanation: It takes the highest willingness to pay first and lowers the price afterwards.

items.label: A video-editing tool gives a basic editor away and charges for extra export formats
items.explanation: A free basic product, with money charged for features that extend it.

items.label: A language app offers free lessons and charges for advanced courses, and a free learner costs it almost nothing
items.explanation: A free basic product that is cheap to serve, with a paid tier above it.

items.label: A theatre charges more for the same seat on a Saturday night and less for students
items.explanation: The same seat is sold at different prices to different segments.

items.label: A software firm charges companies more than schools for the same licence
items.explanation: Similar goods at different prices to different kinds of buyer.

questions.prompt: Garnet Advisory (invented) sets its fees at its costs plus 20%. Clients tell it that they would gladly pay far more, because its advice saves them large sums. What is the likeliest cost of Garnet's approach?
hints: Clients say they would pay far more. What does Garnet's method of setting a price take into account, and what does it leave out?
Cost sets a floor and value a ceiling. Which of the two is Garnet pricing from?
questions.onCorrect: A cost-based price starts from the firm's spending, so it can fall well short of what customers would pay for the value.

acceptedIdeas: It leaves money on the table, since its prices follow its costs and not what clients value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It leaves money on the table, since its prices follow its costs and not what clients value

choices.label: It overcharges clients, since a price built on cost is always above what customers would pay
It makes no difference, since cost-based and value-based prices work out the same
It will lose its clients, since a price based on cost cannot be competitive with rivals
It leaves money on the table, since its prices follow its costs and not what clients value

misconceptions.feedback: A cost-based price can sit well below what customers would pay, as clients say here. It is not always above it.
They are built from different starting points. A cost-based price follows the firm's spending, and a value-based price follows the buyer's willingness to pay.
Nothing here suggests clients will leave. They say they would pay more, so the risk is under-pricing.

questions.prompt: Redgum Coaches (invented) finds that over six years its restricted fares rose far faster in real terms than its cheapest fares. What does this pattern suggest, and what does it leave unsaid?
hints: The data are prices over time for two fare classes. Do they say anything about the reasons for the difference?
A careful reader keeps the pattern apart from the explanation. Which option does that?
questions.onCorrect: A price pattern shows what happened to prices, and the reason behind it needs further evidence.

acceptedIdeas: That segments are priced differently, though the pattern does not show why fares moved
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That segments are priced differently, though the pattern does not show why fares moved

choices.label: That segments are priced differently, though the pattern does not show why fares moved
That competitors forced the cheapest fares down, which the pattern itself proves
That Redgum broke the law, since charging different fares for similar seats is always illegal
That costs rose faster for restricted seats, which the fare figures show directly

misconceptions.feedback: The pattern shows how fares moved, and says nothing about why. A competitor's pressure is one explanation among several.
Different fares for similar seats are a common pricing strategy. The pattern gives no ground for calling it unlawful.
The fares show prices and not costs. A cost explanation is possible, but these figures do not establish it.

questions.prompt: Masters closed with losses of more than $3.2 billion, and some people read that as proof that hardware was a poor industry for Woolworths to enter. Does the failure prove that?
hints: Think of a restaurant that closes in a street where its neighbours do well. Does its closing show that the street is a bad place for restaurants?
A failed entry has several possible causes. Name two that have nothing to do with how profitable the industry is.
questions.onCorrect: A failed entry can come from the industry, the cost of getting in or the entrant's own fit, and the failure alone does not say which.

acceptedIdeas: No, an entry can fail for reasons of the entrant or the entry cost, as well as the industry
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, an entry can fail for reasons of the entrant or the entry cost, as well as the industry

choices.label: Yes, since a business that loses billions for seven years must be unprofitable for everyone in it
No, an entry can fail for reasons of the entrant or the entry cost, as well as the industry
Yes, since Bunnings' lead proves that hardware has no room for a second large chain
No, since the failure of one entrant can never tell us anything about its industry or its firm

misconceptions.feedback: Another firm in the same industry can earn a profit while a new entrant loses money. A loss shows that this entry failed, and not that no firm could succeed.
A strong leader makes entry harder, and it does not prove entry cannot work. The failure may owe more to how the entrant went about it.
A failure does tell us something, but it takes more evidence to know what. The industry, the cost of entry and the entrant's own fit can each be a cause.

questions.prompt: The extract gives a key reason for Masters' failure. Which of the three tests does it bear on most directly, and how?
hints: Ask what the schedules say about how well the new business was fitted to its customers, and which test asks that.
Which test is about the advantage a unit and its parent give each other?
questions.onCorrect: A unit that is poorly fitted to its market gains nothing from its parent, which is what the better-off test looks for.

acceptedIdeas: Better off: schedules that did not fit Australian seasons meant the new unit gained no advantage
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Better off: schedules that did not fit Australian seasons meant the new unit gained no advantage

choices.label: Attractiveness: the schedules show that hardware was an unprofitable industry for every firm in it
Cost of entry: the schedules added to what Woolworths had to spend to get into hardware
None of them, since a scheduling error is a matter of operations and the tests apply only to strategy
Better off: schedules that did not fit Australian seasons meant the new unit gained no advantage

misconceptions.feedback: Schedules set to the wrong seasons are a fault in how this business was run. They say nothing about whether other firms in the industry could earn a profit.
Cost of entry is about what it takes to get in and whether it can be earned back. The schedules bear on whether the new unit had an edge once it was in.
The better-off test asks whether the new unit and the firm gain from each other. A business badly fitted to its market shows that they did not.

extracts.text: A key reason for the failure was the lack of product localisation to the Australian market from company leadership, with product schedules based upon the United States Northern Hemisphere seasons, which do not align with Australia's opposite Southern Hemisphere seasons.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Masters Home Improvement" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.prompt: Bellbird Grocers (invented), a supermarket chain, is weighing an online delivery arm that would use its stores and suppliers against buying a group of hotels. Both industries are profitable and both prices could be earned back. Which move is likelier to pass the better-off test?
hints: What would the delivery arm share with the grocery business, and what would the hotels share with it?
The research Morris and Tripathi cite compares related and unrelated moves. Which is each of these?
questions.onCorrect: A related move has something to leverage, so a unit and its parent are likelier to gain from each other.

acceptedIdeas: The delivery arm, since it shares customers, suppliers and logistics with the grocery arm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The delivery arm, since it shares customers, suppliers and logistics with the grocery arm

choices.label: The delivery arm, since it shares customers, suppliers and logistics with the grocery arm
The hotels, because a much larger and quite different market gives more room to spread its risk
Both equally, because any diversification of a firm spreads risk and so passes the test
Neither, because the better-off test can be applied only after the move has been made

misconceptions.feedback: Spreading risk is not the test. The question is whether the new unit and the firm each gain an advantage from the other, which a very different business is less likely to give.
The better-off test asks for an advantage in each direction. Spreading risk is something an investor can do alone.
The tests are applied before a move, to decide whether to make it. That is what makes them useful.

questions.prompt: Wesfarmers' chair offers this as a reason for owning a diversified portfolio. A sceptical investor says a conglomerate should trade at a discount, because investors can already spread risk by holding several shares. Does the chair's remark, by itself, answer the investor?
hints: What can an investor who holds shares in several separate companies do that the chair's remark describes?
A group is worth more together only if it adds something. What would that be?
questions.onCorrect: Smoothing results is something investors can do alone, so a group must add value in another way to avoid a discount.

acceptedIdeas: No, since investors can spread risk alone, so a group must add something more than smoothing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since investors can spread risk alone, so a group must add something more than smoothing

choices.label: Yes, since spreading risk across businesses is something that investors cannot do for themselves
Yes, since a group's results are always worth more together than the sum of its separate parts
No, since investors can spread risk alone, so a group must add something more than smoothing
No, since weak results in one business show that diversified groups are badly run

misconceptions.feedback: Investors can spread risk by holding shares in several companies. A group has to offer something they cannot do alone.
The conglomerate discount is the observation that a whole is often worth less than its parts, so the claim is not a safe one.
The remark says weakness in one business may be offset by strength in another. It does not say the group is badly run.

extracts.text: Once again, the Group’s results illustrate the value of having a diversified portfolio, where weakness in one business may be compensated by strong performances in other businesses.
extracts.who: Wesfarmers Limited, 2026 Annual Report, Chairman's message
extracts.kind: A company's annual report, written for its shareholders

questions.prompt: The chair offers this as an example of how the Group has changed over time. What does it show?
hints: A share of profit falls when the business shrinks, and also when the rest of the group grows. Which does the extract settle?
Compare the group at listing with the group now. What has happened to its mix?
questions.onCorrect: A portfolio's mix changes as businesses are bought, sold and outgrown, so a share at one date is only a snapshot.

acceptedIdeas: The group's mix has been renewed over time, so its past shares do not describe its present
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The group's mix has been renewed over time, so its past shares do not describe its present

choices.label: That fertiliser was a failed business which the group had to shrink and then give up
The group's mix has been renewed over time, so its past shares do not describe its present
That Wesfarmers itself has shrunk, since a business that earned 55% of profit now earns almost none
That the group is a conglomerate in name only, since a real conglomerate never changes its businesses

misconceptions.feedback: The chair gives no reason for the change. A business can shrink in importance because the others grew, as well as because it failed.
The same report gives revenue of $47.3 billion and a profit after tax of $2.9 billion for 2026. The share fell as the group grew in other businesses.
Changing the mix is part of how a group manages its portfolio. The chair says the group's makeup has changed regularly.

extracts.text: As an example, our fertiliser business contributed around 55 per cent of the Group’s profit at the time of listing. The same business now contributes about one per cent of profits.
extracts.who: Wesfarmers Limited, 2026 Annual Report, Chairman's message
extracts.kind: A company's annual report, written for its shareholders

questions.prompt: Sturt Holdings (invented) bought a vineyard in 2012 and sold it in 2021. Its annual report gives no reason for the sale. A commentator says the group sold it because the vineyard failed. What can be said?
hints: The report says what the group did and not why. What does that allow you to say, and what does it not?
List two reasons other than failure why a group might sell a business.
questions.onCorrect: A portfolio record shows what a group did. Why it did it needs the group's own account or other evidence.

acceptedIdeas: That it bought and sold the vineyard, and any reason needs a source, as failure is one cause
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That it bought and sold the vineyard, and any reason needs a source, as failure is one cause

choices.label: That the vineyard must have failed, since any business that is sold has always failed
That the purchase was a mistake, since a group's portfolio is meant to stay as it was bought
That the group ran short of cash, since groups sell businesses only when they need to raise money
That it bought and sold the vineyard, and any reason needs a source, as failure is one cause

misconceptions.feedback: Groups sell businesses for many reasons, including a better use of the capital or a change in the group's focus. A sale does not show failure.
A group that renews its portfolio will buy and sell over time. A sale on its own does not show that the purchase was wrong.
Raising money is one reason among several, and the report gives none. The claim needs evidence that the facts do not supply.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain (invented) weighs eight growth moves. Which of the four directions is each one?
hints: For each move, ask whether the product is one the chain already sells and whether the customers are ones it already serves.
Both new points to the same direction. Only one new points to one of the two middle directions.
questions.onCorrect: The direction depends on whether the product, the market or both are new, and diversification is the one where both are.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Penetration: more shops in its cities and the offer to current customers. Market development: the new state and the restaurants. Product development: coffee and cooking classes. Diversification: the hotels and the frozen meals for hospitals.

items.label: Opens more shops in the cities where it already trades
items.explanation: The same product to the same customers.

items.label: Runs an offer to get current customers to buy more bread each week
items.explanation: More of the same product to the same market.

items.label: Takes its shops, unchanged, into a state it has never served
items.explanation: The same product in a new market.

items.label: Starts selling its existing bread range to restaurants, a group it has not served
items.explanation: The same product to new customers.

items.label: Adds a coffee range for its current customers
items.explanation: A new product for the existing market.

items.label: Launches cooking classes for customers who already shop with it
items.explanation: A new offering for the market it already has.

items.label: Buys a chain of hotels
items.explanation: A new product in a new market.

items.label: Starts a frozen-meals business that sells to hospitals
items.explanation: Both the product and the market are new.

questions.prompt: Corella Dairy Co-operative (invented) is offered a chain of gyms. The gym industry is profitable, and the price is one the co-operative could earn back. Gyms share no customers, suppliers or skills with dairy. What do the three tests say?
hints: Take the tests one at a time. Which facts in the case bear on each?
What would the gyms gain from the dairy business, and what would dairy gain from the gyms?
questions.onCorrect: A move can pass the industry and price tests and still fail the better-off test when the businesses share nothing.

acceptedIdeas: It passes the first two and probably fails the third, since neither side would gain an advantage
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It passes the first two and probably fails the third, since neither side would gain an advantage

choices.label: It passes all three, since a profitable industry at a price that can be earned back is all the tests ask
It fails the first, since an industry with no link to the firm cannot be attractive to it
It passes the first two and probably fails the third, since neither side would gain an advantage
The tests cannot be applied, since a co-operative is not a firm that can diversify

misconceptions.feedback: The third test asks whether the unit and the firm each gain from the other. A business that shares nothing with the parent is unlikely to.
Attractiveness is about the industry's profit potential, and here it is profitable. The weakness is in the fit, which is the third test.
A co-operative that buys another business is diversifying, and the three tests apply to any group considering a move.

questions.prompt: A diversified retailer that runs hardware stores and a logistics arm (both invented) is choosing among three proposals. The extract is one of three avenues for new capital that Wesfarmers names. Which proposal fits it?
hints: The extract asks for two things: a business next to the existing ones, and a use for what the group already has. Which proposal has both?
What would the retailer's own stores and trucks help it do?
questions.onCorrect: An adjacent opportunity is one the group can serve by leveraging assets and capabilities it already has.

acceptedIdeas: Using its logistics arm and stores to start a trade-supplies delivery service for builders
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Using its logistics arm and stores to start a trade-supplies delivery service for builders

choices.label: Using its logistics arm and stores to start a trade-supplies delivery service for builders
Buying a mining company in another country because its shares look cheap this year
Spreading its capital evenly across every industry listed on the exchange, to cut its risk
Closing its hardware stores and putting all the proceeds into a bank deposit

misconceptions.feedback: A share that looks cheap says nothing about whether the retailer has assets and capabilities to apply to mining.
That is diversification for its own sake, with no link to what the retailer already has.
That is leaving the business, and it does not use existing assets and capabilities to grow a new one.

extracts.text: in adjacent opportunities where we can leverage existing assets and capabilities to develop new sources of long-term growth
extracts.who: Wesfarmers Limited, 2026 Annual Report
extracts.kind: A company's annual report, written for its shareholders

questions.prompt: An IGA store owner buys about three-quarters of its stock through Metcash and sources much of its fresh produce elsewhere. What best explains the pattern?
hints: For which goods does the owner have many easy alternatives to the wholesaler, and for which few?
A wholesaler is worth using where it does something the owner cannot easily do. Which goods fit that?
questions.onCorrect: A firm buys from a specialist where the specialist's scale and range matter, and looks elsewhere where alternatives are many.

acceptedIdeas: A wholesaler's scale and range pay off across most lines, while fresh produce has many other sources
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A wholesaler's scale and range pay off across most lines, while fresh produce has many other sources

choices.label: The owner grows its own fresh produce and contracts out the rest, since it owns the stores that sell both
The owner buys everything from Metcash that it can, and goes elsewhere only when Metcash runs out
A wholesaler's scale and range pay off across most lines, while fresh produce has many other sources
Packaged goods are cheaper to produce than fresh produce, so a wholesaler can always undercut a stall

misconceptions.feedback: The case is about buying. The owner buys fresh produce from other sources, and does not make it.
That describes a habit and gives no reason for it. The pattern follows where Metcash's scale and range matter and where other sources are easy.
Nothing in the case says so. The point is about how many other sources there are, and fresh produce has many.

questions.prompt: Curlew Foods, a group of six independent supermarkets, and Ironbark Foods, one of the largest independent groups (both invented), are each thinking of building a distribution centre to supply themselves. What does the Drakes case suggest?
hints: Drakes was one of the largest independent groups. What did that give it?
A distribution centre has to be paid for. What decides whether a group has enough business to cover the cost?
questions.onCorrect: Making an activity yourself needs enough volume to justify the capital, so the largest independents are the likeliest to manage it.

acceptedIdeas: Ironbark is likelier to justify one, since the capital cost must be spread over enough volume
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ironbark is likelier to justify one, since the capital cost must be spread over enough volume

choices.label: Both are equally able to, since any retailer can supply itself if it is determined enough
Ironbark is likelier to justify one, since the capital cost must be spread over enough volume
Curlew is likelier to, since a smaller group would save more per store by avoiding a wholesaler
Neither can, since the ACCC found that no independent group could replicate Drakes' move

misconceptions.feedback: Drakes' move rested on volume as well as determination. A centre has to be used enough to justify what it costs.
A small group has less volume over which to spread the cost of a centre. The ACCC says the capital had to be justified by scale.
The ACCC said there were likely few that could, and it did not say none. Scale decides which.

questions.prompt: The extract reports a survey of firms that had outsourced tasks. What does it suggest for a firm weighing an outsourcing decision?
hints: Read what the quarter is a quarter of. What did those firms do?
Which option stays within what a survey of reversals can show?
questions.onCorrect: Outsourcing can be reversed, so a decision should weigh control and fit as well as the price quoted.

acceptedIdeas: That outsourcing can fail to work out as planned, so the decision should weigh more than price
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That outsourcing can fail to work out as planned, so the decision should weigh more than price

choices.label: That outsourcing never saves money, since a quarter of the firms that tried it later went back
That reversing a decision shows that the original plan was sound and was simply completed
That a quarter of any firm's activities should be outsourced, since that share worked best
That outsourcing can fail to work out as planned, so the decision should weigh more than price

misconceptions.feedback: A quarter reversing leaves three quarters that did not. The survey does not say that outsourcing never saves money.
A firm that reverses its strategy has changed course. That does not show the first plan succeeded.
The extract gives the share of firms that reversed. It says nothing about how much of a firm should be outsourced.

extracts.text: According to a 2005 Deloitte Consulting survey, a quarter of the companies which had outsourced tasks reversed their strategy.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Outsourcing" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.prompt: Nettle Studio (invented) spends a year training its staff in a client's own unusual software, which no other client uses, and works for that client on a two-year contract. What risk does the studio face when the contract comes up for renewal?
hints: Whose investment can be used for nobody else? Who is then in the weaker position when the contract ends?
What would the studio do with its training if it lost this client?
questions.onCorrect: A specialised investment ties its owner to one customer, who can then press the price down.

acceptedIdeas: The client can press the fee down, because the studio's training cannot be sold to anyone else
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The client can press the fee down, because the studio's training cannot be sold to anyone else

choices.label: The client can press the fee down, because the studio's training cannot be sold to anyone else
The client can cancel at once without cost, since a customer is always free to leave a supplier
The studio can charge what it likes, since the client now depends on its trained staff
There is no risk, since a signed contract settles the terms for good

misconceptions.feedback: That is true of any customer. The particular risk is that the studio has sunk a year into skills that serve only this client.
The party that made the specialised investment is the exposed one. The studio cannot take its training to another client.
A contract covers the period it names. At renewal the bargaining starts again, and the studio with the specialised training is weaker.

questions.prompt: Karri Grain Co-operative (invented) sells nearly all its wheat to one big flour miller. It builds a small mill of its own that could handle a tenth of its crop, and runs it only occasionally. The miller's price offers to the co-operative then improve. What does the case show?
hints: The co-operative still sells most of its wheat to the miller. What changed for the miller anyway?
How did Drakes' move in South Australia affect Metcash's position, according to the ACCC?
questions.onCorrect: A buyer's real option to supply itself can constrain its supplier's pricing even when it is used on only a small part of its needs.

acceptedIdeas: The option to mill its own wheat can limit the miller's pricing, though most wheat still goes to it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The option to mill its own wheat can limit the miller's pricing, though most wheat still goes to it

choices.label: Nothing, since the co-operative still sells nearly all its wheat to the miller and so has no leverage
The option to mill its own wheat can limit the miller's pricing, though most wheat still goes to it
The miller must have lost the co-operative's trade, since a bypass works only if the customer leaves
The co-operative has integrated forward, so its costs will be lower than the miller's at any volume

misconceptions.feedback: A customer that can credibly supply itself has leverage even when it uses the option little. The ACCC says this of Drakes.
The bypass works as a threat. The miller does not need to lose the trade for its pricing to be constrained.
A small mill used occasionally says nothing about costs at any volume. The point is the option it gives.

questions.prompt: These eight situations are invented. Does each favour doing the activity yourself or contracting it out?
hints: Ask of each situation whether it describes a gain from owning the activity or a cost of owning it.
A cost of owning an activity is a reason to contract it out, and a cost of contracting is a reason to own it.
questions.onCorrect: Owning an activity gains margin, independence and control, and costs capital, skills, motivation and flexibility.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Doing it yourself: keeping the supplier's margin, securing a rare input and keeping control of the process. Contracting out: the peripheral task, the missing skill, the guaranteed sales, the talent and the cost of switching away.

items.label: A chain pays a supplier a margin on every carton and wants to keep that margin
items.explanation: Owning the link captures the margin that would otherwise go to the supplier.

items.label: A firm needs a rare input whose price swings sharply from year to year
items.explanation: Owning the supply gives independence when an input is rare or volatile in price.

items.label: The client wants a say over how the work is done, and another firm would own the process
items.explanation: Outsourcing usually leaves the client with little or no control over the process.

items.label: The task is peripheral to the firm and a specialist can do it for much less
items.explanation: Reducing the cost of non-core activity is a common reason to outsource.

items.label: The firm needs a skill it lacks, and building it would distract from its main business
items.explanation: Developing new competencies can compromise a firm's existing ones.

items.label: An in-house supplier's sales are guaranteed, so poor quality can go unnoticed
items.explanation: Guaranteed sales weaken the supplier's motivation, which is a cost of integrating.

items.label: The firm needs talent that it cannot hire for itself
items.explanation: Access to the world's top talent is a reason firms give for outsourcing.

items.label: Switching away from an owned supplier later would be costly
items.explanation: Higher costs of switching are a cost of integrating, which favours contracting.

questions.prompt: Sandpiper Hotels (invented) buys its own laundry and guarantees it all the group's sheets. A few years later the laundry's quality has slipped and nobody in the group complains. Which risk of integration is this?
hints: What pushes an outside supplier to keep its quality up, and is that pressure there for the group's own laundry?
Which risk is about sales that are guaranteed?
questions.onCorrect: An in-house supplier with guaranteed sales has less reason to keep up quality, and the group may not notice.

acceptedIdeas: Weaker motivation to perform, as sales are guaranteed and poor quality passes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Weaker motivation to perform, as sales are guaranteed and poor quality passes

choices.label: Hold-up, since the laundry's equipment can serve no other customer than the group itself
Credible bypass, since the group could always send its sheets to some other laundry
A loss of scale, since a single laundry is always too small to serve a whole hotel group
Weaker motivation to perform, as sales are guaranteed and poor quality passes

misconceptions.feedback: Hold-up is about a specialised investment being bargained down. Here the issue is a supplier that is sure of its sales.
A credible bypass limits a supplier's pricing. This laundry has no pressure on it because it is guaranteed the group's business.
Nothing in the case concerns scale. The fault is slipping quality that nobody is pressed to fix.

questions.prompt: Metcash was asked by the ACCC how likely it is that an IGA retailer would go direct to a supplier. How should a reader weigh its answer?
hints: Who is speaking, and what does that firm gain if independent stores keep buying through it?
A statement from an interested party is a claim. What would you set it beside to test it?
questions.onCorrect: A statement from a firm with a stake in the answer is evidence to be tested against independent evidence.

acceptedIdeas: As the account of a firm with a stake in it, so it is better read beside other evidence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As the account of a firm with a stake in it, so it is better read beside other evidence

choices.label: As settled fact, since a wholesaler knows its own market better than anyone else
As worthless, since a firm answering questions about its own business can never be reliable
As the account of a firm with a stake in it, so it is better read beside other evidence
As proof that every independent store would lose by going direct, whatever its size

misconceptions.feedback: Metcash knows its market well, and it also gains if independents stay with it. A statement from an interested party is a claim to test.
An interested party's account can be accurate. It needs checking against other evidence, and it cannot simply be set aside.
The statement is about many cases and not all. It does not say what a very large group could do, as Drakes did.

extracts.text: In many cases, it’s highly unlikely because for all the reasons that we’ve explained in terms of efficiency and the scale benefit that Metcash brings between the supplier and between often a small independent retailer.
extracts.who: Metcash at an ACCC public hearing, quoted in the Supermarkets inquiry final report (CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.when: quoted in the report of February 2025
extracts.kind: Evidence given by the wholesaler, a party with an interest in the question

questions.prompt: A commentator says Kodak failed because it refused to invest in digital cameras. Which statement do the facts above best support?
hints: Look at what Kodak built and sold before the bankruptcy.
Ask which explanation the facts rule out, and which they leave open.
questions.onCorrect: Kodak did invest in digital, so a refusal can't be the explanation. The trouble lay in what the change did to its existing business, and the lesson comes back to it.

acceptedIdeas: Kodak built digital cameras and led US sales of them, so its failure needs an explanation other than a refusal to invest
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Kodak built digital cameras and led US sales of them, so its failure needs an explanation other than a refusal to invest

choices.label: Kodak built digital cameras and led US sales of them, so its failure needs an explanation other than a refusal to invest
The commentator is right, since a firm that goes bankrupt after building a prototype cannot have taken the technology seriously
Kodak's digital cameras must have been poor products, since a firm with good ones does not file for bankruptcy protection
Kodak was unlucky, since nothing about a firm's own position can explain why newcomers beat it

misconceptions.feedback: The article reports that Kodak was actively involved in developing and producing digital cameras. A prototype followed by a bankruptcy doesn't show a refusal to invest.
The facts say nothing about the cameras' quality. They say Kodak led US sales in 2005, and a firm can lead in sales and still lose its profits.
A firm's position can explain a great deal, as this lesson shows. The facts above rule out one explanation and leave others open.

questions.prompt: A maker of sailing yachts, invented for this question, launches a boat with a new hull that sails far faster than any rival's. It costs more than the leading boats and is sold to the same owners who buy the leader's flagship yachts. Engineers call the design revolutionary. In the lesson's terms, what is it?
hints: Ask who the first customers are before you ask how clever the hull is.
The leader's flagship owners are the leader's best customers. Which kind of innovation starts there?
questions.onCorrect: The boat is sold to the leader's own best customers, which is the sustaining pattern however revolutionary the engineering is.

acceptedIdeas: Sustaining, because it improves what the leader's best customers already buy, however revolutionary the design
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sustaining, because it improves what the leader's best customers already buy, however revolutionary the design

choices.label: Disruptive, because a design this much better is bound to displace the leader's boats in the end, whoever buys it
New-market disruption, because no boat in the market was ever this fast before, so it opens a new market
Sustaining, because it improves what the leader's best customers already buy, however revolutionary the design
Neither, because only a product sold to people who weren't buying anything before counts as an innovation at all

misconceptions.feedback: How good the engineering is doesn't settle the matter. The first automobiles were revolutionary and did not disrupt horse-drawn transport, because disruption depends on where a product enters and what happens next.
A new-market entrant serves customers the leader doesn't serve at all. These buyers already buy the leader's flagship.
Sustaining innovations are innovations too. The word describes a product that improves what current customers already buy.

questions.prompt: In the market for robot pool cleaners, invented for this question, a leader earns most from owners of large pools who buy its top model. Six moves appear. Which kind of innovation is each?
hints: Ask who the first customers are: the leader's best buyers, the buyers it earns least from, or people who weren't buying at all.
A low-end entrant takes customers who are content with less. A new-market entrant takes people who weren't customers.
questions.onCorrect: In each case the answer depends on the entrant's first customers. The leader's best buyers point to sustaining, its least profitable buyers to low-end, and people who weren't buying to new-market.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sustaining: the longer-lasting battery and the sharper navigation. Low-end: the plain cheap robot and the stripped-down robot for budget buyers. New-market: the pocket-sized robot for inflatable pools and the robot for aquarium tanks.

items.label: The leader adds a longer-lasting battery to its top model, for owners who already buy it
items.explanation: It improves what the leader's best customers already buy.

items.label: A newcomer sells a plain robot at a much lower price, which cleans small pools well enough for owners who find the leader's models more than they need
items.explanation: It does less than the leader's models, but enough for customers who don't value the extra.

items.label: A newcomer sells a pocket-sized robot for inflatable backyard pools, whose owners have never bought a cleaning robot
items.explanation: Its first customers weren't buying anything before.

items.label: A rival maker launches a model with sharper navigation, which large-pool owners will pay extra for
items.explanation: It improves the top end for customers who already pay the most.

items.label: A newcomer sells a stripped-down robot without an app to the leader's budget buyers, who rarely upgrade
items.explanation: It starts with the buyers the leader earns least from.

items.label: A newcomer sells a robot that cleans the glass tanks of aquarium shops, which the leader has never sold to
items.explanation: Its first customers sit outside the leader's market.

questions.prompt: A credit committee at an invented regional bank is shown an app that lets people without bank accounts send and receive money by phone. Each user would bring in very little, the market is tiny today, and the committee has a long list of products its best customers have asked for. It declines to fund the app. Which statement best fits the lesson's account of the decision?
hints: Put yourself on the committee's side of the table. What do its best customers want, and what would the app earn at the start?
The lesson says good firms are usually aware of the innovation. What stops them from pursuing it?
questions.onCorrect: The early market is small and thin in profit, and the resources are wanted for sustaining the customers who pay the bills. That is why a well-run firm can look away.

acceptedIdeas: The committee reasoned soundly, since the app's early profit is small and the money is wanted for improvements its best customers asked for
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The committee reasoned soundly, since the app's early profit is small and the money is wanted for improvements its best customers asked for

choices.label: The committee missed the technology, since a well-run firm usually learns of an innovation only after a rival has launched it and won customers
The committee should have asked its existing customers about the app, since listening to customers is the surest guide to where a new market lies
The committee was wrong to decline, since an app that earns little at the start will go on earning little however much it improves or how long it is given
The committee reasoned soundly, since the app's early profit is small and the money is wanted for improvements its best customers asked for

misconceptions.feedback: Christensen's finding, as Wikipedia reports it, runs the other way: good firms are usually aware of the innovation, but their business environment doesn't let them pursue it when it first appears.

Customers who are well served by a firm's current products rarely ask for a niche product. Wikipedia reports Christensen's view that 'stay close to the customer' can be strategically counterproductive here.
Disruptive products start small and improve, and the theory is about what they become. The committee's difficulty is that today's numbers don't show it.

questions.prompt: A national tyre-fitting chain, invented for this question, is mostly franchised, with independent owners running its garages. The chain launches a website that sells tyres directly and sends a mobile van to fit them at the customer's home. Franchisees object that the website takes sales their garages would have made. Which view best fits the lesson?
hints: Think about who gains and who loses when a customer switches from a garage to the website.
Blockbuster's online service was in the same position. What did its franchisees say?
questions.onCorrect: A response to a new model can compete with part of the firm's own business, and when that part belongs to franchisees the firm has partners to deal with as well as customers.

acceptedIdeas: The objection is a real cost of the move, so the chain needs a plan for its franchisees as well as for its customers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The objection is a real cost of the move, so the chain needs a plan for its franchisees as well as for its customers

choices.label: The chain should drop the website, since a response that upsets part of the existing business cannot be the right one
The chain can ignore the objection, since a customer who buys on the website was never a franchisee's customer
The objection is a real cost of the move, so the chain needs a plan for its franchisees as well as for its customers
The objection shows that the website is failing, since franchisees know the market better than the chain does

misconceptions.feedback: Blockbuster's online service also upset franchisees, and Wikipedia reports that Total Access grew past three million customers. A response can be sound and still carry a cost.
A garage loses sales when a customer buys elsewhere, whichever route they take. That is the kind of claim a franchise operator brought against Blockbuster.
An objection from the people the move affects shows it has a cost to them. It says nothing yet about whether the website will win customers.

questions.prompt: A software company's annual filing describes the plan for one of its own products, as in the passage. The same filing warns that revenue from the cloud product that replaces it is typically lower in its first year, and that customers who choose not to move would hurt revenue growth and profit. What best describes the choice the company has made?
hints: Look at the dates. What is the company doing to its own product, and who decided the timetable?
The warnings in the filing name two costs. What are they?
questions.onCorrect: The company is ending a profitable product of its own on a timetable it controls. Its filing names the costs: lower first-year revenue from the replacement, and customers who may not move.

extracts.text: In September 2025, we announced plans to end-of-life our Data Center offering via our Atlassian Ascend initiative. As of March 2026, we no longer sell Data Center products to new customers, and we will stop selling term licenses and expansions to existing customers in March 2028.
extracts.who: Atlassian Corporation, Annual Report on Form 10-K for fiscal 2026
extracts.kind: A company's annual report, written for its investors

acceptedIdeas: It chose to retire its own product on a timetable it sets, accepting lower revenue at first and the risk that some customers do not move
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It chose to retire its own product on a timetable it sets, accepting lower revenue at first and the risk that some customers do not move

choices.label: It was forced out of the product by a rival whose cheaper version has already taken most of its customers and left it no choice
It chose to retire its own product on a timetable it sets, accepting lower revenue at first and the risk that some customers do not move
It made a me-too entry, copying a rival's cloud product after the rival had reached its customers, so that it could survive
It split the market, keeping the old product for loyal customers and selling a new one to everyone else, so that both products continue to be sold for years

misconceptions.feedback: The passage doesn't say a rival forced the move, and the filing's own warnings are about customers who may not migrate.
A me-too entry follows a rival after the rival has reached the leader's customers. The filing describes the company ending its own product, with no rival named.
The passage says the product is being ended: no new customers from March 2026, no new term licences or expansions from March 2028 and, with limited exceptions, no support from March 2029.

questions.prompt: This sentence describes Canva, an Australian design platform launched in 2013. Wikipedia adds that it works on a freemium model and had more than 265 million monthly active users by the end of 2025. Which reading fits the lesson best?
hints: Ask who the first customers were. The sentence tells you who the product was designed for.
What would you need to know about those people to choose between low-end and new-market?
questions.onCorrect: The sentence says who the product was designed for and doesn't say what those people used before. A careful reading names the pattern it resembles and what the evidence leaves open.

extracts.text: The platform uses a drag-and-drop interface designed for its users without professional design training or experience.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Canva" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

acceptedIdeas: It fits a disruptive route, and which one depends on whether those users had been buying professional tools, which the sentence doesn't say
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It fits a disruptive route, and which one depends on whether those users had been buying professional tools, which the sentence doesn't say

choices.label: It is sustaining, because it improves design software for the professionals who already buy it and are its main customers
It fits a disruptive route, and which one depends on whether those users had been buying professional tools, which the sentence doesn't say
It is new-market disruption without doubt, since its 265 million monthly users prove that it displaced the leaders of the industry
It cannot be disruptive, since a freemium product earns too little to challenge the leaders of a market with large profits

misconceptions.feedback: The sentence says the interface is designed for people without professional training, so its first customers aren't the professionals who buy the leaders' tools.
A large user count shows success and doesn't show who was displaced. The article doesn't say that any leader lost customers to Canva.
Disruptors often start where margins are thin. Low earnings at the start don't rule the pattern out.

questions.prompt: These two sources both discuss Uber. Taken together, what do they support about the idea that disruption starts at the low end of a market?
hints: Read what Source A says Uber is, and then what Source B says its author learned from Uber.
Source B says the low end is correlated with something. What is it?
questions.onCorrect: A low-end start tends to go with a business model that leaders find unattractive, and that model is what matters. Uber is a case where the start and the pattern come apart.

extracts.text: Uber is not an example of disruption because it did not originate in a low-end or new market footholds.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Disruptive innovation" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

extracts.text: Uber helped me realize that it isn't that being at the bottom of the market is the causal mechanism, but that it's correlated with a business model that is unattractive to its competitor.
extracts.who: Clayton Christensen, in a Forbes interview quoted in the Wikipedia article "Disruptive innovation" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: A magazine interview with the author of the theory, as quoted by an encyclopedia article

acceptedIdeas: A low-end start goes with disruption, and the theory's author doesn't treat it as the cause
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A low-end start goes with disruption, and the theory's author doesn't treat it as the cause

choices.label: A low-end start goes with disruption, and the theory's author doesn't treat it as the cause
Uber began in a city with an established taxi service, which makes it a clear case of low-end disruption
The author has abandoned the theory, since he accepts that a firm can succeed without starting at the bottom
Both sources agree that Uber is a disruptor, since each of them treats it as an example of the theory

misconceptions.feedback: Source A says the opposite: Uber began in a big city that already had taxis, and it started neither at the low end nor in a new market.
Source B qualifies one part of the theory. It doesn't say that the theory is wrong, and it names another feature that matters.
Source A says Uber is not an example of disruption, and Source B uses Uber to refine the theory without saying it is one.

questions.prompt: Six invented firms each face a newcomer that serves customers they have so far ignored. Which answer from the lesson is each one using?
hints: Ask whether the firm keeps the old business running beside the new one, ends the old one itself, or copies the entrant after it has won customers.
Timing separates one of the kinds from the others: the me-too entrant moves after the rival has already reached its customers.
questions.onCorrect: A leader can set up a separate unit, retire its own product on its own timetable, or copy the entrant late. The first two keep the choice of timing with the leader.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A separate unit: the digital-only title and the no-frills hotel brand. Retiring its own product: the tool maker's battery range and the driving school's online course. A late me-too entry: the mining-services copy and the greeting-card retailer's copy.

items.label: A newspaper group launches a cheaper digital-only title with its own editors and its own price, and leaves the printed paper as it is
items.explanation: A second business with its own price sits beside the first.

items.label: A tool maker names a date on which it will stop selling its mains-powered range and moves its customers to its own battery range
items.explanation: The firm ends its own product on its own timetable.

items.label: A mining-services firm waits until a rival's cheaper service has taken most of its mid-sized customers, then launches a copy of that service
items.explanation: It follows after the rival has reached its customers.

items.label: A hotel chain opens a no-frills brand with separate management and lower rates beside its full-service hotels
items.explanation: The new brand is kept apart from the old one.

items.label: A driving-school franchisor announces the end of its classroom-only course and moves its students to its own online course
items.explanation: It replaces its own product before a rival does.

items.label: A greeting-card retailer brings out a pale copy of an online card start-up's service once the start-up has most of its young customers
items.explanation: It enters late and copies, which Wikipedia says can secure survival but not growth.

questions.prompt: The ACCC calls ALDI a hard discounter. It stocks about 1,800 to 2,000 products, against 15,000 to 25,000 at a standard Coles or Woolworths supermarket, mostly under its own brands, and its stores are in larger centres. Its share of national grocery sales rose from 2.8 per cent in 2006-07 to 8.1 per cent in 2022-23. Which statement do these facts support?
hints: A narrower, cheaper offer is how the lesson describes the start of a low-end entry. What else would the pattern need to show?
Look for what the facts leave open: who the first customers were, and whether the entrant has moved up.
questions.onCorrect: The range and price fit a low-end start, and the sources don't say who ALDI's first customers were or whether it has moved towards the chains' most profitable shoppers.

acceptedIdeas: ALDI's offer fits how a low-end entrant begins, though the facts don't say who its first customers were or whether it has moved up
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ALDI's offer fits how a low-end entrant begins, though the facts don't say who its first customers were or whether it has moved up

choices.label: ALDI is a low-end disruptor that is certain to displace the two chains, since its share has risen from 2.8 to 8.1 per cent
ALDI's offer fits how a low-end entrant begins, though the facts don't say who its first customers were or whether it has moved up
ALDI cannot be a low-end entrant, since a share of 8.1 per cent is far too small to count as a threat to the two large chains
ALDI is a sustaining entrant, since it sells groceries and so must be selling them to the same shoppers who use the chains

misconceptions.feedback: Share gains show growth. Whether the pattern ends in displacement is a prediction the ACCC doesn't make, and the chains' own positions would matter too.
A disruptor's share is small at the start, so a modest share doesn't rule the pattern out. The facts leave the question open for other reasons.
Selling groceries doesn't make the shoppers the same. The facts say nothing about which shoppers ALDI served first.

questions.prompt: Qantas and Ansett were already flying when Virgin Blue arrived. Which statement do the facts above best support?
hints: Ask who the established airlines were when Virgin Blue began, and what happened to one of them.
Look for a statement that the facts support and that doesn't claim more than they show.
questions.onCorrect: A later entrant became a major airline once an established rival failed, so being early did not decide the outcome. The lesson asks what being early can give a firm, and what it can't.

acceptedIdeas: An early start does not decide who leads, since a later entrant grew into a major airline after an established rival failed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An early start does not decide who leads, since a later entrant grew into a major airline after an established rival failed

choices.label: Qantas kept its lead because it was established when Virgin Blue arrived, so the first firm in a market always keeps its lead
An early start does not decide who leads, since a later entrant grew into a major airline after an established rival failed
Virgin Blue's rise was pure luck, since nothing that the airline itself did can explain how it grew so quickly
Ansett's failure shows that the first airline in a market is always the one that goes under in the end

misconceptions.feedback: Qantas was established, but the facts don't say its lead came from moving first. They show a later entrant growing into a major airline.
Wikipedia calls the timing fortunate. It doesn't say that Virgin Blue's own choices counted for nothing.
One failure doesn't make a rule. Ansett's collapse opened space for a later entrant, and the facts say nothing about who began first.

questions.prompt: Seven invented firms each moved into a market first, or are said to have. Which source does each firm's edge come from, if any?
hints: For each firm, ask what a later entrant would have to overcome: a cost it can't reach, a resource it can't get, or customers who won't move.
Two of the firms aren't first movers in the lesson's sense. One of them never entered the market, and the other isn't first at all.
questions.onCorrect: A pioneer's edge needs a source: technology leadership, control of resources or buyer switching costs. A firm that is early without one of these has nothing a later entrant must overcome.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Control of resources: the ferry landing sites and the equipment-hire workshop. Technology leadership: the solar charger process and the patented spraying method. Buyer switching costs: the online tax-return records. None of these: the unshipped product and the second gym.

items.label: The first firm to run ferries on an invented river signs the only two usable landing sites
items.explanation: It controls the sites that a later firm would need.

items.label: A first maker of solar chargers invents a process that cuts its cost per unit below what a later maker can reach, and patents it
items.explanation: It holds a cost advantage that a patent protects.

items.label: Customers of the first online tax-return service keep years of records there and don't want to start again elsewhere
items.explanation: Moving would cost its customers time and effort.

items.label: A firm announces a new product months before anyone else, but never ships it
items.explanation: It never occupied the market, so there is no pioneer's position.

items.label: A second gym opens in a town and wins members with lower fees
items.explanation: Its edge doesn't come from moving first.

items.label: The first equipment-hire firm in a remote region buys the only local workshop and the only spare-parts supplier
items.explanation: It holds the supplies that a later firm would need.

items.label: The first firm to sell a drone crop-spraying service patents the method, and no later firm may use it
items.explanation: The patent keeps its method from later entrants.

questions.prompt: A manager at an invented firm says that being first into home-delivered meal kits will give it a lasting edge. Her firm would have no patent, no exclusive suppliers and no way to tie customers in, and customers could change service at no cost. How would you answer her?
hints: Check her plan against the three sources. Which, if any, would her firm have?
Think about who pays to teach customers what meal kits are, and who gets to use what that teaches.
questions.onCorrect: Without technology, resources or switching costs behind it, her lead would be easy to match. Pioneers often carry the cost of educating the market, and a follower can spend less on the same job.

acceptedIdeas: Her lead would have no source, and her firm would carry the cost of teaching the market while a follower used the lesson
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Her lead would have no source, and her firm would carry the cost of teaching the market while a follower used the lesson

choices.label: She is right, since a first-mover advantage comes from being first, and nothing else has to be true about the firm's position
She is wrong, since a follower always wins by learning from the pioneer's mistakes at no cost to itself, so a pioneer never keeps a lead
She is right, since the first customers will always stay out of loyalty to the first brand they met, whatever it costs them to change
Her lead would have no source, and her firm would carry the cost of teaching the market while a follower used the lesson

misconceptions.feedback: The advantage comes from what being first makes possible. Wikipedia names technology leadership, control of resources and switching costs as the sources, and her firm would have none of them.
Wikipedia says studies differ, and followers do bear costs of their own. The point is that her firm's lead would have no source, which doesn't make a follower's win certain.
Loyalty depends on switching costs or on a brand that performs, and her customers could change service at no cost.

questions.prompt: The ACCC wrote this in its June 2023 report about two later entrants to the domestic market. Which reading does it support?
hints: Read the second sentence closely. What does the ACCC say each airline would need to do?
Ask what the passage claims about the future, and what it leaves open.
questions.onCorrect: The ACCC describes an opportunity and a condition. Both airlines would need to expand significantly before they could be more meaningful competitors, and the passage doesn't say whether they would.

extracts.text: The expansion of Rex and the entry of Bonza in recent years have created the opportunity for the industry to enter a more competitive period. However, both would need to expand significantly if they are to become more meaningful competitors to the Qantas Group and Virgin Australia.
extracts.who: ACCC, Airline competition in Australia, final report (CC BY 4.0 AU)
extracts.kind: A report by the competition regulator on the state of an industry
